**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verses 7–9:**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: Suckle him﴾. The meaning of revelation (wahy) and its various senses has already been discussed. Scholars differ regarding this revelation to the mother of Moses. One group said it was a statement in her dream. Qatadah said it was inspiration (ilham). Another group said it came through an angel who appeared to her. Muqatil said Jibril (Gabriel) brought her this message. On this view, it was a revelation of information, not inspiration. All agree that she was not a prophet (nabiyyah). The sending of an angel to her was like the angel's speaking to the leper, the bald man and the blind man in the well-known hadith, which al-Bukhari and Muslim transmitted. We have mentioned this in the surah of Bara'ah [[See vol. 8, p. 188 and following, first or second edition.]], along with other reports of angels speaking to people without their being prophets. She also greeted Imran ibn Husayn, and he was not thereby a prophet. Her name was Ayarkha, and it is said Ayarkhat, as al-Suhayli reported. Al-Tha'labi said the name of the mother of Moses was Lawha [[It is also said her name was Yukhabidh, or Yukhabil, and other things besides.]], daughter of Hand ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub.

﴿Suckle him﴾: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz read أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ with a kasrah on the nun and an alif of connection (wasl), dropping the hamzah of أَرْضِعْ for lightness, then giving the nun a kasrah because of the meeting of two sukun-bearing letters.

Mujahid said the revelation about suckling came before the birth. Others said it came after. As-Suddi said: When the mother of Moses gave birth, she was commanded to suckle him immediately after the birth and to act toward him as the verse states, because the fear came right after the birth. Ibn Jurayj said: She was commanded to suckle him for four months in an orchard, and when she feared that he would cry out, because her milk was not sufficient for him, she did this. The first view is more apparent, though the latter is supported by His words: ﴿If you fear for him﴾, since idha (if/when) refers to future time.

It is narrated that she made a chest for him from papyrus, sealed it with pitch from the inside, placed Moses in it, and threw it into the Nile of Egypt. Its story has already passed in surah Ta-Ha [[See vol. 11, p. 195 and following, first or second edition.]].

Ibn Abbas said: When the Children of Israel multiplied in Egypt, they grew arrogant over the people and committed sins. So God empowered the Copts over them, and they inflicted the worst torment upon them, until God delivered them through Moses.

Wahb said: It has reached me that Pharaoh slaughtered seventy thousand newborns in his search for Moses. It is also said ninety thousand. It is reported that when she drew near to delivery and the pains of labour seized her, one of the midwives appointed over the pregnant women of the Children of Israel, who was a friend of hers, said: "Let your love for me benefit me today." So she attended to her, and when the child fell to the ground, a light between his eyes overwhelmed her, every joint of her body trembled, and his love entered her heart. Then she said: "I have come to you only to kill your child and inform Pharaoh. But I have found in your son a love such as I have never found before. So guard him." When she went out, Pharaoh's agents came. She wrapped him in a cloth and placed him in a blazing oven, not knowing what she was doing, for her mind had been confused. They searched but found nothing, and they left, while she did not know where he was. Then she heard his crying from the oven, for God had made the fire cool and safe for him.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not fear﴾. There are two interpretations. The first: do not fear that he will drown; this was said by Ibn Zayd. The second: do not fear that he will be lost; this was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

(﴿And do not grieve﴾) Here too there are two interpretations. The first: do not grieve over his separation from you; this was said by Ibn Zayd. The second: do not grieve that he will be killed; this was said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

It was said that she placed him in a chest five spans long and five spans wide, put the key with the chest, and cast it into the sea after she had suckled him for four months. Others said three months, and others eight months, as reported by al-Kalbi.

It is also related that when the carpenter finished making the chest, he informed Pharaoh of the matter. Pharaoh sent men with him to seize the child. But God blinded their eyes and confused their hearts, so they could not find the way. Then the carpenter became certain that this was the child Pharaoh feared, and he believed from that time on. He is the Believer of Pharaoh's family. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Ibn Abbas said: When the chest disappeared from her sight, Satan made her regret, and she said to herself: "If he had been slaughtered before me, and I had shrouded him and buried him, that would have been more beloved to me than throwing him into the sea." Then God said: ﴿We will surely return him to you and make him one of the messengers﴾, meaning to the people of Egypt.

Al-Asma'i related: I heard a Bedouin girl reciting and saying:

*I seek forgiveness of God for all my sins,*
*For I kissed a man not lawful to me;*
*Like a gazelle, soft in its gentleness,*
*The night ended and I had not prayed.*

I said: "May God fight you! How eloquent you are!" She said: "Do you consider this eloquence, when there is His word: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: Suckle him...﴾ and so on? For in a single verse He combined two commands, two prohibitions, two reports and two good tidings."

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might be to them an enemy and a grief﴾. Since their picking him up would lead to his becoming an enemy and a grief to them, the lam in لِيَكُونَ is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), also called the lam of becoming (lam al-sayrurah). For they had picked him up so that he might be a comfort to their eyes, but the outcome was that he became an enemy and a grief to them. Thus the present state is described by its eventual outcome, as the poet said:

*And for death the mothers nurse every suckling,*
*And for the ruin of time we build our houses.*

Another said:

*So for death the mothers raise their young,*
*As for the ruin of time, dwellings are built.*

That is, the end of building is ruin, even though at present it is rejoiced in. Iltiqat (picking up) means finding a thing without seeking it or intending it. The Arabs say of what one finds without seeking or intending: iltaqatahu iltiqatan (he picked it up by chance), and laqitu fulanan iltiqatan (I met so-and-so by chance). The rajiz poet said:

*And a watering place I came upon by chance.*

From this comes luqatah (a found item). The explanation of this in legal rulings has already passed in surah Yusuf [[See vol. 9, p. 134 and following, first or second edition.]], sufficiently.

al-A'mash, Yahya, al-Mufaddal, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read وَحُزْنًا with a damma on the ha and sukun on the zay. The rest read both with a fatha. Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading. He said the tafkhim (in the terminology of the reciters, this means the fatha) is in it. Both are dialects, like العَدَمُ and العُدْمُ, السَّقَمُ and السُّقْمُ, and الرَّشَدُ and الرُّشْدُ.

(﴿Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman﴾), and Haman was his minister, from among the Copts.

(﴿and their soldiers were sinners﴾), that is, disobedient, polytheist and sinful.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said: A comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him﴾. It is reported that Asiyah, the wife of Pharaoh, saw the chest floating on the sea. She ordered that it be brought to her and opened. She found in it a small infant, had mercy on him and loved him. So she said to Pharaoh: "A comfort of the eye for me and for you," meaning he is a comfort of the eye for me and for you. Here قُرَّتُ is the predicate of an implied subject (mubtada' mudmar), as al-Kisa'i said. Al-Nahhas said there is another, distant possibility mentioned by Abu Ishaq: it may be in the nominative as the subject, with the predicate being "do not kill him." It is distant because the meaning becomes that he is known to be a comfort of the eye. Its permissibility is that the meaning may be: if he is a comfort of the eye for me and for you, then do not kill him. It was also said that the sentence is complete at her words "and for you." Al-Nahhas said: The evidence for this is that in the reading of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it reads: "And the wife of Pharaoh said: Do not kill him, a comfort of the eye for me and for you." It is also permissible to read it in the accusative, meaning: do not kill a comfort of the eye for me and for you. She said "do not kill him" and did not say "do not kill him" in the jussive form (lā taqtulhu), because she was addressing Pharaoh as tyrants are addressed, and as they speak of themselves. It was also said that she said "do not kill him" because God brought him from another land and he was not of the Children of Israel.

(﴿It may be that he will benefit us﴾), so we obtain good from him, (﴿or we may take him as a son﴾). She could not bear children, so she asked Pharaoh to give Moses to her as a gift, and he gave him to her. When Pharaoh saw the dream and related it to his priests and scholars, as has already been mentioned, they told him: "A boy from the Children of Israel will destroy your kingdom." So he ordered the Children of Israel to slaughter their infant boys. But he saw that this would cut off their offspring, so he began to slaughter in one year and spare in the next. Thus Harun (Aaron) was born in a year of sparing, and Musa (Moses) was born in a year of slaughter.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And they did not perceive﴾. This is the beginning of a new statement from God, the Exalted, meaning: they did not perceive that their destruction would be caused by him. It was also said that it is part of the woman's speech, meaning: the Children of Israel did not know that we had picked him up, and they did not realise except that he was our child.

The interpreters differed about the time when the wife of Pharaoh said "A comfort of the eye for me and for you." One group said it was when she picked up the chest, when she informed Pharaoh of it. When she informed him, it came to his understanding that the child was from the Children of Israel, and that this was intended so that he might escape the slaughter. So he said: "Bring me the slaughterers." His wife said what has been mentioned, and Pharaoh said: "As for me, no." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If Pharaoh had said yes, he would have believed in Musa, and he would have been a comfort of the eye for him." Al-Suddi said: Rather, she raised him until he grew up. Al-Tha'labi said the name of the mother of Moses was Lawha [[It is also said her name was Yukhabidh, or Yukhabil, and other things besides.]], daughter of Hand ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub.

﴿Suckle him﴾: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz read أَنْ أَرْضِعِيهِ with a kasrah on the nun and an alif of connection (wasl), dropping the hamzah of أَرْضِعْ for lightness, then giving the nun a kasrah because of the meeting of two sukun-bearing letters.

As-Suddi said: When the mother of Moses gave birth, she was commanded to suckle him immediately after the birth and to act toward him as the verse states, because the fear came right after the birth. Ibn Jurayj said: She was commanded to suckle him for four months in an orchard, and when she feared that he would cry out, because her milk was not sufficient for him, she did this. Ibn Abbas said: When the Children of Israel multiplied in Egypt, they grew arrogant over the people and committed sins. So God empowered the Copts over them, and they inflicted the worst torment upon them, until God delivered them through Moses.

Wahb said: It has reached me that Pharaoh slaughtered seventy thousand newborns in his search for Moses. It is also said ninety thousand. It is reported that when she drew near to delivery and the pains of labour seized her, one of the midwives appointed over the pregnant women of the Children of Israel, who was a friend of hers, said: "Let your love for me benefit me today." *I seek forgiveness of God for all my sins,*
*For I kissed a man not lawful to me;*
*Like a gazelle, soft in its gentleness,*
*The night ended and I had not prayed.*

(﴿Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman﴾), and Haman was his minister, from among the Copts.

(﴿and their soldiers were sinners﴾), that is, disobedient, polytheist and sinful.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 10–14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became void⁠—﴾ Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Faragha" means empty of remembrance of everything in the world except the remembrance of Musa. Al-Hasan also, along with Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Zayd, said: "Faragha" means void of revelation, since He had revealed to her, when she was commanded to cast him into the sea, "Do not fear and do not grieve," and the promise He had made to her that He would return him to her and make him one of the messengers. Then Satan said to her: "O mother of Musa, you disliked that Pharaoh should kill Musa, so you drowned him yourself!" Then he informed her that her son had fallen into the hand of Pharaoh, and the magnitude of the trial made her forget what had been the covenant of God with her. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Faragha" means free of grief and sorrow, because she knew that he had not drowned. al-Akhfash also said this. Al-'Ala' ibn Ziyad said: "Faragha" means fleeing (nafiran). al-Kisa'i said: forgetful, bewildered (dhahilan). It was also said: distracted (walihan), narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik: it is the loss of reason. The meaning is that when she heard of his falling into Pharaoh's hand, her reason flew away from excess of anguish and dismay. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿and their hearts are a void⁠﴾, meaning hollow, without intellects, as has been explained in Surah Ibrahim [[See vol. 9, p. 377 ff., first or second edition.]]. This is because hearts are the seats of intellects. Do you not see His saying: ﴿so that they have hearts with which they understand⁠﴾? This is supported by the reading of one who read: "fazi'an" (alarmed). al-Nahhas said: the most sound of these opinions is the first, and those who said it are most knowledgeable of the Book of God, the Mighty and Majestic. So if she was void of everything except the remembrance of Musa, then she was void of revelation. So he handed him to her, and when the child smelled his mother's scent, he took her breast. Ibn Zayd said: they suspected her when she said that, so she said, "and they are sincere to the king." It was also said: when she said, "Shall I direct you to a household who will undertake him for you?" and they were extremely eager to find a nurse whose breast he would accept, they said, "Who is she?" She said, "My mother." It was said to her: "Does she have milk?" She said: "Yes! The milk of Harun," and he had been born in a year when children were not being killed. They said, "You have spoken truly, by God." "And they are sincere to him" means they had compassion and sincerity. It is related that it was said to Moses' mother when he had suckled from her: "How did he suckle from you and not from anyone else?" She said: "I am a woman of good scent and good milk; I can hardly be brought a child without his suckling from me." Abu 'Imran al-Jawni said: Pharaoh used to give Moses' mother a dinar every day. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how was it lawful for her to take a wage for nursing her own child? I say: she did not take it as a wage for the suckling, but it was the property of an enemy combatant which she took by way of permissible acquisition.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We returned him to his mother⁠﴾ meaning, We returned him, and God had turned the heart of the enemy toward him and fulfilled His promise to her.

(So that her eye might be cooled) that is, by her child.

(And she might not grieve) that is, at separation from her child.

(And that she might know that God's promise is true) that is, that she might know its occurrence, for she already knew that his return to her would take place.

(But most of them do not know) meaning most of the people of Pharaoh do not know, i.e., they were heedless of the decree and the evil of the destiny. It was said: meaning most people know that God's promise in all that He promised is true.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when he reached his maturity and became perfect, We gave him judgment and knowledge.⁠﴾ The discussion of "ashudd" has already passed in Surah al-An'am [[See vol. 7, p. 134 ff., first or second edition.]]. The saying of Rabi'ah and Malik that it is puberty is the best of what has been said about it, because of His saying: ﴿until, when they reach marriageable age⁠﴾, and that is the beginning of "ashudd," while its end is thirty-four years; this is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri. "And became perfect": Ibn 'Abbas said: he reached forty years. "Hukm" means wisdom before prophethood. It was also said: understanding of the religion, whose explanation has passed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 131, second edition.]] and elsewhere. "Ilm" means understanding, the saying of al-Suddi. It was also said: prophethood. Mujahid said: fiqh. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: that is, knowledge of what is in his religion and the religion of his forefathers. He had nine of the Children of Israel who listened to him, followed him, and gathered around him, and this was before prophethood.

(And thus do We reward the good-doers) meaning, just as We rewarded Moses' mother when she submitted to God's command, cast her child into the sea, and affirmed God's promise, so We returned her child to her with gifts and treasures while she was secure. Then We bestowed upon him intellect, wisdom and prophethood. And thus do We reward every good-doer.

God Almighty said: ﴿And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness among its people﴾. It was said: When Musa (peace be upon him) came to know the truth that he held in his religion, he criticised what the people of Fir'awn were upon, and this became known from him. They threatened him, so he feared them. Thereafter he did not enter the city of Fir'awn except in fear and concealment.

As-Suddi said: At the time of this story, Musa was still in the position of being attached to Fir'awn. He would ride his mounts, until he was called "Musa, son of Fir'awn." One day Fir'awn rode out and travelled to one of the cities of Egypt called Manf. Muqatil said: It was two farsakhs from Egypt. Then Musa learned that Fir'awn had ridden out, so he rode after him and reached that town at the time of al-qaylulah (the midday rest), which is the time of heedlessness. Ibn 'Abbas said, and he also said: It was between al-'Isha' and al-'Atamah.

Ibn Ishaq said: Rather, the city is Egypt itself. At this time Musa had openly opposed Fir'awn and criticised them for worshipping Fir'awn and idols. So he entered the city of Fir'awn one day at a time of heedlessness among its people. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: It was at midday, while the people were sleeping. Ibn Zayd said: Fir'awn had cast Musa off and expelled him from the city, and he had been absent from it for years. He came while the people were heedless, having forgotten his matter and because their time with him was long past, and that day was a day of festivity. Al-Dahhak said: He sought to enter the city at a time when its people were heedless, and he entered it when he knew that this was the case from them. From him came the killing of the man before he was commanded to kill him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness and He forgave him.

It is said in ordinary speech: "I entered the city when its people were heedless" (dakhaltu al-madinata hina ghafala ahluha), and one does not say "'ala hina ghafala ahluha." The preposition "'ala" is used in this verse because heedlessness is the intended focus. This is like when you say: "I came upon heedlessness ('ala ghaflatin)," and if you wish you may say: "I came upon a time of heedlessness ('ala hina ghaflatin)." Likewise is the verse.

﴿And he found therein two men fighting, one of his own party (hadha min shi'atih)﴾. The meaning is: when an observer looked at them, he would say, "This one is of his party," that is, of the Children of Israel.

﴿And this one of his enemy﴾, that is, of the people of Fir'awn.

﴿So the one from his party sought his help﴾, that is, he sought his support and aid. Likewise He said in the verse after it: ﴿So the one who had sought his help the day before was now crying out to him﴾, that is, he was calling for help against another Copt. Musa helped him because supporting the oppressed is a religious duty in all the religions of the nations, and an obligation in all the sacred laws.

Qatadah said: The Copt wanted to press the Israelite into service to carry firewood for Fir'awn's kitchen, but he refused, so he sought help from Musa. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: He was a baker for Fir'awn.

﴿So Musa struck him﴾. Qatadah said: with his staff. Mujahid said: with his palm, meaning he pushed him. Al-wakz, al-lakz, al-lahz and al-lahd have one meaning, which is striking with the hand gathered together in a closed fist, like the closing of the fingers for the number seventy-three. Ibn Mas'ud read: "fa-lakazahu." It was said: al-lakz is on the jaw, and al-wakz is on the heart. Al-Tha'labi related that in the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud the reading is "fa-nakazahu" with the letter nun, and the meaning is the same. Al-Jawhari said, on the authority of Abu 'Ubaydah: al-lakz is striking with a closed fist on the chest. Abu Zayd said: it is on the whole body. Al-lahz is striking with a gathered hand on the chest, like al-lakz, on the authority of Abu 'Ubaydah also. Abu Zayd said: it is with a closed fist on the jawbones (al-lahazim) and the neck, and a man is called "milhaz," with a kasra on the mim.

Al-Asma'i said: nakazahu means he struck him and pushed him. Al-Kisa'i said: nahazahu is like nakazahu and wakazahu, meaning he struck him and pushed him. And "lahadahu lahdan" means he pushed him in humiliation, so he is "malhud," and likewise "lahadahu." Tarafah said, disparaging a man:

*Slow to answer the caller, quick to indecency, a submissive one, pushed about by the hands of men.* [Note: "Another reading: 'an al-jalā'. Dhalūl is the opposite of ṣa'b. Another reading: 'dhalīl.' Ajmā' is the back of the hand when you gather and close your fingers."]

That is, he is pushed away. It is intensified because of its frequency. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "He (meaning the Prophet ﷺ) pushed me with a push that hurt me," recorded by Muslim.

Musa (peace be upon him) did this, and he did not intend to kill him; he only intended to repel him, but his soul was in it, and this is the meaning of: ﴿and he [Musa] gave him his death (fa-qada 'alayhi)﴾. Whatever you finish and bring to its end, you have "qadaytu 'alayhi." Jarir said, with al-Ashja' meaning the brave one among snakes. The first half of the line is: "Did they, when they saw their own bare feet, [do such things?]":

*The snake bit him, and so the brave one finished him off.*

﴿He said: This is of the work of Satan﴾, that is, of his misleading. Al-Hasan said: Killing the disbeliever was not permitted at that time and in that state, because it was a state of restraint from fighting. ﴿Indeed, he is a clear, misleading enemy﴾ is a predicate following a predicate.

﴿He said: My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾, ﴿so He forgave him﴾. Musa (peace be upon him) regretted that striking, in which the soul was lost, and his regret led him to submit to his Lord and to seek forgiveness for his sin. Qatadah said: By Allah, he knew the way out, so he sought forgiveness. Then he (ﷺ) continued to mention this against himself, although he knew he had been forgiven, until in the Hereafter he would say: "Indeed I killed a soul, for which I was not commanded." He counted it against himself as a sin and said, "I have wronged myself, so forgive me," because it is not befitting for a prophet to kill until he is commanded to do so. Also, the prophets are apprehensive about things about which others are not apprehensive.

An-Naqqash said: He did not kill him deliberately, intending to kill; he only struck him one blow, intending by it to repel his oppression. He said: It has also been said that this was before prophethood. Ka'b said: He was then twelve years old. The killing, moreover, was accidental, since a blow or a punch generally does not kill.

Muslim related from Salim ibn 'Abdullah that he said: "O people of Iraq, how much you ask about the minor matter, and how much you embark upon the major matter! I heard my father 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed, strife will come from here,' and he pointed with his hand towards the east, 'from where the horns of Satan rise, and some of you will strike the necks of others.'" And Musa only killed the one he killed from the family of Fir'awn by mistake, so Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress and tested you with a severe trial﴾.

God Almighty said: ﴿He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me﴾, that is, of knowledge, wisdom and monotheism. ﴿I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾, that is, an aid to the disbelievers. Al-Qushayri said: He did not say "by what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness," because this was before the revelation, and he did not know that Allah had forgiven him that killing. Al-Mawardi said: In "by what You have bestowed upon me" there are two possibilities. One of them is: of forgiveness. Likewise al-Mahdawi and al-Tha'labi mentioned it. Al-Mahdawi said: "By what You have bestowed upon me" means of forgiveness, so You did not punish me. The second possibility is: of guidance. I say: "So He forgave him" indicates forgiveness, and Allah knows best.

Al-Zamakhshari said: God's saying, ﴿by what You have bestowed upon me﴾, may be an oath whose answer is omitted; its estimated meaning is: "I swear by Your bestowal upon me of forgiveness that I will not be a supporter of the criminals." It may also be a plea for mercy, as if he said: "My Lord, protect me by the right of what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness, for then I will not be, if You protect me, a supporter of the criminals." By "supporting the criminals" he meant either accompanying Fir'awn and being included among his company and increasing his numbers, since he used to ride with his riding, like a child with a father, and was called "the son of Fir'awn"; or supporting those whose support leads to sin and wrongdoing, like the support of the Israelite which led to the killing that was not permitted for him to carry out. It has also been said: He meant, "Although I erred in this killing for which I was not commanded, I will not abandon the support of the Muslims against the criminals." On this view the Israelite was a believer, and supporting a believer is obligatory in all the sacred laws. It has been said in some reports that this Israelite was a disbeliever, and he was only called "of his party" because he was an Israelite, and he did not intend agreement in religion. On this view, Musa regretted that he had aided a disbeliever against a disbeliever, so he said: "I will not after this be a supporter of the disbelievers."

It has also been said: This is not a statement of fact but a supplication, meaning: "So I will not after this be a supporter; so do not make me, O my Lord, a supporter of the criminals." Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: "O Allah, so I will never again be a supporter of the criminals." He claimed that this statement was also the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Nahhas said: That it be a statement of fact is preferable and more fitting to the context of the speech, as one says: "I will not disobey You, because You have bestowed favour upon me." This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas in reality, not what al-Farra' related, because Ibn 'Abbas said: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested the second day," and making an exception does not occur in supplication. One does not say: "O Allah, forgive me if You will." The most astonishing thing is that al-Farra' related this from Ibn 'Abbas and then related from him a statement contrary to it.

I say: This meaning has already passed in summary and clarification in Surat al-Naml, and that it is a statement of fact, not a supplication. And on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested with it once more," meaning he did not say, "I will not be (a supporter), if Allah wills." This is like His saying: ﴿And do not incline towards those who have wronged﴾.

The second issue: Salamah ibn Nubayt said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim sent to al-Dahhak the tax of the people of Bukhara and said: "Give it to them." He said: "Excuse me," and he kept asking him to excuse him until he excused him. It was said to him: "What is the harm to you in giving it to them, when you will not take anything from them?" He said: "I do not like to help the oppressors in any part of their affair."

'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Walid al-Wassafi said: I said to 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: "I have a brother who works with his pen, calculating what comes in and goes out, and he has dependants, and if he gave this up he would be in need and would fall into debt?" He said: "Who is the head?" I said: "Khalid ibn 'Abdullah al-Qasri." He said: "Do you not read what the righteous servant said: ﴿My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested with it a second time, and Allah aided him. So your brother should not aid them, for Allah will aid him." 'Ata' said: It is not permissible for anyone to aid an oppressor, to write for him, or to accompany him. If he does any of that, he has become a helper of the wrongdoers.

In a hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: 'Where are the oppressors, the likes of the oppressors, and the helpers of the oppressors, even whoever prepared an inkwell for them or sharpened a pen for them?' They will be gathered in an iron coffin and thrown into Hell." It is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever walks with an oppressed person to help him against his injustice, Allah will make his feet firm upon the Sirat on the Day of Resurrection, the Day when feet will slip; and whoever walks with an oppressor to help him in his oppression, Allah will make his feet slip upon the Sirat, the Day when feet will be overturned." In a hadith: "Whoever walks with an oppressor has committed a sin." Walking with an oppressor is only a sin if one walks with him in order to help him, because he has violated the prohibition of Allah, the Exalted, in His saying: ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 15–19 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he woke up in the city, fearful﴾. It has already been mentioned in "Ta-Ha" [[See vol. 11, p. 202, first or second edition.]] and elsewhere that the prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, do feel fear, in refutation of those who say otherwise, and that fear does not contradict knowledge of Allah nor reliance upon Him. It was said: he woke up fearful that the killing of the man would be attributed to him and he would be seized for it. It was also said: fearful of his people, that they would hand him over. And it was said: fearful of Allah, may He be exalted.

(Yataraqqabu, "watching warily") Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he looked about him in fear. It was also said: he awaited pursuit, and he awaited what people were saying. Qatadah said: "yataraqqabu" means he watched out for pursuit. It was also said: he went out seeking news, and no one had known of the killing of the Copt except the Israelite.

"Asbaha" may carry the sense of "sara" (became), meaning that when he killed he became fearful. It may also mean that he entered upon the morning, that is, the morning of the day following his day. "Khaifan" is in the accusative as the predicate of "asbaha", and if you wish it may be a circumstantial accusative (hal), in which case the adverbial phrase serves as the predicate.

(Then behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was crying out to him for help) That is, behold, his companion the Israelite, whom he had rescued the day before, was fighting another Copt whom he wanted to conscript (yusakhkhirahu) for labour. "Istis'rakh" (crying for help) means seeking aid (istighathah). It derives from "surakh" (a shout), because the one seeking aid shouts and raises his voice to ask for succour. A poet said [[He is Salamah ibn Jandal. "Al-tanabib" (plural of "zunbub") is the dry bony edge of the shin. The intended meaning is the speed of response.]]:

"Whenever a fearful crier came to us, / his cry was like the striking of shin-bones."

It was said: this Israelite who sought help was the one whom the cook of Pharaoh had conscripted to carry firewood to the kitchen; al-Qushayri mentioned this. "Alladhi" is in the nominative as the subject, and "yastasrikhuhu" is in the position of the predicate. It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. "Ams" refers to the day before your day; it is built on kasra because of the meeting of two unvoweled letters. When the definite article or an annexation is attached to it, it becomes declinable and is inflected with ḍamma and fatḥa according to most grammarians, though some grammarians hold that it remains indeclinable even with the definite article. Sibawayh and others relate that some Arabs treat "ams" like a diptotic noun in the nominative case only, and that a poet may be compelled to do this also in the genitive and accusative, as the poet said:

"Indeed I have seen a marvel since yesterday"

Here he put "mudh" (since) into the genitive with "ma madha" (what has passed). The better usage is the nominative, so "ams" in the genitive follows its treatment in the nominative in the second dialect.

(Moses said to him: "Indeed you are clearly a misguided one") "Ghawiyy" means one who is lost or frustrated, that is, because you pick a quarrel with one you cannot withstand. It was also said: a clearly misleading one, manifestly in error; "You killed a man because of you yesterday, and today you summon me to another." "Ghawiyy" is an intensive form (fa'il) from "aghwa yughwi," and it has the sense of "mughwin" (one who misleads), like "wajih" and "alim" meaning "mujiʻ" and "mu'lim." It was also said: "ghawiyy" carries the sense of "ghawin" (erring), meaning that you are erring in fighting one whose harm you cannot repel. Al-Hasan said: he only said to the Copt "you are clearly misguided" because of his conscripting this Israelite, and because he intended to strike him. One says "batasha yabtishu" and "yabtushu," and the damma is more analogical because it is an intransitive verb.

(He said: "O Moses, do you intend to kill me") Ibn Jubayr said: Moses intended to strike the Copt, but the Israelite supposed he meant him, because he had spoken harshly to him, so he said: "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" The Copt heard the words and disclosed them. It was also said: the Israelite intended to strike the Copt, and Moses forbade him, so he feared him and said: "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?"

(You want nothing) That is, you do not want anything.

(But to be a tyrant in the land) That is, a compeller (qitalan). ʿIkrimah and al-Shaʿbi said: a person is not a tyrant until he has killed two souls without right.

(Nor do you want to be among the reformers) That is, among those who set things right between people.

God Almighty said: ﴿And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness among its people﴾. It was said: When Musa (peace be upon him) came to know the truth that he held in his religion, he criticised what the people of Fir'awn were upon, and this became known from him. They threatened him, so he feared them. Thereafter he did not enter the city of Fir'awn except in fear and concealment.

As-Suddi said: At the time of this story, Musa was still in the position of being attached to Fir'awn. He would ride his mounts, until he was called "Musa, son of Fir'awn." One day Fir'awn rode out and travelled to one of the cities of Egypt called Manf. Muqatil said: It was two farsakhs from Egypt. Ibn 'Abbas said, and he also said: It was between al-'Isha' and al-'Atamah.

Ibn Ishaq said: Rather, the city is Egypt itself. At this time Musa had openly opposed Fir'awn and criticised them for worshipping Fir'awn and idols. So he entered the city of Fir'awn one day at a time of heedlessness among its people. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: It was at midday, while the people were sleeping. Ibn Zayd said: Fir'awn had cast Musa off and expelled him from the city, and he had been absent from it for years. He came while the people were heedless, having forgotten his matter and because their time with him was long past, and that day was a day of festivity. Al-Dahhak said: He sought to enter the city at a time when its people were heedless, and he entered it when he knew that this was the case from them. From him came the killing of the man before he was commanded to kill him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness and He forgave him.

It is said in ordinary speech: "I entered the city when its people were heedless" (dakhaltu al-madinata hina ghafala ahluha), and one does not say "'ala hina ghafala ahluha." The preposition "'ala" is used in this verse because heedlessness is the intended focus. This is like when you say: "I came upon heedlessness ('ala ghaflatin)," and if you wish you may say: "I came upon a time of heedlessness ('ala hina ghaflatin)." Likewise is the verse.

﴿And he found therein two men fighting, one of his own party (hadha min shi'atih)﴾. The meaning is: when an observer looked at them, he would say, "This one is of his party," that is, of the Children of Israel.

﴿And this one of his enemy﴾, that is, of the people of Fir'awn.

﴿So the one from his party sought his help﴾, that is, he sought his support and aid. Likewise He said in the verse after it: ﴿So the one who had sought his help the day before was now crying out to him﴾, that is, he was calling for help against another Copt. Musa helped him because supporting the oppressed is a religious duty in all the religions of the nations, and an obligation in all the sacred laws.

Qatadah said: The Copt wanted to press the Israelite into service to carry firewood for Fir'awn's kitchen, but he refused, so he sought help from Musa. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: He was a baker for Fir'awn.

﴿So Musa struck him﴾. Qatadah said: with his staff. Mujahid said: with his palm, meaning he pushed him. Al-wakz, al-lakz, al-lahz and al-lahd have one meaning, which is striking with the hand gathered together in a closed fist, like the closing of the fingers for the number seventy-three. Ibn Mas'ud read: "fa-lakazahu." It was said: al-lakz is on the jaw, and al-wakz is on the heart. Al-Tha'labi related that in the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud the reading is "fa-nakazahu" with the letter nun, and the meaning is the same. Al-Jawhari said, on the authority of Abu 'Ubaydah: al-lakz is striking with a closed fist on the chest. Abu Zayd said: it is on the whole body. Al-lahz is striking with a gathered hand on the chest, like al-lakz, on the authority of Abu 'Ubaydah also. Abu Zayd said: it is with a closed fist on the jawbones (al-lahazim) and the neck, and a man is called "milhaz," with a kasra on the mim.

Al-Asma'i said: nakazahu means he struck him and pushed him. Al-Kisa'i said: nahazahu is like nakazahu and wakazahu, meaning he struck him and pushed him. And "lahadahu lahdan" means he pushed him in humiliation, so he is "malhud," and likewise "lahadahu." Tarafah said, disparaging a man:

*Slow to answer the caller, quick to indecency, a submissive one, pushed about by the hands of men.* [Note: "Another reading: 'an al-jalā'. Dhalūl is the opposite of ṣa'b. Another reading: 'dhalīl.' Ajmā' is the back of the hand when you gather and close your fingers."]

That is, he is pushed away. It is intensified because of its frequency. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "He (meaning the Prophet ﷺ) pushed me with a push that hurt me," recorded by Muslim.

Musa (peace be upon him) did this, and he did not intend to kill him; he only intended to repel him, but his soul was in it, and this is the meaning of: ﴿and he [Musa] gave him his death (fa-qada 'alayhi)﴾. Whatever you finish and bring to its end, you have "qadaytu 'alayhi." Jarir said, with al-Ashja' meaning the brave one among snakes. The first half of the line is: "Did they, when they saw their own bare feet, [do such things?]":

*The snake bit him, and so the brave one finished him off.*

﴿He said: This is of the work of Satan﴾, that is, of his misleading. Al-Hasan said: Killing the disbeliever was not permitted at that time and in that state, because it was a state of restraint from fighting. ﴿Indeed, he is a clear, misleading enemy﴾ is a predicate following a predicate.

﴿He said: My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾, ﴿so He forgave him﴾. Musa (peace be upon him) regretted that striking, in which the soul was lost, and his regret led him to submit to his Lord and to seek forgiveness for his sin. Qatadah said: By Allah, he knew the way out, so he sought forgiveness. Then he (ﷺ) continued to mention this against himself, although he knew he had been forgiven, until in the Hereafter he would say: "Indeed I killed a soul, for which I was not commanded." He counted it against himself as a sin and said, "I have wronged myself, so forgive me," because it is not befitting for a prophet to kill until he is commanded to do so. Also, the prophets are apprehensive about things about which others are not apprehensive.

An-Naqqash said: He did not kill him deliberately, intending to kill; he only struck him one blow, intending by it to repel his oppression. He said: It has also been said that this was before prophethood. Ka'b said: He was then twelve years old. The killing, moreover, was accidental, since a blow or a punch generally does not kill.

Muslim related from Salim ibn 'Abdullah that he said: "O people of Iraq, how much you ask about the minor matter, and how much you embark upon the major matter! I heard my father 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed, strife will come from here,' and he pointed with his hand towards the east, 'from where the horns of Satan rise, and some of you will strike the necks of others.'" And Musa only killed the one he killed from the family of Fir'awn by mistake, so Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress and tested you with a severe trial﴾.

God Almighty said: ﴿He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me﴾, that is, of knowledge, wisdom and monotheism. ﴿I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾, that is, an aid to the disbelievers. Al-Qushayri said: He did not say "by what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness," because this was before the revelation, and he did not know that Allah had forgiven him that killing. Al-Mawardi said: In "by what You have bestowed upon me" there are two possibilities. One of them is: of forgiveness. Likewise al-Mahdawi and al-Tha'labi mentioned it. Al-Mahdawi said: "By what You have bestowed upon me" means of forgiveness, so You did not punish me. The second possibility is: of guidance. I say: "So He forgave him" indicates forgiveness, and Allah knows best.

Al-Zamakhshari said: God's saying, ﴿by what You have bestowed upon me﴾, may be an oath whose answer is omitted; its estimated meaning is: "I swear by Your bestowal upon me of forgiveness that I will not be a supporter of the criminals." It may also be a plea for mercy, as if he said: "My Lord, protect me by the right of what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness, for then I will not be, if You protect me, a supporter of the criminals." By "supporting the criminals" he meant either accompanying Fir'awn and being included among his company and increasing his numbers, since he used to ride with his riding, like a child with a father, and was called "the son of Fir'awn"; or supporting those whose support leads to sin and wrongdoing, like the support of the Israelite which led to the killing that was not permitted for him to carry out. It has also been said: He meant, "Although I erred in this killing for which I was not commanded, I will not abandon the support of the Muslims against the criminals." On this view the Israelite was a believer, and supporting a believer is obligatory in all the sacred laws. It has been said in some reports that this Israelite was a disbeliever, and he was only called "of his party" because he was an Israelite, and he did not intend agreement in religion. On this view, Musa regretted that he had aided a disbeliever against a disbeliever, so he said: "I will not after this be a supporter of the disbelievers."

It has also been said: This is not a statement of fact but a supplication, meaning: "So I will not after this be a supporter; so do not make me, O my Lord, a supporter of the criminals." Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: "O Allah, so I will never again be a supporter of the criminals." He claimed that this statement was also the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Nahhas said: That it be a statement of fact is preferable and more fitting to the context of the speech, as one says: "I will not disobey You, because You have bestowed favour upon me." This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas in reality, not what al-Farra' related, because Ibn 'Abbas said: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested the second day," and making an exception does not occur in supplication. One does not say: "O Allah, forgive me if You will." The most astonishing thing is that al-Farra' related this from Ibn 'Abbas and then related from him a statement contrary to it.

I say: This meaning has already passed in summary and clarification in Surat al-Naml, and that it is a statement of fact, not a supplication. And on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested with it once more," meaning he did not say, "I will not be (a supporter), if Allah wills." This is like His saying: ﴿And do not incline towards those who have wronged﴾.

The second issue: Salamah ibn Nubayt said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim sent to al-Dahhak the tax of the people of Bukhara and said: "Give it to them." He said: "Excuse me," and he kept asking him to excuse him until he excused him. It was said to him: "What is the harm to you in giving it to them, when you will not take anything from them?" He said: "I do not like to help the oppressors in any part of their affair."

'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Walid al-Wassafi said: I said to 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: "I have a brother who works with his pen, calculating what comes in and goes out, and he has dependants, and if he gave this up he would be in need and would fall into debt?" He said: "Who is the head?" I said: "Khalid ibn 'Abdullah al-Qasri." He said: "Do you not read what the righteous servant said: ﴿My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested with it a second time, and Allah aided him. So your brother should not aid them, for Allah will aid him." 'Ata' said: It is not permissible for anyone to aid an oppressor, to write for him, or to accompany him. If he does any of that, he has become a helper of the wrongdoers.

In a hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: 'Where are the oppressors, the likes of the oppressors, and the helpers of the oppressors, even whoever prepared an inkwell for them or sharpened a pen for them?' They will be gathered in an iron coffin and thrown into Hell." It is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever walks with an oppressed person to help him against his injustice, Allah will make his feet firm upon the Sirat on the Day of Resurrection, the Day when feet will slip; and whoever walks with an oppressor to help him in his oppression, Allah will make his feet slip upon the Sirat, the Day when feet will be overturned." In a hadith: "Whoever walks with an oppressor has committed a sin." Walking with an oppressor is only a sin if one walks with him in order to help him, because he has violated the prohibition of Allah, the Exalted, in His saying: ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 15–19 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he woke up in the city, fearful﴾. It has already been mentioned in "Ta-Ha" [[See vol. 11, p. 202, first or second edition.]] and elsewhere that the prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, do feel fear, in refutation of those who say otherwise, and that fear does not contradict knowledge of Allah nor reliance upon Him. It was said: he woke up fearful that the killing of the man would be attributed to him and he would be seized for it. It was also said: fearful of his people, that they would hand him over. And it was said: fearful of Allah, may He be exalted.

(Yataraqqabu, "watching warily") Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he looked about him in fear. It was also said: he awaited pursuit, and he awaited what people were saying. Qatadah said: "yataraqqabu" means he watched out for pursuit. It was also said: he went out seeking news, and no one had known of the killing of the Copt except the Israelite.

"Asbaha" may carry the sense of "sara" (became), meaning that when he killed he became fearful. It may also mean that he entered upon the morning, that is, the morning of the day following his day. "Khaifan" is in the accusative as the predicate of "asbaha", and if you wish it may be a circumstantial accusative (hal), in which case the adverbial phrase serves as the predicate.

(Then behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was crying out to him for help) That is, behold, his companion the Israelite, whom he had rescued the day before, was fighting another Copt whom he wanted to conscript (yusakhkhirahu) for labour. "Istis'rakh" (crying for help) means seeking aid (istighathah). It derives from "surakh" (a shout), because the one seeking aid shouts and raises his voice to ask for succour. A poet said [[He is Salamah ibn Jandal. "Al-tanabib" (plural of "zunbub") is the dry bony edge of the shin. The intended meaning is the speed of response.]]:

"Whenever a fearful crier came to us, / his cry was like the striking of shin-bones."

It was said: this Israelite who sought help was the one whom the cook of Pharaoh had conscripted to carry firewood to the kitchen; al-Qushayri mentioned this. "Alladhi" is in the nominative as the subject, and "yastasrikhuhu" is in the position of the predicate. It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. "Ams" refers to the day before your day; it is built on kasra because of the meeting of two unvoweled letters. When the definite article or an annexation is attached to it, it becomes declinable and is inflected with ḍamma and fatḥa according to most grammarians, though some grammarians hold that it remains indeclinable even with the definite article. Sibawayh and others relate that some Arabs treat "ams" like a diptotic noun in the nominative case only, and that a poet may be compelled to do this also in the genitive and accusative, as the poet said:

"Indeed I have seen a marvel since yesterday"

Here he put "mudh" (since) into the genitive with "ma madha" (what has passed). The better usage is the nominative, so "ams" in the genitive follows its treatment in the nominative in the second dialect.

(Moses said to him: "Indeed you are clearly a misguided one") "Ghawiyy" means one who is lost or frustrated, that is, because you pick a quarrel with one you cannot withstand. It was also said: a clearly misleading one, manifestly in error; "You killed a man because of you yesterday, and today you summon me to another." "Ghawiyy" is an intensive form (fa'il) from "aghwa yughwi," and it has the sense of "mughwin" (one who misleads), like "wajih" and "alim" meaning "mujiʻ" and "mu'lim." It was also said: "ghawiyy" carries the sense of "ghawin" (erring), meaning that you are erring in fighting one whose harm you cannot repel. Al-Hasan said: he only said to the Copt "you are clearly misguided" because of his conscripting this Israelite, and because he intended to strike him. One says "batasha yabtishu" and "yabtushu," and the damma is more analogical because it is an intransitive verb.

(He said: "O Moses, do you intend to kill me") Ibn Jubayr said: Moses intended to strike the Copt, but the Israelite supposed he meant him, because he had spoken harshly to him, so he said: "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" The Copt heard the words and disclosed them. It was also said: the Israelite intended to strike the Copt, and Moses forbade him, so he feared him and said: "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?"

(You want nothing) That is, you do not want anything.

(But to be a tyrant in the land) That is, a compeller (qitalan). ʿIkrimah and al-Shaʿbi said: a person is not a tyrant until he has killed two souls without right.

(Nor do you want to be among the reformers) That is, among those who set things right between people.

God Almighty said: ﴿And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness among its people﴾. It was said: When Musa (peace be upon him) came to know the truth that he held in his religion, he criticised what the people of Fir'awn were upon, and this became known from him. They threatened him, so he feared them. Thereafter he did not enter the city of Fir'awn except in fear and concealment.

As-Suddi said: At the time of this story, Musa was still in the position of being attached to Fir'awn. He would ride his mounts, until he was called "Musa, son of Fir'awn." One day Fir'awn rode out and travelled to one of the cities of Egypt called Manf. Muqatil said: It was two farsakhs from Egypt. Then Musa learned that Fir'awn had ridden out, so he rode after him and reached that town at the time of al-qaylulah (the midday rest), which is the time of heedlessness. Ibn 'Abbas said, and he also said: It was between al-'Isha' and al-'Atamah.

Ibn Ishaq said: Rather, the city is Egypt itself. At this time Musa had openly opposed Fir'awn and criticised them for worshipping Fir'awn and idols. So he entered the city of Fir'awn one day at a time of heedlessness among its people. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: It was at midday, while the people were sleeping. Ibn Zayd said: Fir'awn had cast Musa off and expelled him from the city, and he had been absent from it for years. He came while the people were heedless, having forgotten his matter and because their time with him was long past, and that day was a day of festivity. Al-Dahhak said: He sought to enter the city at a time when its people were heedless, and he entered it when he knew that this was the case from them. From him came the killing of the man before he was commanded to kill him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness and He forgave him.

It is said in ordinary speech: "I entered the city when its people were heedless" (dakhaltu al-madinata hina ghafala ahluha), and one does not say "'ala hina ghafala ahluha." The preposition "'ala" is used in this verse because heedlessness is the intended focus. This is like when you say: "I came upon heedlessness ('ala ghaflatin)," and if you wish you may say: "I came upon a time of heedlessness ('ala hina ghaflatin)." Likewise is the verse.

﴿And he found therein two men fighting, one of his own party (hadha min shi'atih)﴾. The meaning is: when an observer looked at them, he would say, "This one is of his party," that is, of the Children of Israel.

﴿And this one of his enemy﴾, that is, of the people of Fir'awn.

﴿So the one from his party sought his help﴾, that is, he sought his support and aid. Likewise He said in the verse after it: ﴿So the one who had sought his help the day before was now crying out to him﴾, that is, he was calling for help against another Copt. Musa helped him because supporting the oppressed is a religious duty in all the religions of the nations, and an obligation in all the sacred laws.

Qatadah said: The Copt wanted to press the Israelite into service to carry firewood for Fir'awn's kitchen, but he refused, so he sought help from Musa. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: He was a baker for Fir'awn.

﴿So Musa struck him﴾. Qatadah said: with his staff. Mujahid said: with his palm, meaning he pushed him. Al-wakz, al-lakz, al-lahz and al-lahd have one meaning, which is striking with the hand gathered together in a closed fist, like the closing of the fingers for the number seventy-three. Ibn Mas'ud read: "fa-lakazahu." It was said: al-lakz is on the jaw, and al-wakz is on the heart. Al-Tha'labi related that in the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud the reading is "fa-nakazahu" with the letter nun, and the meaning is the same. Al-Jawhari said, on the authority of Abu 'Ubaydah: al-lakz is striking with a closed fist on the chest. Abu Zayd said: it is on the whole body. Al-lahz is striking with a gathered hand on the chest, like al-lakz, on the authority of Abu 'Ubaydah also. Abu Zayd said: it is with a closed fist on the jawbones (al-lahazim) and the neck, and a man is called "milhaz," with a kasra on the mim.

Al-Asma'i said: nakazahu means he struck him and pushed him. Al-Kisa'i said: nahazahu is like nakazahu and wakazahu, meaning he struck him and pushed him. And "lahadahu lahdan" means he pushed him in humiliation, so he is "malhud," and likewise "lahadahu." Tarafah said, disparaging a man:

*Slow to answer the caller, quick to indecency, a submissive one, pushed about by the hands of men.* [Note: "Another reading: 'an al-jalā'. Dhalūl is the opposite of ṣa'b. Another reading: 'dhalīl.' Ajmā' is the back of the hand when you gather and close your fingers."]

That is, he is pushed away. It is intensified because of its frequency. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "He (meaning the Prophet ﷺ) pushed me with a push that hurt me," recorded by Muslim.

Musa (peace be upon him) did this, and he did not intend to kill him; he only intended to repel him, but his soul was in it, and this is the meaning of: ﴿and he [Musa] gave him his death (fa-qada 'alayhi)﴾. Whatever you finish and bring to its end, you have "qadaytu 'alayhi." Jarir said, with al-Ashja' meaning the brave one among snakes. The first half of the line is: "Did they, when they saw their own bare feet, [do such things?]":

*The snake bit him, and so the brave one finished him off.*

﴿He said: This is of the work of Satan﴾, that is, of his misleading. Al-Hasan said: Killing the disbeliever was not permitted at that time and in that state, because it was a state of restraint from fighting. ﴿Indeed, he is a clear, misleading enemy﴾ is a predicate following a predicate.

﴿He said: My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾, ﴿so He forgave him﴾. Musa (peace be upon him) regretted that striking, in which the soul was lost, and his regret led him to submit to his Lord and to seek forgiveness for his sin. Qatadah said: By Allah, he knew the way out, so he sought forgiveness. Then he (ﷺ) continued to mention this against himself, although he knew he had been forgiven, until in the Hereafter he would say: "Indeed I killed a soul, for which I was not commanded." He counted it against himself as a sin and said, "I have wronged myself, so forgive me," because it is not befitting for a prophet to kill until he is commanded to do so. Also, the prophets are apprehensive about things about which others are not apprehensive.

An-Naqqash said: He did not kill him deliberately, intending to kill; he only struck him one blow, intending by it to repel his oppression. He said: It has also been said that this was before prophethood. Ka'b said: He was then twelve years old. The killing, moreover, was accidental, since a blow or a punch generally does not kill.

Muslim related from Salim ibn 'Abdullah that he said: "O people of Iraq, how much you ask about the minor matter, and how much you embark upon the major matter! I heard my father 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed, strife will come from here,' and he pointed with his hand towards the east, 'from where the horns of Satan rise, and some of you will strike the necks of others.'" And Musa only killed the one he killed from the family of Fir'awn by mistake, so Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress and tested you with a severe trial﴾.

God Almighty said: ﴿He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me﴾, that is, of knowledge, wisdom and monotheism. ﴿I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾, that is, an aid to the disbelievers. Al-Qushayri said: He did not say "by what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness," because this was before the revelation, and he did not know that Allah had forgiven him that killing. Al-Mawardi said: In "by what You have bestowed upon me" there are two possibilities. One of them is: of forgiveness. Likewise al-Mahdawi and al-Tha'labi mentioned it. Al-Mahdawi said: "By what You have bestowed upon me" means of forgiveness, so You did not punish me. The second possibility is: of guidance. I say: "So He forgave him" indicates forgiveness, and Allah knows best.

Al-Zamakhshari said: God's saying, ﴿by what You have bestowed upon me﴾, may be an oath whose answer is omitted; its estimated meaning is: "I swear by Your bestowal upon me of forgiveness that I will not be a supporter of the criminals." It may also be a plea for mercy, as if he said: "My Lord, protect me by the right of what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness, for then I will not be, if You protect me, a supporter of the criminals." On this view, Musa regretted that he had aided a disbeliever against a disbeliever, so he said: "I will not after this be a supporter of the disbelievers."

It has also been said: This is not a statement of fact but a supplication, meaning: "So I will not after this be a supporter; so do not make me, O my Lord, a supporter of the criminals." Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: "O Allah, so I will never again be a supporter of the criminals." He claimed that this statement was also the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. One does not say: "O Allah, forgive me if You will." The most astonishing thing is that al-Farra' related this from Ibn 'Abbas and then related from him a statement contrary to it.

I say: This meaning has already passed in summary and clarification in Surat al-Naml, and that it is a statement of fact, not a supplication. And on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested with it once more," meaning he did not say, "I will not be (a supporter), if Allah wills." This is like His saying: ﴿And do not incline towards those who have wronged﴾.

The second issue: Salamah ibn Nubayt said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim sent to al-Dahhak the tax of the people of Bukhara and said: "Give it to them." He said: "Excuse me," and he kept asking him to excuse him until he excused him. It was said to him: "What is the harm to you in giving it to them, when you will not take anything from them?" He said: "I do not like to help the oppressors in any part of their affair."

He said: "Who is the head?" I said: "Khalid ibn 'Abdullah al-Qasri." He said: "Do you not read what the righteous servant said: ﴿My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested with it a second time, and Allah aided him. So your brother should not aid them, for Allah will aid him." 'Ata' said: It is not permissible for anyone to aid an oppressor, to write for him, or to accompany him. If he does any of that, he has become a helper of the wrongdoers.

In a hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: 'Where are the oppressors, the likes of the oppressors, and the helpers of the oppressors, even whoever prepared an inkwell for them or sharpened a pen for them?' They will be gathered in an iron coffin and thrown into Hell." In a hadith: "Whoever walks with an oppressor has committed a sin." Walking with an oppressor is only a sin if one walks with him in order to help him, because he has violated the prohibition of Allah, the Exalted, in His saying: ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾.
