(He said: "O Moses, do you intend to kill me") Ibn Jubayr said: Moses intended to strike the Copt, but the Israelite supposed he meant him, because he had spoken harshly to him, so he said: "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" The Copt heard the words and disclosed them. It was also said: the Israelite intended to strike the Copt, and Moses forbade him, so he feared him and said: "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?"

(You want nothing) That is, you do not want anything.

(But to be a tyrant in the land) That is, a compeller (qitalan). ʿIkrimah and al-Shaʿbi said: a person is not a tyrant until he has killed two souls without right.

(Nor do you want to be among the reformers) That is, among those who set things right between people.

God Almighty said: ﴿And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness among its people﴾. It was said: When Musa (peace be upon him) came to know the truth that he held in his religion, he criticised what the people of Fir'awn were upon, and this became known from him. They threatened him, so he feared them. Thereafter he did not enter the city of Fir'awn except in fear and concealment.

As-Suddi said: At the time of this story, Musa was still in the position of being attached to Fir'awn. He would ride his mounts, until he was called "Musa, son of Fir'awn." One day Fir'awn rode out and travelled to one of the cities of Egypt called Manf. Muqatil said: It was two farsakhs from Egypt. Then Musa learned that Fir'awn had ridden out, so he rode after him and reached that town at the time of al-qaylulah (the midday rest), which is the time of heedlessness. Ibn 'Abbas said, and he also said: It was between al-'Isha' and al-'Atamah.

Ibn Ishaq said: Rather, the city is Egypt itself. At this time Musa had openly opposed Fir'awn and criticised them for worshipping Fir'awn and idols. So he entered the city of Fir'awn one day at a time of heedlessness among its people. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: It was at midday, while the people were sleeping. Ibn Zayd said: Fir'awn had cast Musa off and expelled him from the city, and he had been absent from it for years. He came while the people were heedless, having forgotten his matter and because their time with him was long past, and that day was a day of festivity. Al-Dahhak said: He sought to enter the city at a time when its people were heedless, and he entered it when he knew that this was the case from them. From him came the killing of the man before he was commanded to kill him, so he asked his Lord for forgiveness and He forgave him.

It is said in ordinary speech: "I entered the city when its people were heedless" (dakhaltu al-madinata hina ghafala ahluha), and one does not say "'ala hina ghafala ahluha." The preposition "'ala" is used in this verse because heedlessness is the intended focus. This is like when you say: "I came upon heedlessness ('ala ghaflatin)," and if you wish you may say: "I came upon a time of heedlessness ('ala hina ghaflatin)." Likewise is the verse.

﴿And he found therein two men fighting, one of his own party (hadha min shi'atih)﴾. The meaning is: when an observer looked at them, he would say, "This one is of his party," that is, of the Children of Israel.

﴿And this one of his enemy﴾, that is, of the people of Fir'awn.

﴿So the one from his party sought his help﴾, that is, he sought his support and aid. Likewise He said in the verse after it: ﴿So the one who had sought his help the day before was now crying out to him﴾, that is, he was calling for help against another Copt. Musa helped him because supporting the oppressed is a religious duty in all the religions of the nations, and an obligation in all the sacred laws.

Qatadah said: The Copt wanted to press the Israelite into service to carry firewood for Fir'awn's kitchen, but he refused, so he sought help from Musa. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: He was a baker for Fir'awn.

﴿So Musa struck him﴾. Qatadah said: with his staff. Mujahid said: with his palm, meaning he pushed him. Al-wakz, al-lakz, al-lahz and al-lahd have one meaning, which is striking with the hand gathered together in a closed fist, like the closing of the fingers for the number seventy-three. Ibn Mas'ud read: "fa-lakazahu." It was said: al-lakz is on the jaw, and al-wakz is on the heart. Al-Tha'labi related that in the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud the reading is "fa-nakazahu" with the letter nun, and the meaning is the same. Al-Jawhari said, on the authority of Abu 'Ubaydah: al-lakz is striking with a closed fist on the chest. Abu Zayd said: it is on the whole body. Al-lahz is striking with a gathered hand on the chest, like al-lakz, on the authority of Abu 'Ubaydah also. Abu Zayd said: it is with a closed fist on the jawbones (al-lahazim) and the neck, and a man is called "milhaz," with a kasra on the mim.

Al-Asma'i said: nakazahu means he struck him and pushed him. Al-Kisa'i said: nahazahu is like nakazahu and wakazahu, meaning he struck him and pushed him. And "lahadahu lahdan" means he pushed him in humiliation, so he is "malhud," and likewise "lahadahu." Tarafah said, disparaging a man:

*Slow to answer the caller, quick to indecency, a submissive one, pushed about by the hands of men.* [Note: "Another reading: 'an al-jalā'. Dhalūl is the opposite of ṣa'b. Another reading: 'dhalīl.' Ajmā' is the back of the hand when you gather and close your fingers."]

That is, he is pushed away. It is intensified because of its frequency. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "He (meaning the Prophet ﷺ) pushed me with a push that hurt me," recorded by Muslim.

Musa (peace be upon him) did this, and he did not intend to kill him; he only intended to repel him, but his soul was in it, and this is the meaning of: ﴿and he [Musa] gave him his death (fa-qada 'alayhi)﴾. Whatever you finish and bring to its end, you have "qadaytu 'alayhi." Jarir said, with al-Ashja' meaning the brave one among snakes. The first half of the line is: "Did they, when they saw their own bare feet, [do such things?]":

*The snake bit him, and so the brave one finished him off.*

﴿He said: This is of the work of Satan﴾, that is, of his misleading. Al-Hasan said: Killing the disbeliever was not permitted at that time and in that state, because it was a state of restraint from fighting. ﴿Indeed, he is a clear, misleading enemy﴾ is a predicate following a predicate.

﴿He said: My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾, ﴿so He forgave him﴾. Musa (peace be upon him) regretted that striking, in which the soul was lost, and his regret led him to submit to his Lord and to seek forgiveness for his sin. Qatadah said: By Allah, he knew the way out, so he sought forgiveness. Then he (ﷺ) continued to mention this against himself, although he knew he had been forgiven, until in the Hereafter he would say: "Indeed I killed a soul, for which I was not commanded." He counted it against himself as a sin and said, "I have wronged myself, so forgive me," because it is not befitting for a prophet to kill until he is commanded to do so. Also, the prophets are apprehensive about things about which others are not apprehensive.

An-Naqqash said: He did not kill him deliberately, intending to kill; he only struck him one blow, intending by it to repel his oppression. He said: It has also been said that this was before prophethood. Ka'b said: He was then twelve years old. The killing, moreover, was accidental, since a blow or a punch generally does not kill.

Muslim related from Salim ibn 'Abdullah that he said: "O people of Iraq, how much you ask about the minor matter, and how much you embark upon the major matter! I heard my father 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar say: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed, strife will come from here,' and he pointed with his hand towards the east, 'from where the horns of Satan rise, and some of you will strike the necks of others.'" And Musa only killed the one he killed from the family of Fir'awn by mistake, so Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress and tested you with a severe trial﴾.

God Almighty said: ﴿He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me﴾, that is, of knowledge, wisdom and monotheism. ﴿I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾, that is, an aid to the disbelievers. Al-Qushayri said: He did not say "by what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness," because this was before the revelation, and he did not know that Allah had forgiven him that killing. Al-Mawardi said: In "by what You have bestowed upon me" there are two possibilities. One of them is: of forgiveness. Likewise al-Mahdawi and al-Tha'labi mentioned it. Al-Mahdawi said: "By what You have bestowed upon me" means of forgiveness, so You did not punish me. The second possibility is: of guidance. I say: "So He forgave him" indicates forgiveness, and Allah knows best.

Al-Zamakhshari said: God's saying, ﴿by what You have bestowed upon me﴾, may be an oath whose answer is omitted; its estimated meaning is: "I swear by Your bestowal upon me of forgiveness that I will not be a supporter of the criminals." It may also be a plea for mercy, as if he said: "My Lord, protect me by the right of what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness, for then I will not be, if You protect me, a supporter of the criminals." By "supporting the criminals" he meant either accompanying Fir'awn and being included among his company and increasing his numbers, since he used to ride with his riding, like a child with a father, and was called "the son of Fir'awn"; or supporting those whose support leads to sin and wrongdoing, like the support of the Israelite which led to the killing that was not permitted for him to carry out. It has also been said: He meant, "Although I erred in this killing for which I was not commanded, I will not abandon the support of the Muslims against the criminals." On this view the Israelite was a believer, and supporting a believer is obligatory in all the sacred laws. It has been said in some reports that this Israelite was a disbeliever, and he was only called "of his party" because he was an Israelite, and he did not intend agreement in religion. On this view, Musa regretted that he had aided a disbeliever against a disbeliever, so he said: "I will not after this be a supporter of the disbelievers."

It has also been said: This is not a statement of fact but a supplication, meaning: "So I will not after this be a supporter; so do not make me, O my Lord, a supporter of the criminals." Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: "O Allah, so I will never again be a supporter of the criminals." He claimed that this statement was also the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Nahhas said: That it be a statement of fact is preferable and more fitting to the context of the speech, as one says: "I will not disobey You, because You have bestowed favour upon me." This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas in reality, not what al-Farra' related, because Ibn 'Abbas said: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested the second day," and making an exception does not occur in supplication. One does not say: "O Allah, forgive me if You will." The most astonishing thing is that al-Farra' related this from Ibn 'Abbas and then related from him a statement contrary to it.

I say: This meaning has already passed in summary and clarification in Surat al-Naml, and that it is a statement of fact, not a supplication. And on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested with it once more," meaning he did not say, "I will not be (a supporter), if Allah wills." This is like His saying: ﴿And do not incline towards those who have wronged﴾.

The second issue: Salamah ibn Nubayt said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim sent to al-Dahhak the tax of the people of Bukhara and said: "Give it to them." He said: "Excuse me," and he kept asking him to excuse him until he excused him. It was said to him: "What is the harm to you in giving it to them, when you will not take anything from them?" He said: "I do not like to help the oppressors in any part of their affair."

'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Walid al-Wassafi said: I said to 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: "I have a brother who works with his pen, calculating what comes in and goes out, and he has dependants, and if he gave this up he would be in need and would fall into debt?" He said: "Who is the head?" I said: "Khalid ibn 'Abdullah al-Qasri." He said: "Do you not read what the righteous servant said: ﴿My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested with it a second time, and Allah aided him. So your brother should not aid them, for Allah will aid him." 'Ata' said: It is not permissible for anyone to aid an oppressor, to write for him, or to accompany him. If he does any of that, he has become a helper of the wrongdoers.

In a hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: 'Where are the oppressors, the likes of the oppressors, and the helpers of the oppressors, even whoever prepared an inkwell for them or sharpened a pen for them?' They will be gathered in an iron coffin and thrown into Hell." It is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever walks with an oppressed person to help him against his injustice, Allah will make his feet firm upon the Sirat on the Day of Resurrection, the Day when feet will slip; and whoever walks with an oppressor to help him in his oppression, Allah will make his feet slip upon the Sirat, the Day when feet will be overturned." In a hadith: "Whoever walks with an oppressor has committed a sin." Walking with an oppressor is only a sin if one walks with him in order to help him, because he has violated the prohibition of Allah, the Exalted, in His saying: ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 15–19 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he woke up in the city, fearful﴾. It has already been mentioned in "Ta-Ha" [[See vol. 11, p. 202, first or second edition.]] and elsewhere that the prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, do feel fear, in refutation of those who say otherwise, and that fear does not contradict knowledge of Allah nor reliance upon Him. It was said: he woke up fearful that the killing of the man would be attributed to him and he would be seized for it. It was also said: fearful of his people, that they would hand him over. And it was said: fearful of Allah, may He be exalted.

(Yataraqqabu, "watching warily") Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he looked about him in fear. It was also said: he awaited pursuit, and he awaited what people were saying. Qatadah said: "yataraqqabu" means he watched out for pursuit. It was also said: he went out seeking news, and no one had known of the killing of the Copt except the Israelite.

"Asbaha" may carry the sense of "sara" (became), meaning that when he killed he became fearful. It may also mean that he entered upon the morning, that is, the morning of the day following his day. "Khaifan" is in the accusative as the predicate of "asbaha", and if you wish it may be a circumstantial accusative (hal), in which case the adverbial phrase serves as the predicate.

(Then behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was crying out to him for help) That is, behold, his companion the Israelite, whom he had rescued the day before, was fighting another Copt whom he wanted to conscript (yusakhkhirahu) for labour. "Istis'rakh" (crying for help) means seeking aid (istighathah). It derives from "surakh" (a shout), because the one seeking aid shouts and raises his voice to ask for succour. A poet said [[He is Salamah ibn Jandal. "Al-tanabib" (plural of "zunbub") is the dry bony edge of the shin. The intended meaning is the speed of response.]]:

"Whenever a fearful crier came to us, / his cry was like the striking of shin-bones."

It was said: this Israelite who sought help was the one whom the cook of Pharaoh had conscripted to carry firewood to the kitchen; al-Qushayri mentioned this. "Alladhi" is in the nominative as the subject, and "yastasrikhuhu" is in the position of the predicate. It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. "Ams" refers to the day before your day; it is built on kasra because of the meeting of two unvoweled letters. When the definite article or an annexation is attached to it, it becomes declinable and is inflected with ḍamma and fatḥa according to most grammarians, though some grammarians hold that it remains indeclinable even with the definite article. Sibawayh and others relate that some Arabs treat "ams" like a diptotic noun in the nominative case only, and that a poet may be compelled to do this also in the genitive and accusative, as the poet said:

"Indeed I have seen a marvel since yesterday"

Here he put "mudh" (since) into the genitive with "ma madha" (what has passed). The better usage is the nominative, so "ams" in the genitive follows its treatment in the nominative in the second dialect.

(Moses said to him: "Indeed you are clearly a misguided one") "Ghawiyy" means one who is lost or frustrated, that is, because you pick a quarrel with one you cannot withstand. It was also said: a clearly misleading one, manifestly in error; "You killed a man because of you yesterday, and today you summon me to another." "Ghawiyy" is an intensive form (fa'il) from "aghwa yughwi," and it has the sense of "mughwin" (one who misleads), like "wajih" and "alim" meaning "mujiʻ" and "mu'lim." It was also said: "ghawiyy" carries the sense of "ghawin" (erring), meaning that you are erring in fighting one whose harm you cannot repel. Al-Hasan said: he only said to the Copt "you are clearly misguided" because of his conscripting this Israelite, and because he intended to strike him. One says "batasha yabtishu" and "yabtushu," and the damma is more analogical because it is an intransitive verb.

(He said: "O Moses, do you intend to kill me") Ibn Jubayr said: Moses intended to strike the Copt, but the Israelite supposed he meant him, because he had spoken harshly to him, so he said: "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" The Copt heard the words and disclosed them. It was also said: the Israelite intended to strike the Copt, and Moses forbade him, so he feared him and said: "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?"

(You want nothing) That is, you do not want anything.

(But to be a tyrant in the land) That is, a compeller (qitalan). ʿIkrimah and al-Shaʿbi said: a person is not a tyrant until he has killed two souls without right.

It has also been said: He meant, "Although I erred in this killing for which I was not commanded, I will not abandon the support of the Muslims against the criminals." On this view the Israelite was a believer, and supporting a believer is obligatory in all the sacred laws. It has been said in some reports that this Israelite was a disbeliever, and he was only called "of his party" because he was an Israelite, and he did not intend agreement in religion. On this view, Musa regretted that he had aided a disbeliever against a disbeliever, so he said: "I will not after this be a supporter of the disbelievers."

It has also been said: This is not a statement of fact but a supplication, meaning: "So I will not after this be a supporter; so do not make me, O my Lord, a supporter of the criminals." Al-Farra' said: The meaning is: "O Allah, so I will never again be a supporter of the criminals." He claimed that this statement was also the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Nahhas said: That it be a statement of fact is preferable and more fitting to the context of the speech, as one says: "I will not disobey You, because You have bestowed favour upon me." This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas in reality, not what al-Farra' related, because Ibn 'Abbas said: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested the second day," and making an exception does not occur in supplication. One does not say: "O Allah, forgive me if You will." The most astonishing thing is that al-Farra' related this from Ibn 'Abbas and then related from him a statement contrary to it.

I say: This meaning has already passed in summary and clarification in Surat al-Naml, and that it is a statement of fact, not a supplication. And on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested with it once more," meaning he did not say, "I will not be (a supporter), if Allah wills." This is like His saying: ﴿And do not incline towards those who have wronged﴾.

The second issue: Salamah ibn Nubayt said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muslim sent to al-Dahhak the tax of the people of Bukhara and said: "Give it to them." He said: "Excuse me," and he kept asking him to excuse him until he excused him. It was said to him: "What is the harm to you in giving it to them, when you will not take anything from them?" He said: "I do not like to help the oppressors in any part of their affair."

'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Walid al-Wassafi said: I said to 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: "I have a brother who works with his pen, calculating what comes in and goes out, and he has dependants, and if he gave this up he would be in need and would fall into debt?" He said: "Who is the head?" I said: "Khalid ibn 'Abdullah al-Qasri." He said: "Do you not read what the righteous servant said: ﴿My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "He did not make an exception, so he was tested with it a second time, and Allah aided him. So your brother should not aid them, for Allah will aid him." 'Ata' said: It is not permissible for anyone to aid an oppressor, to write for him, or to accompany him. If he does any of that, he has become a helper of the wrongdoers.

In a hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: 'Where are the oppressors, the likes of the oppressors, and the helpers of the oppressors, even whoever prepared an inkwell for them or sharpened a pen for them?' They will be gathered in an iron coffin and thrown into Hell." It is also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever walks with an oppressed person to help him against his injustice, Allah will make his feet firm upon the Sirat on the Day of Resurrection, the Day when feet will slip; and whoever walks with an oppressor to help him in his oppression, Allah will make his feet slip upon the Sirat, the Day when feet will be overturned." In a hadith: "Whoever walks with an oppressor has committed a sin." Walking with an oppressor is only a sin if one walks with him in order to help him, because he has violated the prohibition of Allah, the Exalted, in His saying: ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 15–19 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he woke up in the city, fearful﴾. It has already been mentioned in "Ta-Ha" [[See vol. 11, p. 202, first or second edition.]] and elsewhere that the prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, do feel fear, in refutation of those who say otherwise, and that fear does not contradict knowledge of Allah nor reliance upon Him. It was said: he woke up fearful that the killing of the man would be attributed to him and he would be seized for it. It was also said: fearful of his people, that they would hand him over. And it was said: fearful of Allah, may He be exalted.

(Yataraqqabu, "watching warily") Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he looked about him in fear. It was also said: he awaited pursuit, and he awaited what people were saying. Qatadah said: "yataraqqabu" means he watched out for pursuit. It was also said: he went out seeking news, and no one had known of the killing of the Copt except the Israelite.

"Asbaha" may carry the sense of "sara" (became), meaning that when he killed he became fearful. It may also mean that he entered upon the morning, that is, the morning of the day following his day. "Khaifan" is in the accusative as the predicate of "asbaha", and if you wish it may be a circumstantial accusative (hal), in which case the adverbial phrase serves as the predicate.

(Then behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was crying out to him for help) That is, behold, his companion the Israelite, whom he had rescued the day before, was fighting another Copt whom he wanted to conscript (yusakhkhirahu) for labour. "Istis'rakh" (crying for help) means seeking aid (istighathah). It derives from "surakh" (a shout), because the one seeking aid shouts and raises his voice to ask for succour. A poet said [[He is Salamah ibn Jandal. "Al-tanabib" (plural of "zunbub") is the dry bony edge of the shin. The intended meaning is the speed of response.]]:

"Whenever a fearful crier came to us, / his cry was like the striking of shin-bones."

It was said: this Israelite who sought help was the one whom the cook of Pharaoh had conscripted to carry firewood to the kitchen; al-Qushayri mentioned this. "Alladhi" is in the nominative as the subject, and "yastasrikhuhu" is in the position of the predicate. It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. "Ams" refers to the day before your day; it is built on kasra because of the meeting of two unvoweled letters. When the definite article or an annexation is attached to it, it becomes declinable and is inflected with ḍamma and fatḥa according to most grammarians, though some grammarians hold that it remains indeclinable even with the definite article. Sibawayh and others relate that some Arabs treat "ams" like a diptotic noun in the nominative case only, and that a poet may be compelled to do this also in the genitive and accusative, as the poet said:

"Indeed I have seen a marvel since yesterday"

Here he put "mudh" (since) into the genitive with "ma madha" (what has passed). The better usage is the nominative, so "ams" in the genitive follows its treatment in the nominative in the second dialect.

(Moses said to him: "Indeed you are clearly a misguided one") "Ghawiyy" means one who is lost or frustrated, that is, because you pick a quarrel with one you cannot withstand. It was also said: a clearly misleading one, manifestly in error; "You killed a man because of you yesterday, and today you summon me to another." "Ghawiyy" is an intensive form (fa'il) from "aghwa yughwi," and it has the sense of "mughwin" (one who misleads), like "wajih" and "alim" meaning "mujiʻ" and "mu'lim." It was also said: "ghawiyy" carries the sense of "ghawin" (erring), meaning that you are erring in fighting one whose harm you cannot repel. Al-Hasan said: he only said to the Copt "you are clearly misguided" because of his conscripting this Israelite, and because he intended to strike him. One says "batasha yabtishu" and "yabtushu," and the damma is more analogical because it is an intransitive verb.

(He said: "O Moses, do you intend to kill me") Ibn Jubayr said: Moses intended to strike the Copt, but the Israelite supposed he meant him, because he had spoken harshly to him, so he said: "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" The Copt heard the words and disclosed them. It was also said: the Israelite intended to strike the Copt, and Moses forbade him, so he feared him and said: "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?"

(You want nothing) That is, you do not want anything.

(But to be a tyrant in the land) That is, a compeller (qitalan). ʿIkrimah and al-Shaʿbi said: a person is not a tyrant until he has killed two souls without right.

(Nor do you want to be among the reformers) That is, among those who set things right between people.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 20–22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And a man came running from the farthest part of the city﴾. Most of the exegetes said: this man was Ḥizqil ibn Ṣabūrā, the believer from the family of Pharaoh, and he was a cousin of Pharaoh. Al-Tha'labi mentioned him. It was also said: he was Ṭālūt, mentioned by al-Suhayli. Al-Mahdawi related from Qatadah: his name was Shim'ūn, the believer from the family of Pharaoh. It was also said: Shamʿān. Al-Daraqutni said: "Shamʿān with the shin marked (with a dot) is not known except as the believer from the family of Pharaoh."

It is related that Pharaoh ordered that Moses be killed, but that man got the news first, so ﴿he said: "O Moses, the chiefs are conspiring against you (ya'tamirūna bika) to kill you"﴾. That is, they are consulting with one another about killing you, over the Copt whom you killed yesterday. It was also said: some of them are commanding others (to kill you). Al-Azhari said: "ta'tamara al-qawm wa-tā'amarū" means some of them commanded others; its parallel is His saying: "and confer among yourselves with good counsel" (ya'tamirū). Al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

"I see that people have invented a custom, and in every new event they confer (yu'tamar)."

﴿So leave; indeed I am to you one of the sincere advisors. So he left it, fearful, watching cautiously﴾, that is, awaiting pursuit.

﴿He said: "My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people."﴾ It was said: the tyrant (al-jabbar) is one who does whatever he wills of striking and killing through injustice, does not consider the consequences, and does not repel with what is better. It was also said: he is the arrogant one who does not humble himself before the command of God, may He be exalted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan, he said: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way."﴾ When Moses, peace be upon him, went out fleeing by himself, alone and fearful, with nothing from provisions, no mount, and no sandals, toward Madyan, because of the kinship between him and them (for Madyan was from the descendants of Abraham, and Moses was from the descendants of Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim), and he saw his condition, his lack of knowledge of the road, and his lacking provisions and other things, he entrusted his affair to God, may He be exalted, saying: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way." This is the state of one who is compelled.

I say: It is related that he sustained himself on the leaves of trees, and that he kept walking until the soles of his feet fell off. Abu Malik said: Pharaoh had sent (men) in pursuit of him and said to them: "Search for him in the mountain passes of the road, for Moses does not know the road." Then a angel came to him riding a horse, carrying a staff (ʿanaza), and said to Moses: "Follow me," so he followed him, and he guided him to the road. It is said that he gave him the staff, and it became his staff. It is also related that his staff had been taken by him for herding the sheep of Madyan, and this is more common and more authentic. Muqatil and al-Suddi said: God sent Jibril to him, and God knows best. The distance between Madyan and Egypt was eight days, as related by Ibn Jubayr and others. The rule of Madyan belonged to someone other than Pharaoh.

There are twenty-four issues (masa'il, points of discussion) in it.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾. Musa, upon him be peace, walked until he arrived at the water of Madyan, meaning he reached it. His arriving at the water means he reached it, not that he entered it. The word "wurud" (arrival) may mean entering the thing arrived at, and it may mean overlooking it and reaching it without entering. So Musa's arrival at this water was by reaching it. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:
"When they came to the water, its surface blue, / they set down the staffs of the settled, who had pitched their tents."
[[The explanation of this verse was given earlier in the margin of vol. 11, p. 137, first or second edition.]]
These meanings were already mentioned in His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will come to it﴾. Madyan is not declined, since it is a well-known town. The poet said [[He is Jarir. Al-'usm (plural of a'sam) is a gazelle with white on its foreleg, or on its forelegs; al-fadir is the old one of them, and it was said: the large one. It is narrated as "from the peaks of the high mountains." Before it: "O mother of Talhah, we have not met the likes of you among those who travel the high lands, nor in the depths of the valley."]]:
"The monks of Madyan, had they seen you, would have come down, / and the white-footed gazelles from the high peaks, the old ones."
It was said: it is a tribe descended from Madyan ibn Ibrahim. The discussion of it has passed in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 247, first or second edition.]]. "Ummah" means a large crowd. "Yasqun" means their livestock. "Min dunihim" means to the side of the direction from which he came; he reached the two women before reaching the ummah. He found them holding back and restraining (tadhudani), meaning they were keeping (their flocks) back and detaining them. From this is his saying, upon him be peace: "Men will surely be driven away (fa-layudhadanna) from my pool." In some copies it is "fa-la tudhadhanna," meaning do not do anything that would cause you to be driven away from it. Ibn al-Athir said: the first is more apt. [[Fa-layudhadanna means "they will surely be driven away." It is also narrated as "fa-la tudhadhanna," meaning "do not do anything that causes you to be driven away." Ibn al-Athir said: the first is more apt.]] In some copies it is "two women holding back, restraining." It is said: dha'da yadhudu when he detained; and "dhudtu al-shay'" means I held the thing back. The poet said [[He is Suwayd ibn Kura', mentioning his refining of his poetry.]]:
"I spend the night at the gate of rhymes, as if / I were holding back with them a herd of wild beasts, startled."
That is: I detain and prevent. It was also said: "tadhudani" means they drive away. The poet said [[He is Jarir, satirizing al-Farazdaq.]]:
"The Banu Tamim have stolen your staff, / so you do not know with which staff to drive back."
That is: they drive away, hold back, and prevent. Ibn Salam said: they were preventing their sheep from mixing with the sheep of the people, so the object was omitted, either to keep it vague for the addressee, or because its knowledge was sufficient. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were holding their sheep back from the water out of fear of the strong herdsmen. Qatadah said: they were holding the people back from their sheep. Al-Nahhas said: the first is better, because after it comes: ﴿They said: We cannot water until the shepherds have driven their flocks away﴾. Had they been holding the people back from their sheep, they would not have informed him of the reason for delaying their watering until the shepherds had finished. When Musa, upon him be peace, saw that from them, ﴿he said: What is your business?﴾, meaning what is your matter. Ru'bah said:

Oh, what a matter! What is his affair and my affair? Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The use of the word "suʾāl" (asking) with "khatb" (affair) is only employed for one who is afflicted, or oppressed, or one who is to be pitied, or one who is involved in something reprehensible; it is as if the matter is entirely one of evil. So the two daughters informed him of their situation, and that their father was an aged old man. The meaning is: because of his weakness he cannot personally undertake the affair of his flock, and because of their own weakness and lack of strength the two of them cannot compete with the strong; their custom was to wait until the people had finished with the water and it had been cleared, and only then would they come to drink. Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "yaṣdura" from "ṣadara," which is the opposite of "warada," meaning the shepherds return. The rest read "yuṣdira" with a dammah on the yaʾ, from "aṣdara," meaning until they bring their livestock back from their watering place. "Ruʿāʾ" is the plural of "rāʿ," like "tājir" and "tijār," and "ṣāḥib" and "ṣiḥāb."

A group said: The wells were uncovered, and the crowding of the people prevented the two of them. When Musa wished to water for them, he pushed the people aside and overpowered them at the water until he had watered. It is because of this overpowering that he did that one of the two described him as strong. Another group said: The two of them used to follow the leftover of the people in the cisterns; if they found some remainder in the trough, that was their watering, and if there was no remainder in it, their flock would go thirsty. Musa felt pity for them, so he went to a well that was covered, while the people were drawing from other than it, and its stone could be lifted only by seven men, as related by Ibn Zayd. Ibn Jurayj said: ten. Ibn 'Abbas said: thirty. Al-Zajjaj said: forty. So he lifted it. He watered for the two women, and because of his lifting of the stone they described him as strong.

It was also said: Their well was one, and he lifted the stone from it after the drawers had separated, since the custom of the two women was to drink the leftovers. 'Amr ibn Maymun related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: When the shepherds had watered, they covered the well with a stone that only ten men could pull up. Musa came, pulled it up, and drew one bucket which needed nothing else, and he watered for them.

The second issue: If it is asked, how was it permissible for the Prophet of Allah, who was Shu'ayb ﷺ, to accept that his two daughters water the livestock? It is said to him: That is not forbidden, and religion does not reject it. As for manliness (murū'ah), people differ on it, customs vary regarding it, the conditions of the Arabs in this differ from those of the non-Arabs, and the way of the desert people is not the way of the settled people, especially when the situation is one of necessity.

The third issue: the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then he turned back to the shade﴾, to the shade of a samurah [[al-samurah: a small tree with small leaves and short thorns, having a yellow fruit which people eat.]], as said by Ibn Mas'ud. He alluded to asking for food with his words: ﴿Indeed, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾. He had not tasted food for seven days, and his belly had stuck to his back, so he alluded to supplication and did not explicitly ask. Thus all the exegetes related that in these words he sought what he might eat. "Khayr" may mean food, as in this verse; it may mean wealth, as He said: ﴿if he leaves behind wealth﴾ and His words: ﴿and indeed, he is intense in love of wealth﴾; it may mean strength, as He said: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾; and it may mean worship, as in the saying: ﴿And We inspired them to do good deeds﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Hunger had reached him, and his color had turned green from eating herbs, and he was the most honored of creation before Allah. It is related that he did not reach Madyan until the soles of his feet had worn away. In this there is a lesson and an indication of the lowliness of this world before Allah. Abu Bakr ibn Tahir said regarding His words "Indeed, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need": meaning, for whatever of Your bounty and wealth You send down, I am in need, that You enrich me with Yourself above all others. I say: What the exegetes mentioned is more fitting, for Allah enriched him only through Shu'ayb.

The fourth issue: the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then came to him one of the two, walking bashfully﴾. In this statement there is an abridgment indicated by this apparent text; Ibn Ishaq estimated it: they went quickly back to their father, though their custom was slowness in watering, and they told him what the man had done for them, so he commanded the elder of his two daughters – and it was said the younger – to call him for him. "So she came," as in this verse. 'Amr ibn Maymun said: She was not a bold woman among women, going out and coming in. It was said: She came veiling her face with the sleeve of her garment, as said by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. It is related that the name of one of them was Layya and the other Safuriyya, daughters of Yathrun, and Yathrun is Shu'ayb ʿalayhi al-salam. It was also said: he was the nephew of Shu'ayb, and that Shu'ayb had died. Most people hold that they were the daughters of Shu'ayb ʿalayhi al-salam, and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ as in Surat al-A'raf, and in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿The companions of the Thicket denied the messengers, when Shu'ayb said to them﴾. Qatadah said: Allah sent Shu'ayb to the companions of the Thicket and to the people of Madyan. The disagreement regarding the name of his father has already passed in al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 247, first or second edition.]]. It is related that when Musa ʿalayhi al-salam came to her with the message, he rose to follow her, and between Musa and her father was a distance of three miles. A wind blew and pressed her garment against her, describing her buttocks, so Musa was reluctant to look at her and said: Walk behind me and guide me to the path with your voice. It was also said: Musa said at the outset: Be behind me, for I am a Hebrew man who does not look at the backs of women, and guide me to the road, right or left. That is the reason for her describing him as trustworthy, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Musa reached the one who had summoned him, and related to him his whole affair from beginning to end, and he comforted him with his words: ﴿Fear not; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾. Madyan lay outside the kingdom of Pharaoh. He brought food near to him, and Musa said: I will not eat; we are a household that does not sell its religion for the filling of the earth with gold. Shu'ayb said: This is not the recompense for the watering, but it is my custom and the custom of my fathers to offer hospitality to guests and to feed people. Then Musa ate.

The fifth issue: the words of the Exalted: ﴿One of them said: O my father, hire him﴾. This is evidence that hiring (ijarah) was known and established among them, and likewise it was in every religious community; it is a necessity of human nature and a benefit of social dealing among people. It contradicts al-Asamm, who was deaf to its hearing.

The sixth issue: the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I wish to marry you﴾, the verse. In it is the guardian's offering of his daughter to a man, and this is an established practice. The righteous one of Madyan offered his daughter to the righteous one of the Children of Israel. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab offered his daughter Hafsah to Abu Bakr and 'Uthman, and a woman offered herself to the Prophet ﷺ. From this is the offering by a man of his ward, and of a woman herself to a righteous man, following the righteous predecessors. Ibn 'Umar said: When Hafsah was widowed, 'Umar said to 'Uthman: If you wish, I will marry you to Hafsah, daughter of 'Umar, and the hadith... al-Bukhari alone related it.

The seventh issue: In this verse is evidence that marriage rests with the guardian, and the woman has no right in it, for the righteous one of Madyan entrusted it to a guardian. This was the view of the jurists of the cities. Abu Hanifah disagreed on this, and it has already passed.

The eighth issue: This verse indicates that a father may marry off his virgin adult daughter without seeking her permission. Malik held this view and cited this verse as proof; it is a strong apparent evidence in the matter, and his citing it indicates that he relied on Israelite narratives, as has already passed. Al-Shafi'i and many scholars agreed with Malik's view on this question. Abu Hanifah said: When a young girl reaches maturity, no one may marry her except with her consent, because she has reached the limit of legal responsibility; but if she is young, he may marry her without her consent, because she has neither permission nor consent, without disagreement.

The ninth issue: The followers of al-Shafi'i used the words "Indeed, I wish to marry you" as proof that the marriage contract depends on the wording of "tazwij" and "inkah." This was also the view of Rabi'ah, Abu Thawr, Abu 'Ubayd, Dawud, and Malik according to one report from him. Our scholars said, according to the well-known view: the marriage is concluded with any wording. Abu Hanifah said: it is concluded with any wording that implies ownership in perpetuity. As for the Shafi'is, they have no proof in the verse, because it is the law of those before us, and they do not hold it to be a proof in anything according to the well-known view among them. As for Abu Hanifah and his companions, al-Thawri, and al-Hasan ibn Hayy, they said: The marriage is concluded with the wording of gift (hibah) and other words, if witnesses were present for it, because divorce takes effect with explicit and indirect wording. They said: Likewise marriage. They said: What was specific to the Prophet ﷺ is the exemption of the marriage from a dowry, not marriage with the wording of gift. Ibn al-Qasim followed them, saying: If he gives his daughter as a gift while intending to marry her off, I do not recall anything from Malik on this, and in my view it is permissible, like sale. Abu 'Umar said: The sound view is that a marriage is not concluded with the wording of gift, just as a gift of any property is not concluded with the wording of marriage. Also, marriage requires explicit wording so that testimony may be given on it, and it is the opposite of divorce, so how can it be analogized to it? They are agreed that marriage is not concluded by saying "I permit you" or "I make lawful for you," and likewise gift. The Prophet ﷺ said: "You have made their private parts lawful by the word of Allah," meaning the Qur'an, and there is no marriage contract in the Qur'an with the wording of gift; rather it contains "tazwij" and "nikah." Permitting marriage with the wording of gift involves annulling part of the particularity of the Prophet ﷺ.

The tenth issue: The words of the Exalted: ﴿One of these two daughters of mine﴾ indicate that this is an offer and not a contract, because if it were a contract he would have specified the one contracted to him. Although scholars differed on the permissibility of sale when one says, "I sell you one of these two slaves of mine for such and such a price," they agreed that this is not permissible in marriage, because it is an option, and no part of options attaches to marriage.

The eleventh issue: Makki said: In this verse are peculiarities of marriage: among them, he did not specify the wife, nor did he set the limit of the term; he made the dowry a hire, and he went in (to her) without paying anything.

I say: These are four issues contained in the eleventh issue. The first of the four issues: Our scholars said: As for the specification, it seems that it occurred in the second stage of the negotiation, and he first presented the matter in general terms, then specified afterward. And it has been said that he...

He married her to him, Safuriyya, and she was the younger one. It is narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "If you are asked which of the two terms Musa fulfilled, say: the better and the more complete of them. And if you are asked which of the two women he married, say: the younger, the one who came walking behind him, and who said: ﴿O my father, hire him. Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾." It has been said: the wisdom in his marrying the younger before the elder, although the elder was more in need of a man, is that he anticipated that he would incline towards her, for he had seen her during his meeting with them and had walked along with her as they approached their father. Had he offered him the elder, he might have shown him a preference while secretly desiring the other. It has been said otherwise, and Allah knows best. In some reports it is related that he married the elder, as recounted by al-Qushayri.

The second issue: as for the mention of the beginning of the term, there is nothing in the verse that requires its omission; rather it is left unmentioned. Either it was agreed upon, or else it begins from the time of the contract.

The third issue: as for marriage through hiring (ijara), it is evident from the verse, and it is a matter that our Law (shar') has established. It also occurred in the hadith of the man who had nothing except some of the Qur'an, which the Imams narrated. In some of its chains: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "What do you memorize of the Qur'an?" He said: "Surat al-Baqara and the one that follows it." He said: "Teach them to her as her mahr, twenty verses, and she is your wife." The scholars differed on this question in three opinions. Malik disliked it, Ibn al-Qasim prohibited it, and Ibn Habib permitted it, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i and his companions. They said: it is permissible for a free person's benefit (manfa'a) to serve as the dower, such as tailoring, building, and teaching the Qur'an. Abu Hanifa said: it is not valid, and he permitted that one marry her by having him serve her with his slave for a year, or house her in his dwelling for a year, because a slave and a house are property, whereas his own service is not property. Abu al-Hasan al-Karkhi said: the marriage contract using the wording of hiring (ijara) is permissible, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿So give them their wages (ujur)﴾. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: it is not valid, because hiring is a time-limited contract, while marriage is perpetual, so the two are contradictory. Ibn al-Qasim said: it is annulled before consummation and is confirmed after it.

Asbagh said: if he has paid something with him, there is disagreement; and if he has not paid, it is more severe. If it is left, it stands in every case, based on the story of Shu'ayb. This was said by Malik, Ibn al-Mawwaz and Ashhab. A group of later and earlier scholars relied on this verse concerning this case. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: this verse includes marriage on the basis of hiring, and the contract is valid, but it is disliked to make the hiring the mahr, and the mahr should be property, as the Exalted said: ﴿that you seek with your wealth, chaste (muhsinin)﴾. This is the view of all our companions.

The fourth issue: as for his words, "and he entered (upon her) and did not pay," people have differed over this: did he enter at the time of the contract or when he traveled? If it was at the contract, then what did he pay? Our scholars have prohibited entering until he pays, even a quarter of a dinar. Ibn al-Qasim said: if he entered before paying, it stands, because the later of our companions said: hastening the dower or some of it is recommended; and on the basis that if the dower was the herding of sheep, then he had already paid by starting the service. If he entered when he traveled, then prolonged waiting in marriage is permissible if it is for the whole lifetime without a condition. [As for if it is with a condition [addition from Ibn al-Arabi's Ahkam al-Quran], it is not permissible unless the purpose is sound, such as preparing for the building or awaiting the wife's readiness to be entered upon if she is young; our scholars explicitly stated this.

The twelfth issue: in this verse there is the combination of hiring and marriage, and our scholars differed on this in three opinions. The first: Abu Zayd said in his Thamaniyya: it is disliked from the outset, but if it occurs, it stands. The second: Malik and Ibn al-Qasim, in the well-known view, said: it is not permissible, and it is annulled before and after consummation, because their purposes differ, like all dissimilar contracts. The third: Ashhab and Asbagh permitted it. Ibn al-Arabi said: this is the correct view, and the verse indicates it. Malik has said that marriage is most like sales, so what is the difference between hiring and sale, or between sale and marriage?

Branch: if he gives her as dower the teaching of permissible poetry, it is valid. Al-Muzani said: such as the words of the poet:
"The servant says: my gain and my wealth... and fear of Allah is the best of what is gained."
If he gives her as dower the teaching of poetry containing satire or obscenity, it is like if he had given her wine or swine as dower.

The thirteenth issue concerns His words, exalted is He: ﴿on condition that you serve me for eight years﴾. The mention of the service was unspecified. Malik said that it is permissible and is understood according to custom (al-'urf), so the service does not need to be specified. This is the apparent meaning of the story of Musa, since he mentioned a general hiring arrangement. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said that it is not permissible unless the service is specified, because it is unknown. Al-Bukhari gave a chapter heading: "Chapter: On one who hires a laborer, specifying the term for him but not specifying the work," citing the words of Allah, ﴿that you serve me for eight years﴾. Al-Muhallab said: "It is not as he titled it, because the work was known among them. It was watering, tilling, herding and similar work of the desert, in the trade of its people. This is customary, even if the specific tasks and their amounts are not stated, such as saying to him, 'You will till such-and-such during the year and herd such-and-such during the year.' This is only according to what is customary in desert service. What is not permissible according to all is that the term be unknown and the work be unknown and not customary; that is not permissible until it is known." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "The scholars of tafsir have mentioned that he specified for him the herding of sheep, but this is not transmitted through a sound chain. However, they said that Salih of Madyan had no work except herding sheep, so what was known of his circumstances stood in place of specifying the service in it."

The fourteenth issue: The scholars agreed that it is permissible to hire a shepherd for known months, at a known wage, to tend a counted number of sheep. If the sheep are counted and specific, our scholars differ in detail. Ibn al-Qasim said: "It is not permissible unless he stipulates a replacement if they die." This is a very weak narration. Salih of Madyan hired Musa to tend his sheep, and he had seen them, yet he did not stipulate a replacement. If the sheep are unspecified, neither named nor particular, it is permissible according to our scholars. Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i said: "It is not permissible because of its uncertainty." Our scholars relied on custom, as we mentioned just above, and that he is given according to what his strength can bear. Some of our scholars added that it is not permissible unless the employer knows the extent of the worker's strength. This is correct, for Salih of Madyan knew the extent of Musa's strength by his lifting of the stone.

The fifteenth issue: Malik said: "The shepherd is not liable for compensation, and he is believed regarding what perishes or is stolen, because he is a trustee, like an agent."

Al-Bukhari gave a chapter heading: "Chapter: If the shepherd or the agent sees a sheep dying or something spoiling, and he rectifies what he fears will spoil." He related the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik, from his father, that they had sheep grazing at Sal' [[Sal': a mountain in Madinah.]]. A slave girl of ours saw a sheep of our flock about to die, so she broke a stone and slaughtered it with it. He said to them, "Do not eat until I ask the Prophet (ﷺ)," or "I will send someone to the Prophet (ﷺ) to ask him." He asked the Prophet (ﷺ), or sent someone to him, and he ordered them to eat it. Abdullah said: "It pleases me that she was a slave girl and that she slaughtered it." Al-Muhallab said: "In it is jurisprudence that the shepherd and the agent are believed regarding what they are entrusted with, until signs of betrayal or lying appear in them. This is the view of Malik and a group of scholars." Ibn al-Qasim said: "If he feared death for a sheep and slaughtered it, he is not liable, and he is believed if he brings it slaughtered. Another said: he is liable until he explains what he said."

The sixteenth issue: Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab differed regarding a shepherd who mated female livestock without the permission of their owners, and they died. Ibn al-Qasim said: "There is no liability on him, because mating is part of preserving and increasing the property." Ashhab said: "He is liable." Ibn al-Qasim's view is more fitting, by the evidence of the hadith of Ka'b. He is not liable for what perishes through his diligent effort, if he is of good character and known for his care of the property. But if he is of wicked and corrupt character, and the owner of the property wishes to make him liable, he may do so, because he is not believed that he saw death in the sheep, given what is known of his wickedness.

The seventeenth issue: What Musa's wage was has not been transmitted. However, Yahya ibn Sallam related that Salih of Madyan made for Musa every young lamb born of a color different from its mother's. Then Allah revealed to Musa, "Cast your staff among them," and they all bore young unlike their kind. Someone other than Yahya said: Rather, he made for him every spotted one born to him, and all of them were born spotted.

Al-Qushayri mentioned that when Shu'ayb hired Musa, he said to him, "Enter such-and-such a house and take a staff from the staves that are in the house." Musa brought out a staff. Adam had brought it out of Paradise, and the prophets inherited it until it came to Shu'ayb. Shu'ayb commanded him to put it back in the house and take another staff. He entered and brought out that same staff. He did this seven times, and each time it did not come into his hand except that one. Shu'ayb knew that he had a matter. In the morning he said to him, "Drive the sheep to the fork of the road. Take the right side, where there is not much grass, and do not take the left, for there is much grass there and a great serpent that does not accept livestock." He drove the livestock to the fork of the road, and they turned toward the left, and he could not control them. Musa slept, and the serpent came out. The staff stood up, its two branches became iron, and it fought the serpent until it killed it, and then it returned to Musa, peace be upon him. When Musa woke up, he saw the staff stained with blood and the serpent slain. He returned to Shu'ayb in the evening. Shu'ayb was blind, so he touched the sheep and found the signs of abundance upon them. He asked him about the story, and he told him. Shu'ayb rejoiced and said, "Every young one these livestock bear this year that is spotted in two colors (qālib lawn, i.e., of two colors), it is yours." All the young of that year came out two-colored, and Shu'ayb knew that Musa had a high station with Allah.

Uyayna ibn Hisn related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Musa hired himself out for the satisfying of his stomach and the chastity of his private parts." Shu'ayb said to him, "You will have from them (i.e., from the offspring of his sheep) whatever comes of them, spotted in color, with none that is barren, none that is shrunken-udder, none that is kamūsh, none that is ḍabūb, and none that is tha'ūl."

Al-Harawi said: "The 'azūz is the barren one, derived from 'izāz, which is hard ground, and the sheep has become 'azza (hard). The fashūsh is one whose milk flows out without milking, because of the width of the urethra. Similar to it are the fatūḥ and the thārūr. Among their proverbs: 'I will deflate you as one deflates a waterskin' (la-afushshannaka fashsh al-waṭb), meaning, I will expel your anger and pride from your head. It is said: fashsh al-siqā' when he expelled the wind from it. From this is the hadith: 'Shaytan blows between the buttocks of one of you until he imagines that he has broken wind,' meaning he blows a faint blow. The kamūsh is the one with a small udder, and it is also the kamīsha; it was so named because its udder shrinks (tuqallus), and from this is said: a man with a narrow waistwrap (kamīsh al-izār). The kashūd is like the kamūsh. The ḍabūb is the one whose urethra is narrow. The ḍabb is milking with strong squeezing. The tha'ūl is the sheep that has an extra teat, and the tha'l is an extra tooth, and that extra one is called the rā'ūl. A man is athal (having an extra teat). The tha'l is the narrowness of the place where milk comes out."

Al-Harawi said: "The explanation of qālib lawn in the hadith is that they came out in colors other than their mothers' colors."

The eighteenth issue: Hiring for an unknown consideration is not permissible, for the birthing of sheep is not known. There are fertile lands where the birthing of sheep, its number, and the soundness of its lambs are known with certainty, such as the lands of Egypt and others. Nevertheless, this is not permissible in our law, because the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade gharar (uncertain transaction), and he forbade the *maḍāmīn* and the *malāqīḥ*. The *maḍāmīn* are what is in the wombs of females, and the *malāqīḥ* are what is in the loins of stallions. Contrary to this, the poet said:

*Mulqūḥa fī baṭni nābin ḥāmil*
(Impregnated in the belly of a pregnant she-camel)

Al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, on Surah 28, verses 23–28 (part 5 of 5):

The explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-Hijr [See vol. 10, p. 17 ff., first or second edition.]. Rashid ibn Ma'mar permitted hiring someone to tend sheep for a third or a quarter of them. Ibn Sirin and 'Ata' said: a person may weave a garment in exchange for a share of it. Ahmad also held this view.

The nineteenth issue: *kafa'ah* (equality between spouses) is taken into account in marriage. The scholars differed over whether it concerns religion, wealth and lineage, or only some of these. The sound view is that it is permissible for a *mawla* (a freed slave or non-Arab convert) to marry Arab women and Qurayshi women, based on the Almighty's words: ﴿Indeed, the most honourable of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you﴾. Moses came to Shu'ayb (the righteous man) of Madyan as a stranger, an outcast, fearful, alone, hungry and naked. Shu'ayb married him to his daughter once he had ascertained Moses' religion and seen his condition, and he disregarded everything else. This issue has already been treated comprehensively, praise be to God.

The twentieth issue: Some have said that what took place from Shu'ayb was not a mention of the woman's *mahr* (dower). Rather, it was a condition he set for himself, in line with the custom of the Bedouin Arabs, who stipulate the bride-price of their daughters and say, "for me, personally, such and such." The dower was left unspecified (*tafwid*), and marriage by *tafwid* is permissible.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: What the Bedouin do is *hulwan* (a payment to the bride's family) and an addition to the dower. It is forbidden and unfitting for prophets. As for when the guardian stipulates something for himself, the scholars have differed over whether something that the husband takes out of his hand and that does not enter the woman's hand is permissible, on two views. One: it is permissible. The other: it is not permissible. What is sound to me is the following division. A woman is either a virgin (*bikr*) or a previously married woman (*thayyib*). If she is a previously married woman, it is permissible, because her marriage is in her own hand, and the guardian only carries out the contract. Taking a fee for this is no obstacle, just as an agent takes a fee for a sale contract. If she is a virgin, the contract is in the guardian's hand, and the payment would be, as it were, a consideration in the marriage paid to someone other than the husband. That is invalid. If it occurs, the marriage is annulled before consummation, and after consummation it stands according to the well-known report. Praise be to God.

The twenty-first issue: When he mentioned the condition and followed it with the voluntary act (of completing ten years), each of the two was given its own ruling. The one did not join the other, and the obligation and the voluntary act were not combined. For this reason, in contracts, the agreed conditions are written first, and then it is said, "and he volunteered such and such." The condition takes its course, and the voluntary act takes its own ruling. The obligatory is separated from the voluntary. It has been said that the wording of Shu'ayb is good in the wording of marriage contracts: "I married her to him" is preferable to "I married him to her," as will be explained in *al-Ahzab* (Surah 33). Shu'ayb made the eight years a condition and left the tenth year to chivalry (*muruwwah*).

The twenty-second issue: God's words: ﴿He said, "That is between me and you. Whichever of the two terms I fulfil, there shall be no transgression against me."﴾ When Shu'ayb finished speaking, Moses, peace be upon him, confirmed it and repeated its meaning as a reinforcement, to make certain that the condition was made for eight years. *Ayyama* is an interrogative in the accusative governed by *qadaytu* ("I fulfilled"). *Al-ajalayn* ("the two terms") is in the genitive, being the object of the addition of *ayy* to them. *Ma* is an extra particle for emphasis, carrying the sense of a conditional, and its answer is ﴿there shall be no transgression﴾. *'Udwan* is accusative, governed by *la* (negation).

Ibn Kaysan said: *ma* is in the genitive position, since *ayy* is added to it, and it is indefinite. *Al-ajalayn* is in apposition to it. Likewise is His words, ﴿So by a mercy from God﴾, where *rahmah* ("mercy") is in apposition to *ma*. Makki said: Ibn Kaysan was careful not to make anything superfluous in the Qur'an, and he sought a way to explain it that removed it from being superfluous.

Al-Hasan recited *ayma* with the *ya'* sukun. Ibn Mas'ud recited, ﴿Which of the two terms, whichever I fulfilled﴾. The majority recited *'udwan* with a *damma* on the *'ayn*. Abu Haywa recited it with a *kasra*. The meaning is: there shall be no liability on me, and no demand for more than that. *'Udwan* is exceeding the limit in what is not obligatory. *Hijaj* means years. The poet said:

*To whom do the dwellings belong at the summit of al-Hijr,*
*worn away by years and by ages?*

The singular is *hijjah*, with a *kasra* on the *ha'*.

﴿And God is Witness over what we say.﴾ It was said: this is from the words of Moses. It was also said: it is from the words of the woman's father. The two righteous men, may God's blessings be upon them both, were content to call God as witness between them and did not call any creature as witness. The scholars have differed over whether witnessing is obligatory in marriage. The twenty-third issue: there are two views. One: the marriage is not concluded except with two witnesses. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i. Malik said: it is concluded without witnesses, because it is a contract of exchange, so witnessing is not a requirement for it. What is required is public announcement and clarity. The difference between marriage and fornication (*sifah*) is the *duff* (tambourine). This issue has already been treated fully in *al-Baqarah* [See vol. 3, p. 79 ff., first or second edition.].

In Bukhari, from Abu Hurayra: a man from the Children of Israel asked another of the Children of Israel to lend him a thousand dinars. He said, "Bring me witnesses, and I will have them witness it." He said, "God suffices as a witness." He said, "Bring me a guarantor." He said, "God suffices as a guarantor." He said, "You have spoken the truth," and he handed him the money. And he mentioned the hadith.

There are twenty-four issues (masa'il, points of discussion) in it.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾. Musa, upon him be peace, walked until he arrived at the water of Madyan, meaning he reached it. His arriving at the water means he reached it, not that he entered it. The word "wurud" (arrival) may mean entering the thing arrived at, and it may mean overlooking it and reaching it without entering. So Musa's arrival at this water was by reaching it. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:
"When they came to the water, its surface blue, / they set down the staffs of the settled, who had pitched their tents."
[[The explanation of this verse was given earlier in the margin of vol. 11, p. 137, first or second edition.]]
These meanings were already mentioned in His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will come to it﴾. Madyan is not declined, since it is a well-known town. The poet said [[He is Jarir. Al-'usm (plural of a'sam) is a gazelle with white on its foreleg, or on its forelegs; al-fadir is the old one of them, and it was said: the large one. It is narrated as "from the peaks of the high mountains." Before it: "O mother of Talhah, we have not met the likes of you among those who travel the high lands, nor in the depths of the valley."]]:
"The monks of Madyan, had they seen you, would have come down, / and the white-footed gazelles from the high peaks, the old ones."
It was said: it is a tribe descended from Madyan ibn Ibrahim. The discussion of it has passed in "al-A'raf" [[See vol. 7, p. 247, first or second edition.]]. "Ummah" means a large crowd. "Yasqun" means their livestock. "Min dunihim" means to the side of the direction from which he came; he reached the two women before reaching the ummah. He found them holding back and restraining (tadhudani), meaning they were keeping (their flocks) back and detaining them. From this is his saying, upon him be peace: "Men will surely be driven away (fa-layudhadanna) from my pool." In some copies it is "fa-la tudhadhanna," meaning do not do anything that would cause you to be driven away from it. Ibn al-Athir said: the first is more apt. [[Fa-layudhadanna means "they will surely be driven away." It is also narrated as "fa-la tudhadhanna," meaning "do not do anything that causes you to be driven away." Ibn al-Athir said: the first is more apt.]] In some copies it is "two women holding back, restraining." It is said: dha'da yadhudu when he detained; and "dhudtu al-shay'" means I held the thing back. The poet said [[He is Suwayd ibn Kura', mentioning his refining of his poetry.]]:
"I spend the night at the gate of rhymes, as if / I were holding back with them a herd of wild beasts, startled."
That is: I detain and prevent. It was also said: "tadhudani" means they drive away. The poet said [[He is Jarir, satirizing al-Farazdaq.]]:
"The Banu Tamim have stolen your staff, / so you do not know with which staff to drive back."
That is: they drive away, hold back, and prevent. Ibn Salam said: they were preventing their sheep from mixing with the sheep of the people, so the object was omitted, either to keep it vague for the addressee, or because its knowledge was sufficient. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were holding their sheep back from the water out of fear of the strong herdsmen. Qatadah said: they were holding the people back from their sheep. Al-Nahhas said: the first is better, because after it comes: ﴿They said: We cannot water until the shepherds have driven their flocks away﴾. Had they been holding the people back from their sheep, they would not have informed him of the reason for delaying their watering until the shepherds had finished. When Musa, upon him be peace, saw that from them, ﴿he said: What is your business?﴾, meaning what is your matter. Ru'bah said:

Oh, what a matter! What is his affair and my affair? Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The use of the word "suʾāl" (asking) with "khatb" (affair) is only employed for one who is afflicted, or oppressed, or one who is to be pitied, or one who is involved in something reprehensible; it is as if the matter is entirely one of evil. So the two daughters informed him of their situation, and that their father was an aged old man. The meaning is: because of his weakness he cannot personally undertake the affair of his flock, and because of their own weakness and lack of strength the two of them cannot compete with the strong; their custom was to wait until the people had finished with the water and it had been cleared, and only then would they come to drink. Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "yaṣdura" from "ṣadara," which is the opposite of "warada," meaning the shepherds return. The rest read "yuṣdira" with a dammah on the yaʾ, from "aṣdara," meaning until they bring their livestock back from their watering place. "Ruʿāʾ" is the plural of "rāʿ," like "tājir" and "tijār," and "ṣāḥib" and "ṣiḥāb."

A group said: The wells were uncovered, and the crowding of the people prevented the two of them. When Musa wished to water for them, he pushed the people aside and overpowered them at the water until he had watered. It is because of this overpowering that he did that one of the two described him as strong. Another group said: The two of them used to follow the leftover of the people in the cisterns; if they found some remainder in the trough, that was their watering, and if there was no remainder in it, their flock would go thirsty. Musa felt pity for them, so he went to a well that was covered, while the people were drawing from other than it, and its stone could be lifted only by seven men, as related by Ibn Zayd. Ibn Jurayj said: ten. Ibn 'Abbas said: thirty. Al-Zajjaj said: forty. So he lifted it. He watered for the two women, and because of his lifting of the stone they described him as strong.

It was also said: Their well was one, and he lifted the stone from it after the drawers had separated, since the custom of the two women was to drink the leftovers. 'Amr ibn Maymun related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: When the shepherds had watered, they covered the well with a stone that only ten men could pull up. Musa came, pulled it up, and drew one bucket which needed nothing else, and he watered for them.

The second issue: If it is asked, how was it permissible for the Prophet of Allah, who was Shu'ayb ﷺ, to accept that his two daughters water the livestock? It is said to him: That is not forbidden, and religion does not reject it. As for manliness (murū'ah), people differ on it, customs vary regarding it, the conditions of the Arabs in this differ from those of the non-Arabs, and the way of the desert people is not the way of the settled people, especially when the situation is one of necessity.

The third issue: the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then he turned back to the shade﴾, to the shade of a samurah [[al-samurah: a small tree with small leaves and short thorns, having a yellow fruit which people eat.]], as said by Ibn Mas'ud. He alluded to asking for food with his words: ﴿Indeed, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾. He had not tasted food for seven days, and his belly had stuck to his back, so he alluded to supplication and did not explicitly ask. Thus all the exegetes related that in these words he sought what he might eat. "Khayr" may mean food, as in this verse; it may mean wealth, as He said: ﴿if he leaves behind wealth﴾ and His words: ﴿and indeed, he is intense in love of wealth﴾; it may mean strength, as He said: ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾; and it may mean worship, as in the saying: ﴿And We inspired them to do good deeds﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Hunger had reached him, and his color had turned green from eating herbs, and he was the most honored of creation before Allah. It is related that he did not reach Madyan until the soles of his feet had worn away. In this there is a lesson and an indication of the lowliness of this world before Allah. Abu Bakr ibn Tahir said regarding His words "Indeed, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need": meaning, for whatever of Your bounty and wealth You send down, I am in need, that You enrich me with Yourself above all others. I say: What the exegetes mentioned is more fitting, for Allah enriched him only through Shu'ayb.

The fourth issue: the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then came to him one of the two, walking bashfully﴾. In this statement there is an abridgment indicated by this apparent text; Ibn Ishaq estimated it: they went quickly back to their father, though their custom was slowness in watering, and they told him what the man had done for them, so he commanded the elder of his two daughters – and it was said the younger – to call him for him. "So she came," as in this verse. 'Amr ibn Maymun said: She was not a bold woman among women, going out and coming in. It was said: She came veiling her face with the sleeve of her garment, as said by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. It is related that the name of one of them was Layya and the other Safuriyya, daughters of Yathrun, and Yathrun is Shu'ayb ʿalayhi al-salam. It was also said: he was the nephew of Shu'ayb, and that Shu'ayb had died. Most people hold that they were the daughters of Shu'ayb ʿalayhi al-salam, and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ as in Surat al-A'raf, and in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿The companions of the Thicket denied the messengers, when Shu'ayb said to them﴾. Qatadah said: Allah sent Shu'ayb to the companions of the Thicket and to the people of Madyan. The disagreement regarding the name of his father has already passed in al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 247, first or second edition.]]. It is related that when Musa ʿalayhi al-salam came to her with the message, he rose to follow her, and between Musa and her father was a distance of three miles. A wind blew and pressed her garment against her, describing her buttocks, so Musa was reluctant to look at her and said: Walk behind me and guide me to the path with your voice. It was also said: Musa said at the outset: Be behind me, for I am a Hebrew man who does not look at the backs of women, and guide me to the road, right or left. That is the reason for her describing him as trustworthy, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Musa reached the one who had summoned him, and related to him his whole affair from beginning to end, and he comforted him with his words: ﴿Fear not; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾. Madyan lay outside the kingdom of Pharaoh. He brought food near to him, and Musa said: I will not eat; we are a household that does not sell its religion for the filling of the earth with gold. Shu'ayb said: This is not the recompense for the watering, but it is my custom and the custom of my fathers to offer hospitality to guests and to feed people. Then Musa ate.

The fifth issue: the words of the Exalted: ﴿One of them said: O my father, hire him﴾. This is evidence that hiring (ijarah) was known and established among them, and likewise it was in every religious community; it is a necessity of human nature and a benefit of social dealing among people. It contradicts al-Asamm, who was deaf to its hearing.

The sixth issue: the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I wish to marry you﴾, the verse. In it is the guardian's offering of his daughter to a man, and this is an established practice. The righteous one of Madyan offered his daughter to the righteous one of the Children of Israel. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab offered his daughter Hafsah to Abu Bakr and 'Uthman, and a woman offered herself to the Prophet ﷺ. From this is the offering by a man of his ward, and of a woman herself to a righteous man, following the righteous predecessors. Ibn 'Umar said: When Hafsah was widowed, 'Umar said to 'Uthman: If you wish, I will marry you to Hafsah, daughter of 'Umar, and the hadith... al-Bukhari alone related it.
