The sixteenth issue: Ibn al-Qasim and Ashhab differed regarding a shepherd who mated female livestock without the permission of their owners, and they died. Ibn al-Qasim said: "There is no liability on him, because mating is part of preserving and increasing the property." Ashhab said: "He is liable." Ibn al-Qasim's view is more fitting, by the evidence of the hadith of Ka'b. He is not liable for what perishes through his diligent effort, if he is of good character and known for his care of the property. But if he is of wicked and corrupt character, and the owner of the property wishes to make him liable, he may do so, because he is not believed that he saw death in the sheep, given what is known of his wickedness.

The seventeenth issue: What Musa's wage was has not been transmitted. However, Yahya ibn Sallam related that Salih of Madyan made for Musa every young lamb born of a color different from its mother's. Then Allah revealed to Musa, "Cast your staff among them," and they all bore young unlike their kind. Someone other than Yahya said: Rather, he made for him every spotted one born to him, and all of them were born spotted.

Al-Qushayri mentioned that when Shu'ayb hired Musa, he said to him, "Enter such-and-such a house and take a staff from the staves that are in the house." Musa brought out a staff. Adam had brought it out of Paradise, and the prophets inherited it until it came to Shu'ayb. Shu'ayb commanded him to put it back in the house and take another staff. He entered and brought out that same staff. He did this seven times, and each time it did not come into his hand except that one. Shu'ayb knew that he had a matter. In the morning he said to him, "Drive the sheep to the fork of the road. Take the right side, where there is not much grass, and do not take the left, for there is much grass there and a great serpent that does not accept livestock." He drove the livestock to the fork of the road, and they turned toward the left, and he could not control them. Musa slept, and the serpent came out. The staff stood up, its two branches became iron, and it fought the serpent until it killed it, and then it returned to Musa, peace be upon him. When Musa woke up, he saw the staff stained with blood and the serpent slain. He returned to Shu'ayb in the evening. Shu'ayb was blind, so he touched the sheep and found the signs of abundance upon them. He asked him about the story, and he told him. Shu'ayb rejoiced and said, "Every young one these livestock bear this year that is spotted in two colors (qālib lawn, i.e., of two colors), it is yours." All the young of that year came out two-colored, and Shu'ayb knew that Musa had a high station with Allah.

Uyayna ibn Hisn related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Musa hired himself out for the satisfying of his stomach and the chastity of his private parts." Shu'ayb said to him, "You will have from them (i.e., from the offspring of his sheep) whatever comes of them, spotted in color, with none that is barren, none that is shrunken-udder, none that is kamūsh, none that is ḍabūb, and none that is tha'ūl."

Al-Harawi said: "The 'azūz is the barren one, derived from 'izāz, which is hard ground, and the sheep has become 'azza (hard). The fashūsh is one whose milk flows out without milking, because of the width of the urethra. Similar to it are the fatūḥ and the thārūr. Among their proverbs: 'I will deflate you as one deflates a waterskin' (la-afushshannaka fashsh al-waṭb), meaning, I will expel your anger and pride from your head. It is said: fashsh al-siqā' when he expelled the wind from it. From this is the hadith: 'Shaytan blows between the buttocks of one of you until he imagines that he has broken wind,' meaning he blows a faint blow. The kamūsh is the one with a small udder, and it is also the kamīsha; it was so named because its udder shrinks (tuqallus), and from this is said: a man with a narrow waistwrap (kamīsh al-izār). The kashūd is like the kamūsh. The ḍabūb is the one whose urethra is narrow. The ḍabb is milking with strong squeezing. The tha'ūl is the sheep that has an extra teat, and the tha'l is an extra tooth, and that extra one is called the rā'ūl. A man is athal (having an extra teat). The tha'l is the narrowness of the place where milk comes out."

Al-Harawi said: "The explanation of qālib lawn in the hadith is that they came out in colors other than their mothers' colors."

The eighteenth issue: Hiring for an unknown consideration is not permissible, for the birthing of sheep is not known. There are fertile lands where the birthing of sheep, its number, and the soundness of its lambs are known with certainty, such as the lands of Egypt and others. Nevertheless, this is not permissible in our law, because the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade gharar (uncertain transaction), and he forbade the *maḍāmīn* and the *malāqīḥ*. The *maḍāmīn* are what is in the wombs of females, and the *malāqīḥ* are what is in the loins of stallions. Contrary to this, the poet said:

*Mulqūḥa fī baṭni nābin ḥāmil*
(Impregnated in the belly of a pregnant she-camel)

Al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, on Surah 28, verses 23–28 (part 5 of 5):

The explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-Hijr [See vol. 10, p. 17 ff., first or second edition.]. Rashid ibn Ma'mar permitted hiring someone to tend sheep for a third or a quarter of them. Ibn Sirin and 'Ata' said: a person may weave a garment in exchange for a share of it. Ahmad also held this view.

The nineteenth issue: *kafa'ah* (equality between spouses) is taken into account in marriage. The scholars differed over whether it concerns religion, wealth and lineage, or only some of these. The sound view is that it is permissible for a *mawla* (a freed slave or non-Arab convert) to marry Arab women and Qurayshi women, based on the Almighty's words: ﴿Indeed, the most honourable of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you﴾. Moses came to Shu'ayb (the righteous man) of Madyan as a stranger, an outcast, fearful, alone, hungry and naked. Shu'ayb married him to his daughter once he had ascertained Moses' religion and seen his condition, and he disregarded everything else. This issue has already been treated comprehensively, praise be to God.

The twentieth issue: Some have said that what took place from Shu'ayb was not a mention of the woman's *mahr* (dower). Rather, it was a condition he set for himself, in line with the custom of the Bedouin Arabs, who stipulate the bride-price of their daughters and say, "for me, personally, such and such." The dower was left unspecified (*tafwid*), and marriage by *tafwid* is permissible.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: What the Bedouin do is *hulwan* (a payment to the bride's family) and an addition to the dower. It is forbidden and unfitting for prophets. As for when the guardian stipulates something for himself, the scholars have differed over whether something that the husband takes out of his hand and that does not enter the woman's hand is permissible, on two views. One: it is permissible. The other: it is not permissible. What is sound to me is the following division. A woman is either a virgin (*bikr*) or a previously married woman (*thayyib*). If she is a previously married woman, it is permissible, because her marriage is in her own hand, and the guardian only carries out the contract. Taking a fee for this is no obstacle, just as an agent takes a fee for a sale contract. If she is a virgin, the contract is in the guardian's hand, and the payment would be, as it were, a consideration in the marriage paid to someone other than the husband. That is invalid. If it occurs, the marriage is annulled before consummation, and after consummation it stands according to the well-known report. Praise be to God.

The twenty-first issue: When he mentioned the condition and followed it with the voluntary act (of completing ten years), each of the two was given its own ruling. The one did not join the other, and the obligation and the voluntary act were not combined. For this reason, in contracts, the agreed conditions are written first, and then it is said, "and he volunteered such and such." The condition takes its course, and the voluntary act takes its own ruling. The obligatory is separated from the voluntary. It has been said that the wording of Shu'ayb is good in the wording of marriage contracts: "I married her to him" is preferable to "I married him to her," as will be explained in *al-Ahzab* (Surah 33). Shu'ayb made the eight years a condition and left the tenth year to chivalry (*muruwwah*).

The twenty-second issue: God's words: ﴿He said, "That is between me and you. Whichever of the two terms I fulfil, there shall be no transgression against me."﴾ When Shu'ayb finished speaking, Moses, peace be upon him, confirmed it and repeated its meaning as a reinforcement, to make certain that the condition was made for eight years. *Ayyama* is an interrogative in the accusative governed by *qadaytu* ("I fulfilled"). *Al-ajalayn* ("the two terms") is in the genitive, being the object of the addition of *ayy* to them. *Ma* is an extra particle for emphasis, carrying the sense of a conditional, and its answer is ﴿there shall be no transgression﴾. *'Udwan* is accusative, governed by *la* (negation).

Ibn Kaysan said: *ma* is in the genitive position, since *ayy* is added to it, and it is indefinite. *Al-ajalayn* is in apposition to it. Likewise is His words, ﴿So by a mercy from God﴾, where *rahmah* ("mercy") is in apposition to *ma*. Makki said: Ibn Kaysan was careful not to make anything superfluous in the Qur'an, and he sought a way to explain it that removed it from being superfluous.

Al-Hasan recited *ayma* with the *ya'* sukun. Ibn Mas'ud recited, ﴿Which of the two terms, whichever I fulfilled﴾. The majority recited *'udwan* with a *damma* on the *'ayn*. Abu Haywa recited it with a *kasra*. The meaning is: there shall be no liability on me, and no demand for more than that. *'Udwan* is exceeding the limit in what is not obligatory. *Hijaj* means years. The poet said:

*To whom do the dwellings belong at the summit of al-Hijr,*
*worn away by years and by ages?*

The singular is *hijjah*, with a *kasra* on the *ha'*.

﴿And God is Witness over what we say.﴾ It was said: this is from the words of Moses. It was also said: it is from the words of the woman's father. The two righteous men, may God's blessings be upon them both, were content to call God as witness between them and did not call any creature as witness. The scholars have differed over whether witnessing is obligatory in marriage. The twenty-third issue: there are two views. One: the marriage is not concluded except with two witnesses. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i. Malik said: it is concluded without witnesses, because it is a contract of exchange, so witnessing is not a requirement for it. What is required is public announcement and clarity. The difference between marriage and fornication (*sifah*) is the *duff* (tambourine). This issue has already been treated fully in *al-Baqarah* [See vol. 3, p. 79 ff., first or second edition.].

In Bukhari, from Abu Hurayra: a man from the Children of Israel asked another of the Children of Israel to lend him a thousand dinars. He said, "Bring me witnesses, and I will have them witness it." He said, "God suffices as a witness." He said, "Bring me a guarantor." He said, "God suffices as a guarantor." He said, "You have spoken the truth," and he handed him the money. And he mentioned the hadith.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 29:

There are three issues here.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When Moses had fulfilled the term﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: A man from the Christians asked me, "Which of the two terms did Moses fulfil?" I said: "I do not know, until I go to the scholar of the Arabs (ḥibr al-ʿarab) and ask him," meaning Ibn ʿAbbas. So I went to him and asked him, and he said: "He fulfilled the more complete and more perfect of the two." I informed the Christian, and he said: "By God, this scholar has spoken the truth." It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked Jibril about this, and he informed him that he fulfilled ten years. Al-Tabari related from Mujahid that he fulfilled ten, and then ten more after them. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: This is weak.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he set out with his family﴾. It has been said that this is evidence that a man may take his family wherever he wishes, because of the authority of qiwamiyyah (guardianship) he has over them and the added degree (of rank) he holds, except that if he binds himself to them to a condition, then "the Muslims are bound by their conditions," and the most deserving of conditions to be fulfilled are those by which you have made lawful the private parts.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He perceived a fire from the side of the Mount﴾, the verse. The discussion of this has preceded in (surah) Ta-Ha. As for al-jidhwah (a brand, a burning ember), with a kasra on the jim, it is the recitation of the majority; Hamzah and Yahya read it with a damma, and ʿAsim, al-Sulami and Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh read it with a fatha. Al-Jawhari said: al-jidhwah, al-jadhwah and al-judhwah all mean a glowing ember, and the plural is jidha, judha and jadha. Mujahid, regarding His saying, exalted is He, "or a brand from the fire," said: that is, a piece of the live coal, and he said: it is in the language of all the Arabs. Abu ʿUbaydah said: al-jadhwah is like al-jidhmah, which is a thick piece of wood, whether or not it has fire at its end. Ibn Muqbil said:

The gatherers of wood for Layla spent the night seeking for her
firm kindling, neither brittle nor smoldering.

And he said:

And he cast upon Qays from the fire a brand,
its heat and its blaze intense upon it.

(It is narrated: "intense upon it its heat and its blazing.")

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 30:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When he came to it﴾, meaning the tree. Its pronoun is placed before its antecedent.

﴿Was called out from the right side of the valley﴾. The first "min" (from) and the second are for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning the call came to him from the bank of the valley, from the direction of the tree. And ﴿from the tree﴾ is a substitution (badal) for his saying ﴿from the bank of the valley﴾, a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion, where the second noun is part of or contained in the first), because the tree was growing on the bank. The shati' (bank) of the valley is its shatt, meaning its side, and its plural is shuttan and shawati'. This was mentioned by al-Qushayri. Al-Jawhari said: "It is said shati' al-awdiyah (the banks of the valleys), and it is not pluralized." And shaata'tu al-rajul means that I walked on one bank while he walked on another bank.

﴿On the right﴾, meaning on the right of Musa (peace be upon him). It is also said: on the right of the mountain.

﴿In the blessed place﴾. Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read "fi al-bu'qah" with a fatha on the ba'. Their saying biqa' indicates bu'qah, just as it is said jafnah and jifan (bowl and bowls). And whoever says bu'qah makes its plural bu'ak, like ghurfah and ghuraf (room and rooms).

﴿From the tree﴾, meaning from the direction of the tree. It is said it was the tree of al-'Ulayqah (dodder). It is said it was the samurah (a kind of acacia). It is said it was al-'awsaj (boxthorn). From it was his staff, as mentioned by al-Zamakhshari. It is also said it was 'unnab (jujube). When the 'awsaj grows large, it is called al-gharqad. In a hadith: "Indeed it is among the trees of the Jews. When 'Isa (Jesus) descends and kills the Jews who are with the Dajjal (Antichrist), no one of them will hide behind a tree except that it will speak and say: 'O Muslim, this is a Jew behind me, come and kill him,' except the gharqad, for it is among the trees of the Jews, so it will not speak." Muslim recorded it.

Al-Mahdawi said: Allah, may He be exalted, spoke to Musa (peace be upon him) from above His Throne, and made him hear His speech from the tree as He willed. It is not permissible to describe Allah, may He be exalted, with movement, cessation, or the like of the attributes of created beings.

Abu al-Ma'ali said: The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) and the people of truth say: whoever Allah speaks to and singles out with the highest rank and the utmost degree, he perceives His eternal speech, which is sanctified above resemblance to letters, sounds, expressions, tones, and varieties of languages, just as whoever Allah singles out with the stations of honor, completes His blessing upon him, and grants him the vision of Him, sees Allah, glory be to Him, transcendent above resemblance to bodies and the judgments of created things. There is no likeness to Him, glory be to Him, in His essence or His attributes. The Muslim community (ummah) agreed that the Lord, may He be exalted, singled out Musa (peace be upon him) and others among the chosen angels with His speech.

Al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq said: The people of truth agreed that Allah, may He be exalted, created in Musa (peace be upon him) a meaning (ma'na) by which he perceived His speech, and that his singling out was in hearing it, and that He is able to do the like for all of His creation. They differed concerning our Prophet (peace be upon him): whether he heard the speech of Allah on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), and whether Jibril heard His speech, on two opinions. The path of one of them is a definitive transmission, and that is missing. They agreed that the hearing of creation of it at the recitation of the Qur'an is in the sense that they heard the expression by which they knew its meaning, not that they heard it in its essence.

Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Kilab said: Musa (peace be upon him) understood the eternal speech of Allah from created sounds which Allah, may He be exalted, brought into existence in some bodies.

Abu al-Ma'ali said: This is rejected. Rather, it is necessary that Musa (peace be upon him) be singled out in perceiving the speech of Allah, as a breach of custom (kharq al-'adah). Had he not said so, Musa (peace be upon him) would have had no distinction in Allah speaking to him. The Lord, may He be exalted, made him hear His mighty speech and created in him a necessary knowledge, until he knew that what he heard was the speech of Allah, and that the One who spoke to him and called him was Allah, Lord of the worlds.

It has been reported in the narratives (al-aqasis) that Musa (peace be upon him) said: "I heard the speech of my Lord with all my limbs, and I did not hear it from one direction only of my directions." This meaning has been fully discussed before in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 1, p. 304, second or third edition.]].

﴿That, O Musa﴾. "An" (that) is in a position of nasb (accusative) by deletion of the preposition, meaning: bi-"an ya Musa" (with "O Musa").

﴿Indeed, I am Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. This is a negation of the lordship (rububiyyah) of any other than Him, glory be to Him. By this speech he became one of the chosen servants of Allah, may He be exalted and majestic, but not one of His messengers, because he does not become a messenger except after His command to convey the message, and the command to it came only after this speech.

And cast down your staff." It is coordinated (ʿutifa) with "an yā Mūsā" (that, O Mūsā), and the discussion of this has already been covered in Surat al-Naml and Surah Ṭā-Hā. "Mudbiran" (turning back) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and likewise the position of His words "wa lam yuʿaqqib" (and did not turn back) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state as well.

"O Mūsā, come forward and do not fear." Wahb said: It was said to him, "Return to where you were." So he returned and wrapped his ḍurrāʿa (a type of garment worn; it is said to be a robe split at the front) around his hand. The angel said to him, "Do you see, if God wished to afflict you with what you are wary of, would your wrapping your hand benefit you?" He said, "No, but I am weak; I was created from weakness." Then he uncovered his hand and put it into the mouth of the serpent, and it returned to being a staff.

"Indeed you are of those who are secure" — that is, from what you were wary of.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿Insert your hand into your bosom﴾, the verse, its discussion has already preceded.

(And draw your arm close to you against fear.) "Min" (from) is connected to "wallā" (he turned), meaning he turned back, fleeing, out of fear. Hafs, al-Sulami, 'Isa ibn 'Amr and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "min al-rahb" with a fatha on the rā' and a sukūn on the hā'. Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans except Hafs read it with a ḍamma on the rā' and a jazm on the hā'. The rest read it with a fatha on both the rā' and the hā'. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, based on His saying ﴿and they call upon Us in hope and fear﴾, and all of these are dialects, and it means fear. The meaning is: when the matter of your hand and its radiance frightens you, insert it into your bosom and return it, and it will return to how it was. It was also said: God commanded him to press his hand to his chest, and the fear of the serpent would leave him. This is related from Mujahid and others, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "No one who is struck by terror after Musa, peace be upon him, puts his hand into his bosom and places it on his chest, except that the terror leaves him." It is related from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may God have mercy on him, that a scribe was writing before him, and a gust of wind escaped from him, so he was embarrassed and broke down. He stood up and struck the ground with his pen. 'Umar said to him: "Take your pen and draw your arm close to you, and let your fright be relieved, for I have never heard it from anyone more than I have heard it from myself." It was also said: the meaning is press your hand to your chest, so that God removes what is in your chest of fear. Musa used to tremble with fear, either from the people of Pharaoh or from the serpent. Drawing in the wing means calm, as in His saying ﴿and lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾, meaning gentleness, and likewise His saying ﴿and lower your wing to those who follow you among the believers﴾, that is, be gentle with them. Al-Farra' said: by the wing he meant his staff. Some scholars of meanings said: al-rahb means the sleeve, in the dialect of Himyar and Banu Hanifa. Muqatil said: a Bedouin woman asked me for something while I was eating, so I filled my palm and gestured to her, and she said: "Here, in my rahb," meaning in my sleeve. Al-Asma'i said: I heard a Bedouin saying to another, "Give me your rahb." So I asked him about al-rahb, and he said: "The sleeve." On this basis, its meaning is: draw your hand to you and bring it out of the sleeve, because he had taken the staff while his hand was in his sleeve. His saying ﴿Insert your hand into your bosom﴾ indicates that it is the right hand, because the bosom is on the left. This was mentioned by al-Qushayri. I say: what they explained as pressing the hand to the chest indicates that the bosom's place is the chest. Its explanation has passed in Surat al-Nur. [[See vol. 12, p. 231, first or second edition.]] Al-Zamakhshari said: Among the strange interpretations is that al-rahb means the sleeve in the dialect of Himyar, and that they say "give me from what is in your rahb." I wonder how this is sound in the language! Has it been heard from the reliable, trustworthy authorities whose Arabic is accepted? Then I wonder how it fits in the verse, and how its detailed application is, like the rest of the words of the revelation, given that Musa, may blessings be upon him, on the night of the intimate conversation was wearing nothing but a zurmanqa [[The zurmanqa: a woollen robe, a non-Arabic word arabicized.]] of wool that had no sleeves. Al-Qushayri said: His saying ﴿and draw your wing to you﴾ means the two hands, if we say that it intended security from the fear of the serpent. It was also said: ﴿and draw your wing to you﴾ means gather yourself and prepare to bear the burdens of the message. I say: according to this, it was said: ﴿you are among the secure﴾, that is, among the messengers, based on His saying ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾. Ibn Bahr said: By this interpretation he became a messenger through this statement. It was also said that he became a messenger only through the saying: (These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs), and the proofs are the hand and the staff. Ibn Kathir read "fa-dhānnāni" with a shadda on the nūn, and the rest read it with a light nūn. Abu 'Umara narrated from Abu al-Fadl from Abu Bakr from Ibn Kathir, "fa-dhānnāyika" with the shadda and the yā'. Also from Abu 'Amr, he said: the dialect of Hudhayl is "fa-dhāniyka" with a light nūn and a yā', and the dialect of Quraysh is "fa-dhānika," as Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read. Regarding its explanation there are five opinions. It was said: he shaddaded the nūn as a substitute for the dropped alif in dhānika, which is the dual of dhā in the nominative, and it is nominative as a subject, and the alif of dhā is deleted because the dual alif was added to it, and he did not regard the meeting of two sukūns, because the original is fadhāānika, so the first alif was deleted as a substitute for the strong nūn. It was said: the shadda is for emphasis, as they added the lām to that. Makki said: it was also said that whoever shaddaded it built it on the dialect of those who say that in the singular, so when he built it he kept the lām after the dual nūn, then assimilated the lām into the nūn according to the rule of assimilating the second into the first, while the original is that the first is always assimilated into the second, except that a cause prevents it, and then the second is assimilated into the first. The cause that prevented the first from being assimilated into the second is that if this were done, there would be a shadda lām in the place of the nūn that indicates the dual, and the form of the dual would change, so the second was assimilated into the first for this reason, and it became a shadda nūn. It has also been said that when he reached that, the lām was kept before the nūn, then the first was assimilated into the second according to the principles of assimilation, and it became a shadda nūn. It was also said: it was shaddaded to distinguish it from the apparent form that drops the nūn with an added pronoun, because dhānni is not made into an idāfa. It was also said: to distinguish between the declinable noun and it. The same is the reason for the shadda of the nūn in "alladhānni" and "hadhānni." Abu 'Amr said: Abu 'Amr singled out this letter for shadda, rather than every dual of its kind, because of the fewness of its letters, so he read it with the heavy form. As for whoever reads "fadhānīka" with a yā' and a light nūn, the original in his view is "fadhānnika" with the shadda, so he replaced the second nūn with a yā' to avoid doubling, as they say: "lā amlāhu" for "lā amallu," so they replaced the second lām with an alif. As for whoever reads with a yā' after the heavy nūn, his reasoning is that he prolonged the kasra of the nūn, so the yā' was produced from it.

His saying: ﴿So send him with me as a helper﴾, meaning a supporter, derived from "ardtuhu," that is, I helped him. Al-ridʾ is help. The poet said:

Did you not see that Asram was my helper... and the best of people in scarcity and wealth

Al-Nahhas said: "Ardahu" and "radahu" mean he helped him, and he dropped its hamza for lightness, and Nafi' read with it, and it has the meaning of the hamzated form. Al-Mahdawi said: it is also possible that the omission of the hamza is from their saying "ardā 'ala al-mi'a," that is, it exceeded it, and it seems the meaning is: send him with me as an increase in confirming me. This was said by Muslim ibn Jundub. He recited the poet's line:

And a spear of dark wood, as if its knots are the seeds of the qasab date, has exceeded a span over ten.

Thus al-Mawardi recited this verse: "qad ardā." Al-Ghaznawi and al-Jawhari in al-Sihah recited "qad armā," [[Armā and arbā are two dialects.]] and he said: al-qasb is hard, and al-qasb is a dry date that crumbles in the mouth, hard-stoned. He describes a lance: "And a dark spear..." the verse. Al-Jawhari said: radu'a al-shay' yardu'u ruda'atan means it became bad, so it is radi', that is, corrupt, and ardatuhu means I corrupted it. Ardatuhu also means "a'antuhu," as you say: "ardatuhu bi-nafsi," meaning I was a helper to him, and the ridʾ is the help. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So send him with me as a helper who will confirm me﴾. Al-Nahhas said: Radatuhu has also been transmitted, rid'an, and the plural of ridʾ is ardā'. 'Asim and Hamzah read "yuṣaddiqunī" with a ḍamma, and the rest read it with a jazm. This is the choice of Abu Hatim, on the basis of it being a response to the supplication. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the ḍamma as a circumstantial clause from the hā' in "fa-arsilhu," meaning send him as a helper confirming at the time of confirmation, like His saying: ﴿Send down upon us a table from heaven, which will be [for us]﴾, meaning being, a circumstance turned to the future. It may also be an adjective of "ridʾan."

(Indeed I fear that they will deny me.) If I have no minister and no helper, because they hardly understand me. So [He] said, may He, the Mighty and Majestic, to him: (We will strengthen your arm through your brother), meaning We will strengthen you with him. This is a figure of speech, because the strength of the hand is through the upper arm. Ṭarafa said:

Sons of Lubayna, you are not a hand, except a hand that has no upper arm.

It is said in prayer for good: "May God strengthen your arm." And in its opposite: "May God break your arm."

(And We will give you both an authority) meaning a proof and an evidence.

(So they will not reach you) with harm (by Our signs) meaning you will both be protected from them. "By Our signs" may be stopped at "unto you both," and there would be a transposition in the speech. It was also said: the estimate is "you two and whoever follows you are the victors" by Our signs. This was said by al-Akhfash and al-Tabari. Al-Mahdawi said: In this is the placing of the complement before the relative, unless it is estimated as "you two are victorious by Our signs, you two and whoever follows you are the victors." By "the signs" he meant all His miracles.

Did you not see that Asram was my helper... and the best of people in scarcity and wealth

Al-Mahdawi said: it is also possible that the omission of the hamza is from their saying "ardā 'ala al-mi'a," that is, it exceeded it, and it seems the meaning is: send him with me as an increase in confirming me. And a spear of dark wood, as if its knots are the seeds of the qasab date, has exceeded a span over ten.

Thus al-Mawardi recited this verse: "qad ardā." Al-Ghaznawi and al-Jawhari in al-Sihah recited "qad armā," [[Armā and arbā are two dialects.]] and he said: al-qasb is hard, and al-qasb is a dry date that crumbles in the mouth, hard-stoned. This is a figure of speech, because the strength of the hand is through the upper arm. Ṭarafa said:

The Qur'an verse: ﴿Insert your hand into your bosom﴾, the verse, its discussion has already preceded.

(And draw your arm close to you against fear.) "Min" (from) is connected to "wallā" (he turned), meaning he turned back, fleeing, out of fear. Hafs, al-Sulami, 'Isa ibn 'Amr and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "min al-rahb" with a fatha on the rā' and a sukūn on the hā'. Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans except Hafs read it with a ḍamma on the rā' and a jazm on the hā'. The rest read it with a fatha on both the rā' and the hā'. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, based on His saying ﴿and they call upon Us in hope and fear﴾, and all of these are dialects, and it means fear. The meaning is: when the matter of your hand and its radiance frightens you, insert it into your bosom and return it, and it will return to how it was. It was also said: God commanded him to press his hand to his chest, and the fear of the serpent would leave him. This is related from Mujahid and others, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "No one who is struck by terror after Musa, peace be upon him, puts his hand into his bosom and places it on his chest, except that the terror leaves him." He stood up and struck the ground with his pen. 'Umar said to him: "Take your pen and draw your arm close to you, and let your fright be relieved, for I have never heard it from anyone more than I have heard it from myself." It was also said: the meaning is press your hand to your chest, so that God removes what is in your chest of fear. **Verse 36**

*"So when Moses came to them with Our clear signs"*: that is, manifest and evident. *(They said, "This is nothing but fabricated magic")*: invented and made up. *("We never heard of this among our forefathers of old.")* It has also been said that these signs, and the proofs by which Moses argued for the affirmation of tawhid (the oneness of God), are rational arguments. It has also been said that they are his miracles.

*"And Moses said"*: the common qira'ah (canonical recitation) reads it with the waw (wa-qala). Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read *qala* without the waw, and it is so in the mushaf (codex) of the people of Makkah. *("My Lord knows best who comes with guidance")*: that is, with right guidance.

*("...from Him, and whose will be the good outcome of the abode.")* The Kufans, except Asim, read *yakunu* with the ya', and the rest read it with the ta'. This has already been discussed.

*("...the good outcome of the abode")*: that is, the abode of recompense.

*(Indeed, the "h" in innahu is a pronoun of the matter and affair)*: *("...the wrongdoers will not prosper.")*

**Verse 38**

*"And Pharaoh said, 'O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself.'"* Ibn Abbas said: between this and his saying, *"I am your Lord, the Most High,"* there were forty years. The enemy of Allah was lying; rather, he knew that there was a Lord beyond him, who is the Creator of him and of his people: *"And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, 'Allah.'"* He said: *("So kindle for me, O Haman, a fire over the clay")*: that is, bake for me the bricks. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him. Qatadah said: he was the first to make bricks and build with them.

When Pharaoh ordered his vizier Haman to build the tower, Haman gathered the workers, said to be fifty thousand builders apart from the followers and hired labourers. He ordered the baking of bricks and lime, the sawing of wood and the driving of nails. They built, raised the structure and erected it to such a height that no building had reached it since Allah created the heavens and the earth. The builder could not stand at its top, until Allah willed to test them with it. As-Suddi related that Pharaoh climbed the roof and shot an arrow towards the sky, and it returned stained with blood, so he said, "I have killed the God of Moses." It has also been said: they are leaders whom those with lessons take as examples, and from whom the people of insight draw admonition.

*("They call to the Fire")*: that is, to the deeds of the people of the Fire. *("And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped.")*

**Verse 42**

*("And We followed them in this world with a curse")*: that is, We commanded the servants to curse them, so whoever mentions them curses them. It has also been said: that is, We obliged them to be cursed, that is, to be distanced from good.

*("And on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.")* That is, among those destroyed and abhorred. This was said by Ibn Kaysan and Abu Ubaydah. Ibn Abbas said: those whose appearance is disfigured by blackness of faces and blueness of eyes. It has also been said: among those kept far away. It is said: *qabbahahu Allah*, meaning Allah removed him from every good, and *qabahahu* and *qabbahahu* mean he made him ugly. Abu Amr said: *qabahtu wajhahu*, with the lightened form, means *qabbahtu* (I made his face ugly). The poet said:

*"Surely Allah has cursed all the Baraajim (tribes),*
*And cursed Yarbu', and cursed Daarim."*

*Yawm* (day) is in the accusative on the basis of the place of *"in this world"*, and the conjunction is dispensed with in His saying *"among the despised,"* as it is dispensed with in His saying *"They will say, 'They were three, the fourth of them being their dog.'"* It is also possible that the governing word for *yawm* is an implied verb indicated by His saying *"they are among the despised,"* so it is like His saying *"The day they see the angels, there will be no good news that day for the criminals."* It is also possible that the governing word for *yawm* is His saying *"they are among the despised,"* even though the adverbial phrase precedes it. It is also possible that it is an object by way of expansion, as if He said: *"And We followed them in this world with a curse, and a curse on the Day of Resurrection."*

**Verse 36**

*"So when Moses came to them with Our clear signs"*: that is, manifest and evident. *(They said, "This is nothing but fabricated magic")*: invented and made up. *("We never heard of this among our forefathers of old.")* It has also been said that these signs, and the proofs by which Moses argued for the affirmation of tawhid (the oneness of God), are rational arguments. It has also been said that they are his miracles.

*"And Moses said"*: the common qira'ah (canonical recitation) reads it with the waw (wa-qala). Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read *qala* without the waw, and it is so in the mushaf (codex) of the people of Makkah. *("My Lord knows best who comes with guidance")*: that is, with right guidance.

*("...from Him, and whose will be the good outcome of the abode.")* The Kufans, except Asim, read *yakunu* with the ya', and the rest read it with the ta'. This has already been discussed.

*("...the good outcome of the abode")*: that is, the abode of recompense.

*(Indeed, the "h" in innahu is a pronoun of the matter and affair)*: *("...the wrongdoers will not prosper.")*

**Verse 38**

*"And Pharaoh said, 'O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself.'"* Ibn Abbas said: between this and his saying, *"I am your Lord, the Most High,"* there were forty years. The enemy of Allah was lying; rather, he knew that there was a Lord beyond him, who is the Creator of him and of his people: *"And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, 'Allah.'"* He said: *("So kindle for me, O Haman, a fire over the clay")*: that is, bake for me the bricks. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him. Qatadah said: he was the first to make bricks and build with them.

When Pharaoh ordered his vizier Haman to build the tower, Haman gathered the workers, said to be fifty thousand builders apart from the followers and hired labourers. He ordered the baking of bricks and lime, the sawing of wood and the driving of nails. They built, raised the structure and erected it to such a height that no building had reached it since Allah created the heavens and the earth. The builder could not stand at its top, until Allah willed to test them with it. As-Suddi related that Pharaoh climbed the roof and shot an arrow towards the sky, and it returned stained with blood, so he said, "I have killed the God of Moses." It is narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him), sent by Allah the Exalted at the time of his saying, struck the tower with his wing and cut it into three pieces: one piece fell upon Pharaoh's army and killed a million of them, one piece fell into the sea, and one piece fell in the west, and everyone who had worked on it was destroyed. Allah knows best the authenticity of this.

*("And indeed, I think him to be among the liars.")* The *zann* (supposition) here means doubt, so he disbelieved on the basis of doubt, because he had seen of the proofs what would not be unclear *[[la yukhayyil: i.e., not unclear]]* to one of sound nature.

**Verse 39**

*"And he was arrogant"*: that is, he magnified himself. *("He and his soldiers")*: that is, from faith in Moses.

*("...in the land without right")*: that is, by transgression; that is, he had no argument that could repel what Moses had brought.

*("And they thought that they would not be returned to Us.")*: that is, they imagined that there was no return and no resurrection. Nafi', Ibn Muhaysin, Shaybah, Humayd, Ya'qub, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *la yarji'un* with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the jim, in the form of the active verb. The rest read *yurja'un* in the passive form. The former is the choice of Abu Ubayd, and the latter is the choice of Abu Hatim.

Wahb and as-Suddi said: the place where Allah drowned them, on the side of al-Qulzum, is called Batn Murayrah, and it is angry to this day. Muqatil said: it means the River Nile. *("So look, O Muhammad,")* *("...how was the end of the wrongdoers.")* that is, the final outcome of their affair.

**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾**, meaning the Torah (al-Tawrat), said Qatadah. Yahya ibn Sallam said: it is the first book, meaning the Torah, in which the obligations (al-fara'id), the prescribed penalties (al-hudud) and the rulings (al-ahkam) were revealed. It was also said that "the Book" here refers to six of the seven oft-repeated (al-mathani) verses which Allah sent down upon His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn Abbas, and he narrated it as a marfu' report.

**﴿after We had destroyed the former generations﴾.** Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah did not destroy a people, nor a generation, nor a nation, nor the people of a town, with a punishment from the sky or from the earth since He sent down the Torah to Moses, except for the town that was transformed into monkeys. Have you not seen His saying, exalted is He: 'And We gave Moses the Book after We had destroyed the former generations'?" That is, after the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud. It was also said: that is, after We drowned Pharaoh and his people and caused Qarun to be swallowed up by the earth.

**﴿as clear insights for mankind﴾**, meaning We gave him the Book as insights, so that people might gain understanding. **﴿And guidance﴾** from misguidance for whoever acts upon it, **﴿and mercy﴾** for whoever believes in it, **﴿that they may remember﴾**, meaning that they might recall this blessing and thereby remain firm in their faith in this world, and trust in their reward in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 44–45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you were not﴾, meaning: you were not, O Muhammad, (on the western side), meaning on the western side of the mountain. The poet said:

"He gave you, who gave guidance to the Prophet, a light that adorns the western pulpit."

(When We decreed to Moses the command), when We charged him with Our command and prohibition, and bound him to Our covenant. It is also said: meaning, when We decreed to Moses your affair and mentioned you with the best mention.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "When We decreed" means: We informed that the nation of Muhammad is the best of nations.

(And you were not among the witnesses), meaning: among those present. His saying, exalted is He: (But We brought into being generations), meaning after Moses, (and the lifetime grew long for them), until they forgot the remembrance of Allah, meaning His covenant and His command. Its parallel is: "So the term grew long for them and their hearts became hard." The apparent meaning of this requires that mention of our Prophet, peace be upon him, had occurred at that time, and that Allah would send him, but the period grew long and hardness prevailed, so the people forgot that. It is also said: We gave Moses the Book and took covenants from his people, then the covenant grew long and they disbelieved, so We sent Muhammad as a renewer of the religion and a caller of creation to it. His saying, exalted is He: (And you were not a dweller among the people of Madyan), meaning residing as Moses and Shu'ayb resided among them. Al-'Ajjaj said:

"So he spent the night where the resident guest enters"

meaning the guest who stays. And His saying: (reciting to them Our verses), meaning reminding them of the promise and the threat.

(But We were sending messengers), meaning We sent you among the people of Makkah, and We gave you a Book containing these reports, and had it not been for that, you would not have known them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you were not on the side of the Mount when We called﴾. That is, just as you were not present on the western side when Allah sent Musa to Pharaoh, likewise you were not present on the side of the Mount when We called Musa when he came to the appointed time with the seventy. 

Amr ibn Dinar related it, traced back to the Prophet, saying: "It was called out: O community of Muhammad, I answered you before you called upon Me, and I gave you before you asked Me." That is His saying: ﴿And you were not on the side of the Mount when We called﴾.

Abu Hurayrah said, and in a narration from Ibn Abbas, that Allah said: "O community of Muhammad, I have answered you before you call upon Me, I have given you before you ask Me, I have forgiven you before you seek forgiveness from Me, and I have shown mercy to you before you seek mercy from Me." Wahb said: The reason is that when Allah mentioned to Musa the virtue of Muhammad and his community, he said: "My Lord, show them to me." Allah said: "You will not reach them, but if you wish, I will call out to them and make you hear their voice." He said: "Yes, my Lord." Then Allah, may He be exalted, said: "O community of Muhammad!" and they answered from the loins of their fathers. He said: "I have answered you before you call upon Me." The meaning of the verse according to this is: You were not on the side of the Mount when We spoke to Musa, and We called out to your community and informed him of the mercy We had written for you and for your community until the end of the world.

(But) We did it (as a mercy) from Us to you. Al-Akhfash said: "a mercy" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning: but We showed mercy to you, a mercy. Al-Zajjaj said: it is an object of purpose, meaning He did that for you for the sake of mercy. Al-Nahhas said: that is, you did not witness the stories of the prophets, nor were they recited to you, but We sent you and revealed them to you as a mercy.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the predicate of "kana", the sense being: but it was a mercy. He said: the nominative is also permissible, in the sense of "it is a mercy." Al-Zajjaj said: the nominative is in the sense of: but doing that is a mercy.

(So that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you) meaning the Arabs; that is, you did not witness those reports, but We revealed them to you as a mercy toward those to whom you were sent, so that you might warn them with them (so that they may remember).

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verses 47–48:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And had it not been that a misfortune should afflict them﴾. He means the Quraysh. It is also said: the Jews.

*Musibah* (a calamity) means a punishment and a vengeance, ﴿for what their hands have put forward﴾, that is, from disbelief and sins. He specified "the hands" because most earning is done by them. The answer to *lawla* (if not / had it not been) is omitted; the meaning is: "Had it not been that a punishment would afflict them because of their earlier sins, ﴿they would say: Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger﴾," that is, "why did You not send..." (*hallа*, "why not"). "Had We not sent the messengers..." It is also said: "We would have hastened the punishment upon them, and the sending of messengers is a removal of the excuse of the disbelievers, as was mentioned previously in [the commentary on] *Subhan* and at the end of *Ta-Ha*."

﴿So that we might follow Your signs﴾: *nasb* (accusative) as an answer to the *takhsis* (a particle of specification).

﴿And become﴾: it is conjoined to it.

﴿Among the believers﴾: among those who affirm the truth. Whoever argued from this verse, saying that reason makes faith and gratitude obligatory, [did so] because He said: "for what their hands have put forward," and that necessitates punishment once the obligation is established before the sending of the messengers, and that is only through reason. Al-Qushayri said: "The correct view is that the omitted [clause] is: 'Had it not been that...', so that there would be no need to renew the messengers; that is, these disbelievers are not excused, since the earlier laws and the call to monotheism reached them. But the time has lengthened, so if We were to punish them, one of them might say, 'The time since the messengers has been long,' and he would think that this is an excuse, though they have no excuse after the news of the messengers has reached them. Rather, We have completed the removal of the excuse, and We have completed the clarification, so We have sent you, O Muhammad, to them." Allah has decreed that He does not punish any servant except after the completion of clarification, the proof, and the sending of messengers.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us﴾, meaning Muhammad ﷺ, ﴿they said﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa﴾, that is, "why was he not given..." (*lawla*, "why not"): of the staff and the white hand, and the Qur'an was sent down to him all at once, like the Torah. This had reached them about Musa before Muhammad. So Allah, may He be exalted, said: (﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before? They said: "Two sorcerers who support each other"﴾). [[Recitation of Nafi': "sahiran tazahara" (two sorcerers who support each other), and the author follows this.]] *Tazahara* means that Musa and Muhammad cooperated in magic.

Al-Kalbi said: "The Quraysh sent to the Jews and asked them about the sending of Muhammad and his affair. They said: 'We find him in the Torah with his description and attributes.' When the answer came back to them, 'they said: two sorcerers who support each other.'" It was also said by some people: "The Jews taught the polytheists, and they said: 'Say to Muhammad: why were you not given the like of what Musa was given, for he was given the Torah in one single bestowal.'" So this argument is directed at the Jews; that is, "Did these Jews not disbelieve in what was given to Musa, when they said about Musa and Harun, 'they are two sorcerers,'" and ﴿Indeed, we are disbelievers in both of them﴾, that is, "we are disbelievers in each one of them."

The Kufans read *sihran* (two sorts of magic) without an *alif*, that is, the Gospel and the Qur'an. It is also said: the Torah and the Furqan (the Criterion), as stated by al-Farra'. It is also said: the Torah and the Gospel, as stated by Abu Ruzayn. The rest read *sahiran* with an *alif*. In this there are three opinions:

First: Musa and Muhammad, peace be upon them. This is the view of the polytheist Arabs, and it was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

Second: Musa and Harun. This is the view of the Jews about them both at the beginning of the prophetic mission, and it was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd. Then the speech is an argument against them. This indicates that what is omitted in His saying, "Had it not been that a misfortune should afflict them," is: "Had We not renewed the sending of the messengers." For the Jews acknowledged the prophethoods, but they distorted and altered [the message], and they deserved punishment. So He said: "We have completed the removal of their excuse by sending Muhammad ﷺ."

Third: 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. This is the view of the Jews today, and it was said by Qatadah.

It was also said: "Did not all the Jews disbelieve in what was given to Musa in the Torah, of the mention of the Messiah, and the mention of the Gospel and the Qur'an? So they saw Musa and Muhammad as two sorcerers, and the two Books as two sorceries."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And had it not been that a misfortune should afflict them﴾. He means the Quraysh. It is also said: the Jews.

*Musibah* (a calamity) means a punishment and a vengeance, ﴿for what their hands have put forward﴾, that is, from disbelief and sins. He specified "the hands" because most earning is done by them. The answer to *lawla* (if not / had it not been) is omitted; the meaning is: "Had it not been that a punishment would afflict them because of their earlier sins, ﴿they would say: Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger﴾," that is, "why did You not send..." (*hallа*, "why not"). "Had We not sent the messengers..." It is also said: "We would have hastened the punishment upon them, and the sending of messengers is a removal of the excuse of the disbelievers, as was mentioned previously in [the commentary on] *Subhan* and at the end of *Ta-Ha*."

﴿So that we might follow Your signs﴾: *nasb* (accusative) as an answer to the *takhsis* (a particle of specification).

﴿And become﴾: it is conjoined to it.

﴿Among the believers﴾: among those who affirm the truth. Whoever argued from this verse, saying that reason makes faith and gratitude obligatory, [did so] because He said: "for what their hands have put forward," and that necessitates punishment once the obligation is established before the sending of the messengers, and that is only through reason. Al-Qushayri said: "The correct view is that the omitted [clause] is: 'Had it not been that...', so that there would be no need to renew the messengers; that is, these disbelievers are not excused, since the earlier laws and the call to monotheism reached them. But the time has lengthened, so if We were to punish them, one of them might say, 'The time since the messengers has been long,' and he would think that this is an excuse, though they have no excuse after the news of the messengers has reached them. Rather, We have completed the removal of the excuse, and We have completed the clarification, so We have sent you, O Muhammad, to them." Allah has decreed that He does not punish any servant except after the completion of clarification, the proof, and the sending of messengers.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us﴾, meaning Muhammad ﷺ, ﴿they said﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa﴾, that is, "why was he not given..." (*lawla*, "why not"): of the staff and the white hand, and the Qur'an was sent down to him all at once, like the Torah. This had reached them about Musa before Muhammad. So Allah, may He be exalted, said: (﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before? They said: "Two sorcerers who support each other"﴾). [[Recitation of Nafi': "sahiran tazahara" (two sorcerers who support each other), and the author follows this.]] *Tazahara* means that Musa and Muhammad cooperated in magic.

Al-Kalbi said: "The Quraysh sent to the Jews and asked them about the sending of Muhammad and his affair. They said: 'We find him in the Torah with his description and attributes.' When the answer came back to them, 'they said: two sorcerers who support each other.'" It was also said by some people: "The Jews taught the polytheists, and they said: 'Say to Muhammad: why were you not given the like of what Musa was given, for he was given the Torah in one single bestowal.'" So this argument is directed at the Jews; that is, "Did these Jews not disbelieve in what was given to Musa, when they said about Musa and Harun, 'they are two sorcerers,'" and ﴿Indeed, we are disbelievers in both of them﴾, that is, "we are disbelievers in each one of them."

The Kufans read *sihran* (two sorts of magic) without an *alif*, that is, the Gospel and the Qur'an. It is also said: the Torah and the Furqan (the Criterion), as stated by al-Farra'. It is also said: the Torah and the Gospel, as stated by Abu Ruzayn. The rest read *sahiran* with an *alif*. In this there are three opinions:

First: Musa and Muhammad, peace be upon them. This is the view of the polytheist Arabs, and it was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

Second: Musa and Harun. This is the view of the Jews about them both at the beginning of the prophetic mission, and it was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd. Then the speech is an argument against them. This indicates that what is omitted in His saying, "Had it not been that a misfortune should afflict them," is: "Had We not renewed the sending of the messengers." For the Jews acknowledged the prophethoods, but they distorted and altered [the message], and they deserved punishment. So He said: "We have completed the removal of their excuse by sending Muhammad ﷺ."

Third: 'Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. This is the view of the Jews today, and it was said by Qatadah.

It was also said: "Did not all the Jews disbelieve in what was given to Musa in the Torah, of the mention of the Messiah, and the mention of the Gospel and the Qur'an? So they saw Musa and Muhammad as two sorcerers, and the two Books as two sorceries."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 49–51:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guidance than both of them, and I will follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ That is: Say, O Muhammad, if you (O assembly of polytheists) disbelieve in these two Books, "then bring a Book from Allah that is better guidance than both of them, and I will follow it," so that this will be an excuse for you in disbelief, "if you are truthful" in your claim that they are both sorcery. Or: "Bring a book that is better guidance than the books of Musa and Muhammad, peace be upon them." And this strengthens the reading of the Kufans, "sihranī" (two sorceries). As for "atteba'hu" (I will follow it), al-Farra' said: it is in the nominative (raf'), because it is an attribute of "Kitab," and "kitab" is indefinite. He said: and if you apocopate it (jazm), which is the preferred form, then it is conditional (shart).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they do not respond to you﴾, O Muhammad, to bring a Book from Allah, ﴿then know that they only follow their desires﴾, that is, the opinions of their hearts and what they find pleasing, which Satan makes attractive to them, and they have no proof.

﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah﴾, that is, there is no one more astray than him, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have certainly conveyed to them the word﴾, that is, We made one part follow another, and We sent messenger after messenger. Al-Hasan read "wassalna" with a light (mukhaffaf) form. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: the meaning of "wassalna" is "We completed," like your joining (silatuka) a thing. Ibn 'Uyayna and al-Suddi said: "We made clear." This is also said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: "We detailed (fassalna)." And thus he used to read it. Ibn Zayd said: We conveyed to them news of this world with news of the Hereafter, until it is as if they were in the Hereafter while in this world. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: We connected (walayna), followed up, and sent down the Qur'an with its parts following one another: promise and threat, stories, lessons, advice and admonitions, in the hope that they would remember and prosper. Its root is from joining ropes to one another (wasl al-hibal). The poet said:

So say to the sons of Marwan, what is the matter with a covenant (dhimma)
and a weak cord that is continually joined (yuwassal)?

And Imru' al-Qays said:

Dariri, like the top (khadhrif) of a boy whose hand spins it,
his two hands turning it with a joined thread.

The pronoun in "lahum" (for them) refers to the Quraysh, according to Mujahid. It was also said that it refers to the Jews, and it was said that it refers to all of them. The verse is a rebuttal of those who said, "Why was the Qur'an not given to Muhammad all at once?"

﴿So that they may remember﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that they may remember Muhammad and believe in him. It was also said: that they may remember and fear that what befell those before them will befall them. This was said by 'Ali ibn 'Isa. It was also said: that they may take warning from the Qur'an against worshipping idols. This was related by al-Naqqash.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 52–53:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾. He informs that a group among those who were given the Book from the Children of Israel, before the Qur'an, believe in the Qur'an, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and Salman. It also includes those of the scholars of the Christians who embraced Islam, and they were forty men who came with Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib to Medina, thirty-two men from Abyssinia, and eight men who came from al-Sham, and they were the imams of the Christians. Among them were Bahira the monk, Abraha, al-Ashraf, Amir, Ayman, Idris and Nafi. Thus al-Mawardi named them. And Allah the Exalted revealed this verse concerning them, and the one after it: ﴿These will be given their reward twice, for what they endured with patience﴾. This is what Qatadah said. And from him also: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, Tamim al-Dari, al-Jarud al-ʿAbdi and Salman al-Farisi, who embraced Islam, so this verse was revealed concerning them. And from Rifaʿa al-Qurazi: it was revealed concerning ten people, I being one of them. ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: it was revealed concerning the Negus and his companions, and he sent twelve men, and they sat with the Prophet (ﷺ), and Abu Jahl and his companions were near them, and they believed in the Prophet (ﷺ). When they rose from his presence, Abu Jahl and those with him followed them, and said to them: "May Allah disappoint you as a caravan, and disgrace you as a delegation. You did not wait before you confirmed him, and we have seen no caravan more foolish or more ignorant than you." They said: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, ﴿we do not seek the ignorant﴾, ﴿for us are our deeds and for you are your deeds﴾. This has been mentioned in full in "al-Ma'idah" [[See vol. 6, p. 255 onward, first or second edition.]] at His saying: ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger﴾. And Abu al-ʿAliyah said: these are a people who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) before he was sent, and some of them met him.

(مِنْ قَبْلِهِ) i.e. before the Qur'an. It was said: before Muhammad (peace be upon him). (هُمْ بِهِ) i.e. in the Qur'an or in Muhammad (peace be upon him) (يُؤْمِنُونَ) they believe.

(وَإِذا يُتْلى عَلَيْهِمْ قالُوا آمَنَّا بِهِ إِنَّهُ الْحَقُّ مِنْ رَبِّنا) i.e. when the Qur'an is recited to them, they say: we confirm what is in it. ﴿Indeed, we were Muslims before it﴾ i.e. before its revelation, or before the mission of Muhammad (peace be upon him), (مُسْلِمِينَ) i.e. monotheists, or believers that Muhammad would be sent and the Qur'an would be revealed upon him.

There are four issues in this passage.

**The first issue** concerns God's words: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, because they were patient﴾. It is established in Sahih Muslim, from Abu Musa, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Three will be given their reward twice: a man from the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and then encountered the Prophet (ﷺ), believed in him, followed him and affirmed him, for him is a double reward; a slave who fulfils the right of God, Mighty and Majestic, and the right of his master, for him is a double reward; and a man who had a slave-girl, provided well for her, then educated her well, then freed her and married her, for him is a double reward." Al-Sha'bi said to the Khurasani: "Take this hadith without payment, for a man would travel even for less than this to Madina." It is also related by al-Bukhari.

Our scholars said: since each of these persons was addressed with two commands from two directions, each of them merits two rewards. The People of the Book was addressed from the direction of his prophet, and then he was addressed from the direction of our Prophet, responded and followed him, so he has the reward of both religions. Likewise the slave is commanded from the direction of God, the Exalted, and from the direction of his master. The master of the slave-girl, when he fulfilled what he was addressed with regarding her upbringing and her education, gave her life through training. Then when he freed her and married her, he gave her life through the freedom which he conferred upon her by raising her to his own station. He has thus carried out what he was commanded regarding her, so the reward of each of them is two rewards. Furthermore, each of the two rewards is multiplied in itself, since a good deed is rewarded tenfold, so the rewards are multiplied.

For this reason it has been said that a slave who fulfils the right of his master and the right of God, the Exalted, is better than a free person. This is the view preferred by Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others. In the Sahih it is related from Abu Hurayra that he said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "For the righteous slave there are two rewards." By Him in whose hand is the soul of Abu Hurayra, were it not for jihad in the way of God, the Hajj and kindness to my mother, I would love to die while being a slave. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: "We have been informed that Abu Hurayra would not perform the Hajj until his mother died, because of his companionship with her." Also in the Sahih, from Abu Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "How excellent for the slave is that he dies while worshipping God well and serving his master well; how excellent for him."

**The second issue** concerns God's words ﴿because they were patient﴾. It is general in regard to their patience in their religion, then in this (religion), and in the harm they suffer from the disbelievers and others.

**The third issue** concerns God's words ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾. That is, they repel. One says "daraʾtu" (I repelled) when I pushed back, and "al-darʾ" means repelling. In a hadith: "Avert the hudud (legal penalties) through doubts." It has been said: they repel harm through forbearance and good speech. It has also been said: they repel sins through repentance and seeking forgiveness. On the first view, it is a description of noble character: whoever says something bad to them that is not mentioned, they meet with good speech that repels it. This is a verse of conciliation, from the early period of Islam, and it was abrogated (naskh, i.e., replaced) by the verse of the sword. Its ruling remains in what falls short of disbelief, to be practised by the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) until the Day of Resurrection. From this is his (ﷺ) saying to Mu'adh: "Follow the bad deed with a good deed and it will erase it, and deal with people with good character." Among good character is repelling what is disliked and harmful, and patience with harshness by turning away from it and speaking gently.

**The fourth issue** concerns God's words ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾. He praised them for spending from their wealth in acts of obedience and in what the Sharia prescribes, and in this there is encouragement to give charity. Spending may also be done with the body, through fasting and prayer. Then He praised them also for turning away from frivolity, as He says: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾, that is, when they hear what the polytheists say to them of harm and abuse, they turn away from it, meaning they do not occupy themselves with it. ﴿They say: "To us our deeds, and to you your deeds. Peace be upon you."﴾ That is, a disengagement, like His saying: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾ That is, to us is our religion and to you is your religion.

(﴿Peace be upon you﴾) That is, a safety for you from us, for we do not fight you and we do not revile you, and it has nothing to do with greeting. Al-Zajjaj said: this was before the command to fight.

(﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾) That is, we do not seek them out for dispute, argument and abuse.

Also in the Sahih, from Abu Hurayra, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "How excellent for the slave is that he dies while worshipping God well and serving his master well; how excellent for him."

**The second issue** concerns God's words ﴿because they were patient﴾. It is general in regard to their patience in their religion, then in this (religion), and in the harm they suffer from the disbelievers and others.

**The third issue** concerns God's words ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾. That is, they repel. One says "daraʾtu" (I repelled) when I pushed back, and "al-darʾ" means repelling. In a hadith: "Avert the hudud (legal penalties) through doubts." It has been said: they repel harm through forbearance and good speech. It has also been said: they repel sins through repentance and seeking forgiveness. On the first view, it is a description of noble character: whoever says something bad to them that is not mentioned, they meet with good speech that repels it. This is a verse of conciliation, from the early period of Islam, and it was abrogated (naskh, i.e., replaced) by the verse of the sword. Its ruling remains in what falls short of disbelief, to be practised by the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) until the Day of Resurrection. From this is his (ﷺ) saying to Mu'adh: "Follow the bad deed with a good deed and it will erase it, and deal with people with good character." Among good character is repelling what is disliked and harmful, and patience with harshness by turning away from it and speaking gently.

**The fourth issue** concerns God's words ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾. He praised them for spending from their wealth in acts of obedience and in what the Sharia prescribes, and in this there is encouragement to give charity. Spending may also be done with the body, through fasting and prayer. Then He praised them also for turning away from frivolity, as He says: ﴿And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾, that is, when they hear what the polytheists say to them of harm and abuse, they turn away from it, meaning they do not occupy themselves with it. ﴿They say: "To us our deeds, and to you your deeds. Peace be upon you."﴾ That is, a disengagement, like His saying: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾ That is, to us is our religion and to you is your religion.

(﴿Peace be upon you﴾) That is, a safety for you from us, for we do not fight you and we do not revile you, and it has nothing to do with greeting. Al-Zajjaj said: this was before the command to fight.

(﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾) That is, we do not seek them out for dispute, argument and abuse.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The Muslims are unanimous that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib. I say: The correct statement is that most of the exegetes (mufassirun) are unanimous that it was revealed concerning the matter of Abu Talib, the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is the wording of the hadith of al-Bukhari and Muslim. The discussion of this has already preceded in "Bara'ah" [[See vol. 8, p. 272 and what follows, first or second edition.]]. Abu Rawq said: His saying, ﴿but Allah guides whom He wills﴾, is an allusion to al-Abbas. Qatadah also said this.

﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾. Mujahid said: [He knows] those for whom it has been decreed that they will be guided. It was said: The meaning of "whom you love" is whom you wished to be guided. Jubayr ibn Mut'im said: No one heard the revelation being delivered to the Prophet (ﷺ) except Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, for he heard Jibril saying: "O Muhammad, recite: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 57–58:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: If we follow the guidance with you, we shall be snatched away from our land.﴾ This is the saying of the polytheists of Makkah. Ibn 'Abbas said: The one who said this among the Quraysh was al-Harith ibn 'Uthman ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf al-Qurashi. He said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We know that what you say is true, but what prevents us from following the guidance with you and believing in you is our fear that the Arabs will snatch us away from our land" — meaning Makkah — "because they are united against us, and we have no strength against them." This was among their pretexts, so Allah, exalted is He, answered what they had raised as an excuse, saying: ﴿Did We not establish for them a sanctuary secure (haram aminan)?﴾ That is, a place of security. This is because in the Jahiliyyah the Arabs would raid one another and kill one another, while the people of Makkah were secure wherever they were, by the sanctity of the Haram. So He informed them that He had made them secure by the sanctity of the House, and had kept their enemy away from them, so they do not fear that the Arabs will violate the sanctity in fighting them. Al-takhattuf (snatching) means seizing swiftly, and it has already been discussed. Yahya ibn Salam said: It means, "You were secure in My sanctuary, eating My provision, and worshipping other than Me. Will you fear when you worship Me and believe in Me?"

﴿To it are brought the fruits of every thing﴾: that is, to it are gathered the fruits of every land and city, according to Ibn 'Abbas and others. It is said: jaba al-ma' fi al-hawd, meaning he gathered the water into the basin, and al-jabiyah is the great basin. Nafi' read "tujba" with the ta', because of "the fruits" (al-thamarat). And al-Yaqub with the ya', because of His saying "every thing" (kull shay'), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this. He said: Because a barrier came between the feminine noun and its verb; and also, the thamarat is a plural, and is not a true feminine.

﴿A provision from Us﴾: that is, from Our presence.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾: that is, they do not reason; that is, they are heedless of drawing inference, and that He who provided for them and made them secure in the past, while they were in disbelief, will provide for them if they embrace Islam, and will keep the disbelievers away from them in their Islam. "Rizqan" is in the accusative as an object of purpose. It is permissible to make it accusative as a verbal noun in meaning, since the meaning of "tujba" is "turzaq" (is provided). And it has been read "tujbani" with the nun, from al-junan, and its transitivity with ila, as in your saying: yajni ila fihi, and yujna ila al-khafah. [[al-Khafah is the pouch; and from the hadith, "The believer is like the pouch of grain."]]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed which exulted in its livelihood!﴾ He clarifies for one who imagines that if he believed, the Arabs would fight him, that the fear in abandoning belief is greater, for how many a people disbelieved and then destruction befell them. Al-bata (exultation) and al-tughyan (overweening) with regard to blessing, said al-Zajjaj. "Ma'ishataha": that is, in its livelihood. When the "fi" is omitted, the verb becomes transitive, said al-Mazini, like His saying: "And Musa chose from his people seventy men." Al-Farra' said: It is accusative as a specification (tafsir). He said, as you say: abtarta malaka and batirtahu. Its parallel in his view is "except one who makes foolish his own self" (illa man safiha nafsahu), and likewise in his view "if they remit to you willingly a thing of it, a self" (fa-in tibna lakum 'an shay'in minhu nafsan). The accusative of definite nouns as specification is impossible according to the Basrans, because the meaning of specification and distinction is that it be a single indefinite noun denoting a genus. It was also said: it is accusative by "batirat," and the meaning of "batirat" is "jahilat" (was ignorant), so the meaning is: it was ignorant of the gratitude for its livelihood.

﴿So those are their dwellings, not inhabited after them except a little﴾: that is, after the destruction of its people, they were not inhabited except a few of the dwellings, and most of them are ruins. The exception refers to the dwellings, that is, some of them are inhabited, said al-Zajjaj. This was objected to: it was said, if the exception referred to the dwellings he would have said "illa qalil," because you say: "The people did not strike except a little," raising it if the one struck was little; and if you put it in the accusative, "little" is an attribute of the striking, that is, "they did not strike except a little striking." So the meaning then is: "Those are their dwellings, which were not inhabited except by travellers and passers along the road for a day or part of a day," that is, they were not inhabited after them except for a little habitation. And Ibn 'Abbas likewise said: None inhabited them except the traveller or the passer on the road for a day or an hour.

﴿And We were the inheritors﴾: that is, of what they left behind after their destruction.
