Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 59–61:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities﴾, i.e., the disbelieving cities.

(Until He sends in their mother [the main city] a messenger) It is read with a damma and with a kasra on the hamza, following the genitive (ittiba' al-jarr). It means Makkah. And "a messenger" means Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It was also said: "in their mother" means in their greatest one, "a messenger" who warns them. Al-Hasan said: "in its first ones." I say: Makkah is the greatest of the cities because of its sanctity and because it is the first of them, in accordance with His saying, may He be exalted: "Indeed, the first House established for mankind" [Qur'an 3:96]. It was singled out as the greatest for the sending of the Messenger within it, because messengers are sent to the notables, and they live in the cities, and the city is the "mother" of what surrounds it. This meaning has already passed at the end of surah Yusuf [see vol. 9, p. 274, first or second edition].

(Reciting to them Our verses) "Reciting" is in the position of a qualifier, i.e., reciting, that is, informing them that the punishment will descend upon them if they do not believe.

(And We would never destroy the cities) The nun is dropped because of the annexation, like "dhalimi anfusihim" [Qur'an 2:... as a construct]. (Unless its people were wrongdoers) That is, We did not destroy them except when they had deserved destruction, due to their persistence in disbelief after the proof was established against them. In this is a clarification of His justice and His sanctity above injustice. He, may He be exalted, informs that He does not destroy them except when they deserve destruction through their wrongdoing, and He does not destroy them while they are wrongdoers except after the confirmation of the proof and the obligation through the sending of messengers, and He does not make His knowledge of their conditions a proof against them. He declares Himself far above destroying them while they are not wrongdoers, as the Mighty One who speaks said: "And your Lord would never destroy the cities unjustly while their people are reformers" [Qur'an 11:117]. In His saying "unjustly" He explicitly states that if He were to destroy them while they were reformers, that would be an injustice from Him toward them, and that His state in His self-sufficiency and wisdom is incompatible with injustice. He indicated this by the negative particle together with its lam, as He, may He be exalted, said: "And Allah would never waste your faith" [Qur'an 2:143].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whatever you have been given of things﴾, O people of Makkah, (then it is the enjoyment of the worldly life and its adornment) That is, you enjoy it for the duration of your life, or for a period within your life; then either you will depart from it, or it will depart from you.

(And what is with Allah is better and more lasting) That is, more excellent and more enduring, meaning the Hereafter, which is Paradise.

(Then will you not reason?) That what remains is better than what perishes. Abu 'Amr read "ya'qilun" with the yaa'. The rest read with the taa' as direct address, and this is the preferred reading because of His saying: "And whatever you have been given."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is one to whom We have promised a good promise and who will meet it﴾, meaning Paradise and the reward therein, (like one We have given enjoyment of the worldly life) so he is given some of what he wished.

(Then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forth) That is, into the Fire. Its parallel is His saying: "And if not for the grace of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth" [Qur'an 37:57]. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib and Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Jahl. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it was revealed concerning Hamzah and 'Ali, and Abu Jahl and 'Umarah ibn al-Walid. It was also said: concerning 'Ammar and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, as al-Suddi said. Al-Qushayri said: the correct view is that it was revealed concerning the believer and the disbeliever in general terms. Al-Tha'labi said: in sum, it was revealed concerning every disbeliever who was given enjoyment in the world with health and wealth while in the Hereafter he has the Fire, and concerning every believer who endured the trials of the world, trusting in the promise of Allah, and in the Hereafter he has Paradise.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And on the day He calls them﴾, meaning: Allah calls out on the Day of Resurrection to these polytheists, ﴿and says, "Where are My partners,"﴾ according to your claim that they would help you and intercede for you.

(﴿Those against whom the Word has been justified will say﴾), meaning: the word of punishment has been justified against them, and they are the leaders. This is what al-Kalbi said. Qatadah said: they are the devils.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 28, verses 68–70**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses﴾. This is connected to the mention of the associates: "Worship them" and "choose them as intercessors." That is, the choosing rests with Allah, the Exalted, regarding the intercessors, not with the polytheists.

It was also said that this is an answer to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, when he said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?﴾ He meant himself, supposing so, and 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if.

It was also said that this is an answer to the Jews when they said: "If the messenger to Muhammad were other than Gabriel, we would believe in him."

Ibn 'Abbas said: The meaning is: Your Lord creates from His creation whatever He wills, and chooses from among them whomever He wills for His obedience.

Yahya ibn Salam said: The meaning is: Your Lord creates from His creation whatever He wills, and chooses whomever He wills for His prophethood.

Al-Naqqash related that the meaning is: Your Lord creates from His creation whatever He wills, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), and chooses the Ansar for His religion.

I say: In the *Musnad* of al-Bazzar there is a hadith, raised to the Prophet and authentic, from Jabir: "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, chose my companions over the worlds, apart from the prophets and messengers. And He chose for me from among my companions four, namely Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, and made them my companions. In all my companions there is good. And He chose my community over the rest of the nations, and chose for me from my community four generations."

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna related from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, from his father, concerning His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses﴾. He said: From the cattle, the sheep; and from the birds, the pigeon. The complete pause (*waqf al-tamam*, the pause where the sentence is complete) is at "and chooses."

'Ali ibn Sulayman said: This is a complete pause, and it is not permissible for "ma" to be in the accusative position governed by "chooses," because if it were in the accusative position, a pronoun would have to return to it, and there is none.

He said: In this there is a refutation of the Qadariyya (*al-Qadariyya*, the early school denying divine predestination in human acts).

Al-Nahhas said: The complete pause is at "and chooses," meaning: and chooses the messengers.

﴿They have no choice﴾, meaning: those whom they choose do not send anyone.

Abu Ishaq said: "And chooses" is the complete pause for "the chosen," and it is permissible for "ma" to be in the accusative position governed by "chooses," and the meaning would be: and chooses that in which they have a choice.

Al-Qushayri said: The correct view is the first, because they agree on pausing at His saying "and chooses."

Al-Mahdawi said: It is more fitting with the doctrine of the *Ahl al-Sunnah* (the people of the Sunnah, the mainstream Sunni tradition). The "ma" in His saying "they have no choice" is a general negation of all things in which the servant might have any share, apart from his acquisition (*iktisab*) by the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "They have no choice" is an explanation of His saying "and chooses," because its meaning is: He chooses what He wills. For this reason the conjunction is not used. The meaning is: indeed the choice belongs to Allah, the Exalted, in His acts, and He knows best the wisdom in them. That is, none of His creation has the right to choose over Him.

Al-Zajjaj and others permitted that "ma" be in the accusative governed by "chooses."

Al-Tabari denied that "ma" is a negation, lest the meaning be that they had no choice in the past while it is theirs in the future, and because no statement of negation had preceded it.

Al-Mahdawi said: This does not necessarily follow, because "ma" negates the present and the future just as "laysa" (is not) does, and for this reason it acts as it does. Also, the verses used to descend upon the Prophet (ﷺ) according to what was asked about and according to what they were insisting upon in their deeds, even if that is not stated in the text.

According to al-Tabari, the sense of the verse is: and He chooses, for His guardianship, the best of His creation. This is because the polytheists used to choose the best of their wealth and make it for their gods. So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses﴾, for guidance, from His creation, whoever has had happiness preceded for him in His knowledge, just as the polytheists chose the best of their wealth for their gods. On this view, "ma" refers to those who have reason, and it means "the one who." "The choice" is the subject of the inchoative, "for them" is the predicate, and the clause is the predicate of "kana" (was). He compared it to your saying: "Zayd, his father is departing," and this is weak, since there is no pronoun in the sentence returning to the subject of "kana" except by assuming an ellipsis, which is permissible but distant.

The meaning of what al-Tabari said has been related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Tha'labi said: "Ma" is a negation, meaning: they do not have the choice over Allah. This is more correct, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair﴾.

Mahmud al-Warraq said:

*Put your trust in the Merciful in every need you desire, for Allah decrees and determines.*

*When the Lord of the Throne wills a matter for His servant, it befalls him, and the servant has no choosing of his own.*

*A man may perish from the very thing he fears, and by the praise of Allah he is saved from where he does not fear.*

[Note in the edition: In some copies of the original: "and the servant has no choosing." The correction is from the Khayriyya copy.] [Note: Perhaps the correct line is: "and saved from what he does not fear." This is what the meaning of reliance (*tawakkul*) indicates.]

Another poet said:

*The servant is full of impatience, and the Lord is full of decree, and fortune has its turns, and provision is apportioned.*

*The good in full is what our Creator chooses, and in choosing otherwise is blame and misfortune.*

Some scholars said: It is not fitting for anyone to set out upon a matter of the affairs of this world until he asks Allah for the good choice in it, by praying two rak'ahs, the prayer of *istikhara* (the prayer of seeking guidance). In the first rak'ah, after the Fatiha, he recites "Say: O disbelievers" (Surah al-Kafirun), and in the second rak'ah "Say: He is Allah, One" (Surah al-Ikhlas).

Some shaykhs preferred that he recite in the first rak'ah "Your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses, they have no choice" (up to the end of the verse), and in the second rak'ah "It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair." All of this is good.

Then he supplicates after the salam with this supplication, which al-Bukhari related in his *Sahih* from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to teach us the *istikhara* in all matters, just as he taught us a surah of the Qur'an. He said: "When one of you is concerned about a matter, let him pray two rak'ahs other than the obligatory prayer, then let him say: O Allah, I seek Your choice by Your knowledge, and I seek power from You by Your power, and I ask You of Your great bounty. For You have power and I have no power, You know and I do not know, and You are the Knower of the unseen. O Allah, if You know that this matter is good for me in my religion, my livelihood and the outcome of my affair (or he said: in the immediate and the distant of my affair), then decree it for me, make it easy for me, then bless it for me. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 28, verses 68–70**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses﴾. This is connected to the mention of the associates: "Worship them" and "choose them as intercessors." That is, the choosing rests with Allah, the Exalted, regarding the intercessors, not with the polytheists.

It was also said that this is an answer to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, when he said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two cities?﴾ He meant himself, supposing so, and 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi from al-Ta'if.

It was also said that this is an answer to the Jews when they said: "If the messenger to Muhammad were other than Gabriel, we would believe in him."

Ibn 'Abbas said: The meaning is: Your Lord creates from His creation whatever He wills, and chooses from among them whomever He wills for His obedience.

Yahya ibn Salam said: The meaning is: Your Lord creates from His creation whatever He wills, and chooses whomever He wills for His prophethood.

Al-Naqqash related that the meaning is: Your Lord creates from His creation whatever He wills, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), and chooses the Ansar for His religion.

I say: In the *Musnad* of al-Bazzar there is a hadith, raised to the Prophet and authentic, from Jabir: "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, chose my companions over the worlds, apart from the prophets and messengers. And He chose for me from among my companions four, namely Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, and made them my companions. In all my companions there is good. And He chose my community over the rest of the nations, and chose for me from my community four generations."

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna related from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, from his father, concerning His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses﴾. He said: From the cattle, the sheep; and from the birds, the pigeon. The complete pause (*waqf al-tamam*, the pause where the sentence is complete) is at "and chooses."

'Ali ibn Sulayman said: This is a complete pause, and it is not permissible for "ma" to be in the accusative position governed by "chooses," because if it were in the accusative position, a pronoun would have to return to it, and there is none.

He said: In this there is a refutation of the Qadariyya (*al-Qadariyya*, the early school denying divine predestination in human acts).

Al-Nahhas said: The complete pause is at "and chooses," meaning: and chooses the messengers.

﴿They have no choice﴾, meaning: those whom they choose do not send anyone.

Abu Ishaq said: "And chooses" is the complete pause for "the chosen," and it is permissible for "ma" to be in the accusative position governed by "chooses," and the meaning would be: and chooses that in which they have a choice.

Al-Qushayri said: The correct view is the first, because they agree on pausing at His saying "and chooses."

Al-Mahdawi said: It is more fitting with the doctrine of the *Ahl al-Sunnah* (the people of the Sunnah, the mainstream Sunni tradition). The "ma" in His saying "they have no choice" is a general negation of all things in which the servant might have any share, apart from his acquisition (*iktisab*) by the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "They have no choice" is an explanation of His saying "and chooses," because its meaning is: He chooses what He wills. For this reason the conjunction is not used. The meaning is: indeed the choice belongs to Allah, the Exalted, in His acts, and He knows best the wisdom in them. That is, none of His creation has the right to choose over Him.

Al-Zajjaj and others permitted that "ma" be in the accusative governed by "chooses."

Al-Tabari denied that "ma" is a negation, lest the meaning be that they had no choice in the past while it is theirs in the future, and because no statement of negation had preceded it.

Al-Mahdawi said: This does not necessarily follow, because "ma" negates the present and the future just as "laysa" (is not) does, and for this reason it acts as it does. Also, the verses used to descend upon the Prophet (ﷺ) according to what was asked about and according to what they were insisting upon in their deeds, even if that is not stated in the text.

According to al-Tabari, the sense of the verse is: and He chooses, for His guardianship, the best of His creation. This is because the polytheists used to choose the best of their wealth and make it for their gods. So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿Your Lord creates whatever He wills and chooses﴾, for guidance, from His creation, whoever has had happiness preceded for him in His knowledge, just as the polytheists chose the best of their wealth for their gods. On this view, "ma" refers to those who have reason, and it means "the one who." "The choice" is the subject of the inchoative, "for them" is the predicate, and the clause is the predicate of "kana" (was). He compared it to your saying: "Zayd, his father is departing," and this is weak, since there is no pronoun in the sentence returning to the subject of "kana" except by assuming an ellipsis, which is permissible but distant.

The meaning of what al-Tabari said has been related from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Tha'labi said: "Ma" is a negation, meaning: they do not have the choice over Allah. This is more correct, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair﴾.

Mahmud al-Warraq said:

*Put your trust in the Merciful in every need you desire, for Allah decrees and determines.*

*When the Lord of the Throne wills a matter for His servant, it befalls him, and the servant has no choosing of his own.*

*A man may perish from the very thing he fears, and by the praise of Allah he is saved from where he does not fear.*

[Note in the edition: In some copies of the original: "and the servant has no choosing." The correction is from the Khayriyya copy.] [Note: Perhaps the correct line is: "and saved from what he does not fear." This is what the meaning of reliance (*tawakkul*) indicates.]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 74–75:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the Day He calls them, He will say, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ He repeated this pronoun because the two states differ. They are called once and it is said to them, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?" and they call upon the idols, but they do not respond, and their bewilderment becomes evident [in another copy: their grief becomes evident]. Then they are called a second time and they remain silent. This is a rebuke and an increase in disgrace. The calling here is not from Allah, because Allah the Exalted does not speak to the disbelievers, according to His words: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Rather, He commands whoever rebukes and confounds them, and establishes the proof against them at the place of reckoning. It was also said: it is possible that it is from Allah, and His words ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾ refer to the time when it is said to them: ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾. And He said "My partners" because they had assigned to them a share of their wealth.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We will draw out from every nation a witness﴾, that is, a prophet, according to Mujahid. It was also said: they are the just witnesses of the Hereafter who testify against the servants concerning their deeds in this world. The first view is more apparent, due to His words: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and We bring you as a witness against these?﴾ The witness of every nation is its messenger who testifies against it. And "shahid" also means present, that is, We bring forth their messenger who was sent to them.

(﴿Then We will say, "Produce your proof."﴾) That is, your argument.

(﴿Then they will know that the truth belongs to Allah﴾) That is, they will know the truthfulness of what the prophets brought.

(﴿And what they used to fabricate will vanish from them﴾) That is, it will go away from them and become void.

(﴿What they used to fabricate﴾) That is, what they used to invent of falsehood against Allah the Exalted, that He has associates who are worshipped.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 74–75:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the Day He calls them, He will say, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ He repeated this pronoun because the two states differ. They are called once and it is said to them, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?" and they call upon the idols, but they do not respond, and their bewilderment becomes evident [in another copy: their grief becomes evident]. Then they are called a second time and they remain silent. This is a rebuke and an increase in disgrace. The calling here is not from Allah, because Allah the Exalted does not speak to the disbelievers, according to His words: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Rather, He commands whoever rebukes and confounds them, and establishes the proof against them at the place of reckoning. It was also said: it is possible that it is from Allah, and His words ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾ refer to the time when it is said to them: ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾. And He said "My partners" because they had assigned to them a share of their wealth.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We will draw out from every nation a witness﴾, that is, a prophet, according to Mujahid. It was also said: they are the just witnesses of the Hereafter who testify against the servants concerning their deeds in this world. The first view is more apparent, due to His words: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and We bring you as a witness against these?﴾ The witness of every nation is its messenger who testifies against it. And "shahid" also means present, that is, We bring forth their messenger who was sent to them.

(﴿Then We will say, "Produce your proof."﴾) That is, your argument.

(﴿Then they will know that the truth belongs to Allah﴾) That is, they will know the truthfulness of what the prophets brought.

(﴿And what they used to fabricate will vanish from them﴾) That is, it will go away from them and become void.

(﴿What they used to fabricate﴾) That is, what they used to invent of falsehood against Allah the Exalted, that He has associates who are worshipped.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 28, verses 76–77 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Musa﴾. When He said, exalted is He, "What you have been given is but the enjoyment of this worldly life and its adornment," He made clear that Qarun was given it, was deceived by it, and it did not protect him from the punishment of Allah, just as it did not protect Pharaoh. You, O polytheists, are not greater in number or wealth than Qarun and Pharaoh. Pharaoh's soldiers and his wealth did not benefit him, and Qarun's kinship to Musa did not benefit him, nor did his treasures. Al-Nakha'i, Qatadah and others said: he was the paternal cousin of Musa, and he was "Lahhan" (the skilful reciter). He was Qarun ibn Yasbar ibn Qahith ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub, and Musa was the son of Imran ibn Qahith. Ibn Ishaq said: he was the paternal uncle of Musa, the full brother of his father and mother. It was also said: he was the son of Musa's maternal aunt. His name is not declined because of foreignness (ajamiyyah) and definiteness (ta'rif). Whatever is on the pattern of fa'ul and is non-Arabic, and does not accept the definite article "al-", is not declined when definite, but is declined when indefinite. If it accepts the definite article "al-", it is declined if it is the name of a male, such as Tawus and Raqud. Al-Zajjaj said: if Qarun were derived from qarantu al-shay' (I joined the thing), it would be declined.

(Fa-baghā 'alayhim) His transgression (baghy) was that he lengthened the hem of his garment by a span. This was said by Shahr ibn Hawshab. In a hadith: "Allah will not look at the one who drags his garment out of arrogance." It was also said: his transgression was his disbelief in Allah, mighty and majestic. This was said by al-Dahhak. It was said: his transgression was his belittling of them by reason of his abundance of wealth and children. This was said by Qatadah. It was said: his transgression was his attribution of what Allah had given him of treasures to himself, by his own knowledge and cunning. This was said by Ibn Bahr. It was said: his transgression was his saying, "If prophethood is for Musa and the altar and the offering are for Harun, then what is for me?" It is narrated that when Musa brought them across the sea, and prophethood went to Musa while the priesthood went to Harun, who would offer the offering and be the head among them, and the offering was assigned to Musa, Musa handed it over to his brother. Qarun felt resentment in himself and envied them both. He said to Musa: "The command belongs to you two, and there is nothing for me. How long must I endure?" Musa said: "This is the doing of Allah." He said: "By Allah, I will not believe you until you bring a sign." So Musa ordered the leaders of the Children of Israel that each of them should bring his staff. He bound them together and placed them in the tent in which revelation used to descend upon him. They used to guard their staffs at night. In the morning, behold, the staff of Harun was moving, and it had green leaves, and it was of almond wood. Qarun said: "This is no more wondrous than the sorcery you practise." (Fa-baghā 'alayhim) means from al-baghy, which is injustice. Yahya ibn Salam and Ibn al-Musayyib said: Qarun was a wealthy man who worked for Pharaoh over the Children of Israel, so he transgressed against them and oppressed them, and he was one of them. A seventh saying: it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: when Allah ordered the stoning of the adulterer, Qarun set out to a prostitute, gave her money, and persuaded her to claim against Musa that he had committed adulty with her and that he had made her pregnant. This weighed heavily on Musa, and he made her swear by Allah, who split the sea for the Children of Israel and sent down the Torah to Musa, that she should speak the truth. Allah then gave her understanding, and she said: "I bear witness that you are innocent, and that Qarun gave me money and persuaded me to say what I said. You are the truthful one and Qarun is the liar." Allah then placed Qarun's affair in Musa's hands and commanded the earth to obey him. He came to Qarun, who was saying to the earth: "O earth, take him!" It was taking him bit by bit while he cried out: "O Musa!" until he sank into the earth, he and his house and his companions who followed his way. It is narrated that Allah, exalted is He, revealed to Musa: "My servants have cried out to you and you did not have mercy on them. Indeed, had they called upon Me, they would have found Me near and responsive." Ibn Jurayj said: we have been told that they are swallowed up every day to the depth of a man's height, and they will not reach the bottom of the earth until the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned in the Kitab al-Faraj: Ibrahim ibn Rashid narrated to me, saying: Dawud ibn Mihran narrated to me, from al-Walid ibn Muslim, from Marwan ibn Janah, from Yunus ibn Maysarah ibn Halbas, who said: Qarun met Yunus in the darkness of the sea. Qarun called out to Yunus, saying: "O Yunus, repent to Allah, for you will find Him at the first step you take towards Him." Yunus said: "What has prevented you from repenting?" He said: "My repentance was placed in the hands of my cousin, and he refused to accept it from me." In a report: when Qarun reaches the bottom of the seventh earth, Israfil will blow into the Trumpet. And Allah knows best. Al-Suddi said: the name of the prostitute was Sabarta, and Qarun offered her two thousand dirhams. Qatadah said: he had crossed the sea with Musa, and he was called "al-Munawwar" (the Illuminated) because of his beautiful appearance in the Torah, but the enemy of Allah was a hypocrite, just as al-Samiri was a hypocrite.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him of the treasures﴾. Ata' said: he came into possession of much of the treasures of Yusuf, peace be upon him. Al-Walid ibn Marwan said: he used to practise alchemy (al-kimiya').

(Ma inna mafatihahu) "Inna" with its noun and predicate forms the relative clause (sila) of "ma", and "ma" is the object of "atayna-hu". Al-Nahhas said: I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman say: how ugly is what the Kufans say about relative clauses. It is not permissible for the relative clause of alladhi and its sisters to be "inna" and what it governs, and the Qur'an has "ma inna mafatihahu". Mafatih is the plural of mifta', with a kasra, which is that by which something is opened. Whoever says miftah has the plural mafatih. Whoever says that they are the treasuries, its singular is mafttah with a fatha.

(La tanu'u bil-'usbah) The best that has been said about it is that the meaning is latunii' al-'usbah, that is, it bends them by its weight. When the ta' took a fatha, the ba' entered, as they said: "He takes away with the misery" (yadhhabu bil-bu's), and "the one who takes away the misery" (madhhab al-bu's). So it became "latanu'u bil-'usbah", and so the 'usbah bends, that is, rises up heavily, like your saying: "Stand with us," meaning "make us stand". One says: nā'a yanū'u nawān, when he rises with a burden. The poet said [[This is Dhu al-Rummah. He means that her buttocks bend her towards the ground because of their bulk and the abundance of flesh on her hips.]]:
"Her hindquarters bow her down, so her rising is with difficulty, and she walks slowly, and soon she is breathless."
Another said:
"I was seized and could not control myself, and I was bent and did not rise, as if I were shackled by the length of time."
And anā'anī means: it made me heavy, according to Abu Zayd. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the saying "latanu'u bil-'usbah" is inverted, and the meaning is "latanu'u bihā al-'usbah", that is, the group rises with it. Abu Zayd: nuwtu bil-himl means I rose up with the load. The poet said:
"We found a successor, an evil successor, a slave who, when he rises with the load, stands still."
The first meaning is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih and al-Suddi. It is also the view of al-Farra', and al-Nahhas preferred it. Just as one says: dhahabtu bihi and adhhabtuhu (I took him away), ji'tu bihi and aji'tuhu (I brought him), and nuwtu bihi and anha'tuhu (I made him rise). As for their saying: "lahu 'indi ma sā'ahu wa nā'ahu" (I have for him what displeases him and what burdens him), it is an echoing pair (itba'), and it should have been said "wa anā'ahu", like "hanna'anī al-ta'ām wa marra'anī" (it made me enjoy the food and made me digest it), and "akhdhuhu ma qadama wa ma hadatha" (taking from him what is old and what is new). It was also said that it is derived from al-nā'y, which is distance. From it is the poet's saying:
"They keep away from us, yet their affection does not keep away; the heart is held captive by them wherever they are."
Budayl ibn Maysarah recited "la-yanu'u" with the ya', meaning: the one of them, or the one mentioned, bends, so it was understood according to the meaning. Abu 'Ubaydah said: I said to Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj about his saying:
"In it are lines of black and white, as if on the skin there is the pattern of white leprosy."
If you meant the lines, say "ka'annahā"; if you meant the black and the white, say "ka'annahumā". He said: I meant all of that. There is disagreement about the 'usbah, which is the group whose members support one another, and it has eleven sayings. The first: three men, said by Ibn 'Abbas. From him also: from three to ten. Mujahid said: the 'usbah here is what lies between twenty and fifteen. From him also: what lies between ten and fifteen. From him also: from ten to five. Al-Tha'labi mentioned the first, al-Qushayri and al-Mawardi the second, and al-Mahdawi the third. Abu Salih, al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: forty men. Al-Suddi: what lies between ten and forty. Qatadah also said this. 'Ikrimah said: some say forty, and some say seventy. This is the view of Abu Salih, that the 'usbah is seventy men, mentioned by al-Mawardi, and al-Tha'labi mentioned the first from him. It was said: sixty men. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: six or seven. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: what lies between three and nine, which is a group (nafar). Al-Kalbi said: ten, based on the saying of the brothers of Yusuf, "and we are a group (usbah)". Muqatil also said this. Khaythamah said: I found in the Gospel that the keys of the treasuries of Qarun were a load of sixty mules, white-faced and with white markings, and that they would bend under them because of their weight. No single key exceeded a finger in size. For each key there was a treasure of wealth, which, if it were divided among the people of Basra, would have sufficed them. Mujahid said: the keys were made of camel hide. It was also said: of cow hide, so that they would be light for him. They were carried with him when he rode on seventy mules, as al-Qushayri mentioned. It was also said: on forty mules, and this is the view of al-Dahhak. From him also: the keys are their containers. Abu Salih said likewise: the meaning of the keys is the treasuries. And Allah knows best.

(Idh qala lahu qawmuhu) That is, the believers among the Children of Israel, said by al-Suddi. Yahya ibn Salam said: "the people" here means Musa. This was said by al-Farra'. It is a plural used to mean a singular, like His saying: "those to whom the people said" (alladhina qala lahumu al-nas), when it was in fact Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, as has passed.

(La tafrah) That is, do not exult and do not be insolent.

(Inna Allaha la yuhibbu al-farihin) That is, the insolent (al-bataranin). This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. The poet said:
"I am not one who rejoices when fortune delights me, nor one who laments when its changing turns against me."
Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: do not rejoice in wealth, for one who rejoices in wealth does not give its due. Mubashshir ibn 'Abd Allah said: "la tafrah" means "la tufsid" (do not corrupt). The poet said [[Abu 'Ubaydah recited it for Bi'as al-'Udhri.]]:
"When you do not cease to discharge a trust, and you carry another, the deposits have corrupted you (afrahatka al-wada'i)."
That is, they have corrupted you. Abu 'Amr said: afrahahu al-dayn means the debt weighed him down. And he recited: "idha anta..." (the verse). And afrahahu also means it gladdened him, so it is a homonym. Al-Zajjaj said: al-farihin and al-farihin are the same. Al-Farra' distinguished between them, saying: al-farihin means those who are in a state of joy, and al-farihin means those who will rejoice in the future. He claimed that similar to this are tama' (greedy) and tami' (greedy), and mayyit (dead) and ma'it (dead). What the verse of Allah, mighty and majestic, says contradicts what he said: "Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die" (innaka mayyitun wa innahum mayyitun), and He did not say ma'itun. Mujahid also said: the meaning of "la tafrah" is "la tabgh" (do not transgress), and "Indeed Allah does not love the rejoicing ones" means the transgressors. Ibn Bahr said: "la tabkhal" (do not be stingy), for Allah does not love the stingy.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And seek, in what Allah has given you, the Final Abode﴾. That is, seek in what Allah has given you of this world the Final Abode, which is Paradise, for it is the right of the believer to spend the world on what benefits him in the Hereafter, not on arrogance and transgression.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 76–77 (part 2 of 2):

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not forget your share of the world﴾, there is difference of opinion. Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: Do not waste your life by not doing righteous deeds in your worldly life, since the Hereafter is only attained through deeds; so a person's share is his lifespan and his righteous deed within it. The discourse on this interpretation is one of severe admonition. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: its meaning is, do not waste your portion of your worldly life by failing to enjoy the lawful and seek it, and by neglecting the consequences of your worldly life. The discourse on this interpretation contains some gentleness toward him and the rectifying of the matter he desires. This is what must be employed with the one being admonished, lest aversion arise from severity; so said Ibn 'Atiyyah.

I say: Ibn 'Umar combined these two interpretations in his saying: "Work for your world as if you will live forever, and work for your Hereafter as if you will die tomorrow." And from al-Hasan: "Send forward the surplus, and keep back what suffices." Malik said: it is eating and drinking without extravagance. It was also said: he meant by his share the shroud. So this is a continuous admonition, as if they said: Do not forget that you will leave all your wealth except your share, which is this shroud. Similar to this is the saying of the poet:
Your share of all that you gather over the ages
is a cloak in which you are wrapped, and embalming spices.
And another said:
It is contentment; do not seek a substitute for it,
in it is bliss, and in it is rest for the body.
Look at the one who possessed the whole world,
did he depart from it with anything but cotton and a shroud?
Ibn al-'Arabi said: The most marvelous of what is in this, in my view, is the saying of Qatadah: "And do not forget your lawful share, for it is your share of the world," and how excellent this is.

(And do good as Allah has done good to you): i.e., obey Allah and worship Him as He has bestowed favor upon you.
From this is the hadith: "What is excellence (ihsan)?" He said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him." It was also said: it is a command to maintain ties with the needy. Ibn al-'Arabi said: concerning it there are many sayings, the sum of which is using the blessings of Allah in obedience to Allah. Malik said: it is eating and drinking without extravagance. Ibn al-'Arabi said: I think Malik intended to refute those who exceed in worship and asceticism, for the Prophet (ﷺ) loved sweets, drank honey, used roasted meat, and drank cold water. This meaning has already passed in more than one place.

(And seek not corruption in the earth): i.e., do not act in disobedience. (Indeed, Allah does not love the corrupters.)

Budayl ibn Maysarah recited "la-yanu'u" with the ya', meaning: the one of them, or the one mentioned, bends, so it was understood according to the meaning. Abu 'Ubaydah said: I said to Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj about his saying:
"In it are lines of black and white, as if on the skin there is the pattern of white leprosy."
If you meant the lines, say "ka'annahā"; if you meant the black and the white, say "ka'annahumā". He said: I meant all of that. There is disagreement about the 'usbah, which is the group whose members support one another, and it has eleven sayings. The first: three men, said by Ibn 'Abbas. From him also: from three to ten. Mujahid said: the 'usbah here is what lies between twenty and fifteen. From him also: what lies between ten and fifteen. From him also: from ten to five. Al-Tha'labi mentioned the first, al-Qushayri and al-Mawardi the second, and al-Mahdawi the third. Abu Salih, al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: forty men. Al-Suddi: what lies between ten and forty. Qatadah also said this. 'Ikrimah said: some say forty, and some say seventy. This is the view of Abu Salih, that the 'usbah is seventy men, mentioned by al-Mawardi, and al-Tha'labi mentioned the first from him. It was said: sixty men. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: six or seven. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: what lies between three and nine, which is a group (nafar). Al-Kalbi said: ten, based on the saying of the brothers of Yusuf, "and we are a group (usbah)". Muqatil also said this. Khaythamah said: I found in the Gospel that the keys of the treasuries of Qarun were a load of sixty mules, white-faced and with white markings, and that they would bend under them because of their weight. No single key exceeded a finger in size. For each key there was a treasure of wealth, which, if it were divided among the people of Basra, would have sufficed them. Mujahid said: the keys were made of camel hide. It was also said: of cow hide, so that they would be light for him. They were carried with him when he rode on seventy mules, as al-Qushayri mentioned. It was also said: on forty mules, and this is the view of al-Dahhak. From him also: the keys are their containers. Abu Salih said likewise: the meaning of the keys is the treasuries. And Allah knows best.

(Idh qala lahu qawmuhu) That is, the believers among the Children of Israel, said by al-Suddi. Yahya ibn Salam said: "the people" here means Musa. This was said by al-Farra'. It is a plural used to mean a singular, like His saying: "those to whom the people said" (alladhina qala lahumu al-nas), when it was in fact Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, as has passed.

(La tafrah) That is, do not exult and do not be insolent.

(Inna Allaha la yuhibbu al-farihin) That is, the insolent (al-bataranin). This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. The poet said:
"I am not one who rejoices when fortune delights me, nor one who laments when its changing turns against me."
Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: do not rejoice in wealth, for one who rejoices in wealth does not give its due. Mubashshir ibn 'Abd Allah said: "la tafrah" means "la tufsid" (do not corrupt). The poet said [[Abu 'Ubaydah recited it for Bi'as al-'Udhri.]]:
"When you do not cease to discharge a trust, and you carry another, the deposits have corrupted you (afrahatka al-wada'i)."
That is, they have corrupted you. Abu 'Amr said: afrahahu al-dayn means the debt weighed him down. And he recited: "idha anta..." (the verse). And afrahahu also means it gladdened him, so it is a homonym. Al-Zajjaj said: al-farihin and al-farihin are the same. Al-Farra' distinguished between them, saying: al-farihin means those who are in a state of joy, and al-farihin means those who will rejoice in the future. He claimed that similar to this are tama' (greedy) and tami' (greedy), and mayyit (dead) and ma'it (dead). What the verse of Allah, mighty and majestic, says contradicts what he said: "Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die" (innaka mayyitun wa innahum mayyitun), and He did not say ma'itun. Mujahid also said: the meaning of "la tafrah" is "la tabgh" (do not transgress), and "Indeed Allah does not love the rejoicing ones" means the transgressors. Ibn Bahr said: "la tabkhal" (do not be stingy), for Allah does not love the stingy.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And seek, in what Allah has given you, the Final Abode﴾. That is, seek in what Allah has given you of this world the Final Abode, which is Paradise, for it is the right of the believer to spend the world on what benefits him in the Hereafter, not on arrogance and transgression.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 76–77 (part 2 of 2):

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not forget your share of the world﴾, there is difference of opinion. Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: Do not waste your life by not doing righteous deeds in your worldly life, since the Hereafter is only attained through deeds; so a person's share is his lifespan and his righteous deed within it. The discourse on this interpretation is one of severe admonition. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: its meaning is, do not waste your portion of your worldly life by failing to enjoy the lawful and seek it, and by neglecting the consequences of your worldly life. The discourse on this interpretation contains some gentleness toward him and the rectifying of the matter he desires. This is what must be employed with the one being admonished, lest aversion arise from severity; so said Ibn 'Atiyyah.

I say: Ibn 'Umar combined these two interpretations in his saying: "Work for your world as if you will live forever, and work for your Hereafter as if you will die tomorrow." And from al-Hasan: "Send forward the surplus, and keep back what suffices." Malik said: it is eating and drinking without extravagance. It was also said: he meant by his share the shroud. So this is a continuous admonition, as if they said: Do not forget that you will leave all your wealth except your share, which is this shroud. Similar to this is the saying of the poet:
Your share of all that you gather over the ages
is a cloak in which you are wrapped, and embalming spices.
And another said:
It is contentment; do not seek a substitute for it,
in it is bliss, and in it is rest for the body.
Look at the one who possessed the whole world,
did he depart from it with anything but cotton and a shroud?
Ibn al-'Arabi said: The most marvelous of what is in this, in my view, is the saying of Qatadah: "And do not forget your lawful share, for it is your share of the world," and how excellent this is.

(And do good as Allah has done good to you): i.e., obey Allah and worship Him as He has bestowed favor upon you.
From this is the hadith: "What is excellence (ihsan)?" He said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him." It was also said: it is a command to maintain ties with the needy. Ibn al-'Arabi said: concerning it there are many sayings, the sum of which is using the blessings of Allah in obedience to Allah. Malik said: it is eating and drinking without extravagance. Ibn al-'Arabi said: I think Malik intended to refute those who exceed in worship and asceticism, for the Prophet (ﷺ) loved sweets, drank honey, used roasted meat, and drank cold water. This meaning has already passed in more than one place.

(And seek not corruption in the earth): i.e., do not act in disobedience. (Indeed, Allah does not love the corrupters.)

He said, "I have only been given it because of knowledge I possess." That is, the knowledge of the Torah. It was reported that he was among the people who recited it best and knew it best. He was one of the seventy scholars whom Musa (Moses) chose for the appointed time.

Ibn Zayd said: meaning, "I have only been given it because of His knowledge of my merit and His approval of me." So His words "*indi* (with me / in my possession)" mean: "with me is the knowledge that Allah the Exalted gave me these treasures, knowing that I deserved them because of a merit in me."

It was also said: "I was given it on knowledge from me of the ways of trade and gain." This was said by Ali ibn Isa. But he did not realise that if Allah had not made it easy for him to acquire them, they would never have been gathered with him.

Ibn Abbas said: "On knowledge I possess of the craft of gold-making," and he pointed to the knowledge of *al-kimiya'* (alchemy).

al-Naqqash related that Musa, peace be upon him, taught him a third of the craft of alchemy, Yusha' a third, and Harun a third. Qarun deceived the two of them, though he was on their faith, until he learned what they had, practised alchemy, and his wealth increased.

It was also said that Musa taught alchemy to three men: Yusha' ibn Nun, Kalib ibn Yufinna [[In the original sources "Talut", which is a distortion. The correction is from the books of tafsir.]], and Qarun. al-Zajjaj preferred the first opinion and rejected the view of those who said that Qarun practised alchemy. He said: "Because alchemy is false and has no reality."

It was also said that Musa taught alchemy to his sister, who was Qarun's wife, and Musa's sister taught Qarun. And Allah knows best.

His words, ﴿Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations﴾, that is, with punishment.

(*min al-qurun*) "of the generations," that is, the past disbelieving nations.

(*man huwa ashaddu minhu quwwatan wa aktharu jam'an*) "who were stronger than him in might and greater in gathering," that is, of wealth. Had wealth been a sign of superiority, Allah would not have destroyed them. It was also said: "might" means instruments, and "gathering" means helpers and supporters. The speech came as a rebuke from Allah the Exalted to Qarun, meaning: "Did Qarun not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations..."

(*wa la yus'alu 'an dhunubihimu al-mujrimun*) "The guilty will not be asked about their sins," that is, they will not be asked in the manner of seeking to make amends, as He said: "...nor will they be asked to make amends," and "so they are not among those who are made to make amends." Rather, they will be asked in the manner of rebuke and reproach, as He said: "By your Lord, We will surely question them all." This was said by al-Hasan. Mujahid said: the angels will not be asked tomorrow about the guilty, for they are recognised by their marks; they will be gathered with black faces and blue eyes. Qatadah said: the guilty will not be asked about their sins because they are obvious and numerous; rather, they will enter the Fire without reckoning. It was also said: the guilty of this nation will not be asked about the sins of the past nations who were punished in this world. It was also said: Allah destroyed those generations that He destroyed with knowledge of their sins, so He had no need to ask them about their sins.

﴿So he went out before his people in his finery﴾ meaning: before the Children of Israel, in what he regarded as adornment of the goods of the worldly life, such as garments, mounts, and grooming, on a day of festivity. Al-Ghaznawi said: "on a Saturday." "In his finery" means "with his finery." A poet said:

"When the hearts of the people fly away in fear of death, they plant (their) souls alongside (them)" [[In one copy: "they throw (their) souls." In another copy: "they plant the souls with the molars." We have not found it.]]

That is, "with the souls." He went out with seventy thousand of his followers, wearing *al-mu'asfarat* (garments dyed with safflower), and he was the first to have garments dyed in this way. Al-Suddi said: "with a thousand white slave-girls, on white mules, with saddles of gold, over *qutuf al-urjuwan* (saddle-cloths of urjuwan)." Ibn Abbas said: "He went out on grey mules." Mujahid said: "on white palfreys with saddles of urjuwan, and they wore *al-mu'asfarat*, and that was the first day the safflower-dyed garment was seen." Qatadah said: "He went out on four thousand beasts, wearing red garments, among them a thousand white mules with red saddle-cloths." Ibn Jurayj said: "He went out on a grey she-mule covered with urjuwan, and with him three hundred slave-girls on grey mules, wearing red garments." Ibn Zayd said: "He went out with seventy thousand men wearing *al-mu'asfarat*." Al-Kalbi said: "He went out in a green garment which Allah had sent down to Musa from Paradise, but Qarun stole it from him." Jabir ibn Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "His finery was *al-qirmiz*." I say: *al-qirmiz* is a red dye like *al-urjuwan*, and *al-urjuwan* in the language is a red dye. This was mentioned by al-Qushayri.

(Those who desired the life of this world said: "Would that we had the like of what has been given to Qarun. Indeed, he is possessed of a great fortune.") That is, a great share of worldly goods. It was then said: this is the speech of the believers of that time, who wished for the like of his wealth out of desire for this world. It was also said: it is the speech of peoples who did not believe in the Hereafter nor desired it, and they are the disbelievers.

﴿But those who had been given knowledge said﴾ — and they were the rabbis of the Children of Israel — ﴿to those who had wished for his position: "Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better"﴾ meaning Paradise,

(for those who believe and do righteous deeds; and it is not granted except to the patient). That is, righteous deeds are not granted, or Paradise is not granted in the Hereafter, except to those who are patient in obedience to Allah. The pronoun in *yulaqqaha* (its being granted) is permissible because it refers to "the reward of Allah" (*thawab Allah*), which is the subject of what is meant.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verse 81–82:

God's words: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾. Muqatil said: When Musa (Moses) commanded the earth, it swallowed him, and the Children of Israel said: "He only destroyed him so that he could inherit his wealth, for he was the son of his paternal uncle, the brother of his father." So God caused the earth to swallow him, his home, and all his wealth after three days. Then God revealed to Musa: "I will never again return obedience of the earth to anyone after you, ever." It is said: khasafa al-makan yakhsifu khusufan (the place) "went down into the earth," and Allah khasafa bihi al-ardh khasfan, meaning He made him disappear into it. From this is God's words: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home﴾. Khasafa he (himself) into the earth, and khusifa bihi (he was caused to be swallowed). Khusuf al-qamar (the eclipse of the moon) is its kusuf (eclipse). Tha'lab said: "kasafat al-shams wa khasafa al-qamar (the sun was eclipsed and the moon was eclipsed)" — this is the most correct usage. Al-khasf also means decrease, as it is said: "So-and-so accepted al-khasf," meaning accepted the deficiency.

(﴿Then there was not for him any company﴾) meaning a group and a band.

(﴿who could help him against Allah. Nor was he among those who could defend themselves﴾) i.e., those who could protect themselves against what the khasf (swallowing) had befallen him. It is narrated that Qarun was sinking every day by the height of a man, until when he reached the bottom of the lowest earth, Israfil would blow into the Trumpet, as has already been mentioned, and Allah knows best.

God's words: ﴿And those who had longed for his position the day before began to say﴾ meaning they began to regret that wish, and (they said: "Wayka'anna Allah") [wayka'anna: "wai" is a particle of regret]. Al-Nahhas said: The best of what has been said about this is the view of al-Khalil, Sibawayh, Yunus and al-Kisa'i, that the people became alert or were alerted, and so they said "way" (wai), and the Arabs who express regret say "way" in the midst of their regret. Al-Jawhari said: "Wai" is an expression of wonder; it is said "waika" and "wai li-Abdullah." "Wai" may also precede "ka'anna," both the light and the heavy forms, and you say: "Wayka'anna Allah." Al-Khalil said: It is separated, you say "wai," then you begin and say "ka'anna." Al-Tha'labi said: Al-Farra' said it is a particle of affirmation, like your saying: "Do you not see the handiwork and kindness of Allah?" It is mentioned that a Bedouin woman said to her husband: "Where is your son, woe to you?" He said: "Wai, ka'annahu wara' al-bayt" (wai, it is as if he is behind the house), meaning, "Do you not see him?" Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan said: "Waika" is an introductory and affirmative expression, its implied meaning being: "Indeed Allah expands the provision." It was also said: it is an alert, in the position of "alla" in your saying "alla taf'al" (will you not do?) and "amma" in your saying "amma ba'd" (as for what follows). The poet said [it is Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl]:

They asked me for divorce when they saw me, my wealth having become little; you came to me with a disaster.
Wai, ka'anna whoever has wealth is loved, and whoever is poor lives in hardship.

Qutrub said: It is originally "waylaka," the lam was dropped and the kaf of address was attached to "wai." Antarah said:

And indeed it healed my soul and removed its sickness: the saying of the horsemen, "Waika, Antar, advance!"

Al-Nahhas and others rejected this, saying: the meaning is not sound on this basis, because the people did not address anyone so as to say to him "woe to you"; and if it were so, it would have been "innahu" with a kasra. Also, dropping the lam from "wailaka" is not permissible. Some said: the estimate is "wailaka i'lam annahu" (woe to you, know that he...), so "i'lam" (know) is implied. Ibn al-A'rabi: "Wayka'anna Allah" means "i'lam" (know). It was also said: its meaning is "alam tara anna Allah" (do you not see that Allah...). Al-Qutabi said: its meaning is "rahmatun laka" (mercy for you) in the dialect of Himyar. Al-Kisa'i said: "wai" in it carries the sense of wonder; it is also narrated from him that one may pause on "wai" and say it is an expression of grief. Whoever says "waika" and pauses on the kaf, its meaning is: "I marvel that Allah expands provision, and I marvel that the disbelievers do not prosper." The kaf should be a particle of address, not a noun, since "wai" is not something that takes a pronominal suffix. It is written joined because, as its use became frequent, it was treated together with what follows as one word.

(﴿Had it not been that Allah had been gracious to us﴾) with faith and mercy, and had He not protected us from the like of what Qarun had, of rebellion and arrogance, "He would have caused the earth to swallow us." Al-A'mash read: "Lawla mannu Allahi alayna." Hafs read: "Lakhasafa bina" with the active form. The rest read it in the passive form (lam yusamma fa'iluhu, the agent unnamed), and this is the choice of Abu Ubayd. In the reading of Abdullah it is "La nakhsifa bina," as you say "inṭaliq bina" (let us set off). Likewise al-A'mash and Talhah ibn Musarrif read it. Abu Hatim chose the reading of the majority for two reasons: the first is His words: "So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home"; the second is His words: "Had it not been that Allah had been gracious to us," since attributing it to Allah, the Exalted, is more fitting, given the nearness of His name to it.

(﴿And [they said]: "Wayka'annahu, the disbelievers do not prosper"﴾) with Allah.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 28, verses 83–84:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is the Last Abode; We assign it to those who do not seek exaltation on earth, nor corruption.﴾ He means Paradise. He said this to magnify it and to exalt its status, meaning: that is the one you have heard mentioned and whose description has reached you. (*We assign it to those who do not desire exaltation on earth*), that is, elevation and arrogance against faith and the believers. (*Nor corruption*), meaning acting in acts of disobedience. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil. ʿIkrimah and Muslim al-Bitin said it is seizing wealth unjustly. al-Kalbi said it is calling people to other than the worship of God. Yahya ibn Sallam said it is the killing of the prophets and the believers.

(*And the outcome is for the God-conscious*). al-Dahhak said: Paradise. Abu Muʿawiya said: the one who does not desire exaltation is the one who does not grieve over its humiliation and does not compete for its honour. The most exalted of them in the sight of God is the most humble of them, and the most honoured of them on the Day (of Judgement) is the one who most clung to humility in this world.

Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna narrated from Ismaʿil ibn Abi Khalid, who said: ʿAlī ibn al-Husayn passed by some poor people who were eating crusts of bread, while he was riding. He greeted them, and they invited him to their food. He recited this verse, "That is the Last Abode; We assign it to those who do not seek exaltation on earth nor corruption," then he dismounted and ate with them. Then he said: "I have answered your invitation, so answer mine." He took them to his home, fed them, clothed them, and sent them away. This was related by Abu al-Qasim al-Tabarani, Sulayman ibn Ahmad, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna narrated to us, and he mentioned it.

It has also been said: the expression "the Last Abode" includes both reward and punishment. The meaning is that only the God-conscious benefit from that abode, while whoever is not God-conscious, that abode is against him and not for him, because it harms him and does not benefit him.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, he will have better than it﴾ has been discussed in surah al-Naml (*Surat al-Naml*). ʿIkrimah said: nothing is better than *lā ilāha illā Allāh* ("there is no god but God"). The meaning is that whoever comes with *lā ilāha illā Allāh*, he will have better than it (from the Abode).

(*And whoever comes with an evil deed*), that is, with polytheism (*shirk*), (*those who committed evil deeds will not be recompensed except for what they used to do*), meaning: they will be punished in a manner befitting His knowledge.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 28, verses 85–88:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, He who has ordained the Quran for you will surely bring you back to a place of return.﴾ He concluded the surah with good news to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) that he would be returned to Makkah, victorious over his enemies. It was also said that this is good news to him of Paradise, but the first view is more common. This is the statement of Jabir ibn Abdullah, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others. Al-Qutabi said: the ma'ad (place of return) of a man is his homeland, because he sets out and then returns to it. Muqatil said: the Prophet (ﷺ) left the cave at night as a emigrant to Madinah, by a route other than the usual one, fearing pursuit. When he returned to the road and reached al-Juhfah, he recognized the road to Makkah and longed for it. Jibril said to him: "Indeed, Allah says: 'Indeed, He who has ordained the Quran for you will surely bring you back to a place of return,'" meaning: back to Makkah, dominant over it. Ibn Abbas said: this verse was revealed at al-Juhfah, and it is neither Makki nor Madani. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas that "to a place of return" means: to death. Also from Mujahid, Ikrimah, al-Zuhri and al-Hasan: the meaning is "will surely bring you back to the Day of Resurrection," and this is the choice of al-Zajjaj. It is said: "between me and you is the ma'ad," meaning the Day of Resurrection, because people return on that day alive. And "fard" (ordained) means "sent down." Also from Mujahid, Abu Malik and Abu Salih: "to a place of return" means: to Paradise. This is the statement of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and also Ibn Abbas, because he entered it on the night of the Isra'. It was also said: because his father Adam came out of it.

﴿Say: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance and who is in manifest error.﴾ That is, say to the disbelievers of Makkah when they say, "Indeed, you are in manifest error": "My Lord knows best who has come with guidance and who is in manifest error," whether I or you. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you﴾, that is, you did not know that We would send you to the creation and reveal the Quran to you.

﴿except as a mercy from your Lord﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: this is a disjunctive exception, meaning "but."

﴿So never be a supporter of the disbelievers﴾, that is, a helper and an assistant to them. This has already been mentioned in this surah.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And let them not turn you away from the signs of Allah after they have been sent down to you﴾, meaning their statements, their lies and their harm. Do not turn toward them, but proceed with your command and your affair. Ya'qub read "yasuddanka" with the nun marked as jussive. It is also read "yusiddunnaka" from asadda, with the meaning of saddah, which is a dialect of Kalb. The poet said [it is Dhu al-Rummah]:

"People who turned others away from them with the sword,
Turning away like irrigation channels from the noses of the thirsty camels." [Another narration: "from the noses of the hazim (sand-dunes)."]

﴿And call to your Lord﴾, that is, to monotheism. This includes conciliation and reconciliation. All of this was abrogated by the verse of the sword. The reason for this verse is that Quraysh used to call the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to venerate their idols, and at that point Satan cast into his recitation the matter of the cranes, as previously mentioned [see vol. 12, p. 79 ff., first or second edition]. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not invoke with Allah any other god﴾, that is, do not worship anything alongside Him, for there is no god but Him. It is a negation of every object of worship and an affirmation of worship of Him alone.

﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾. Mujahid said: its meaning is "except Him." Al-Sadiq said: "His religion." Abu al-Aliyah and Sufyan said: that is, except what is intended by it His Face, meaning what is sought by it through devotion. He said:

"I seek forgiveness from Allah for a sin I cannot count,
Lord of the servants, to Him is the face and the deed."

Muhammad ibn Yazid said: al-Thawri narrated to me, saying: I asked Abu Ubaydah about the verse "Everything is perishing except His Face," and he said: "except His standing (jah)," just as you say that so-and-so has a face (wajh) among the people, meaning standing (jah).

﴿To Him belongs the judgment﴾ in the first life and the Hereafter, ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "wajhahu" is in the accusative as an exception. If it were outside the Quran, it would be "illa wajhuhu" in the nominative, meaning: everything other than His Face is perishing, as the poet said [it is Amr ibn Kulthum; it is also narrated for Suwar ibn al-Mudarrib; the examples of Sibawayh]:

"Every brother departs from his brother, by the life of your father, except the two Farqads."

The meaning: every brother other than the two Farqads departs from his brother. "And to Him you will be returned" means you will be returned to Him.

The Surah of al-Qasas is complete, and praise be to Allah.
